title: முல்லை payiram-10
theme: The mullai fifty's first decade: after the prefatory verse, the friend and the waiting wife read the rainy season, its cloud, thunder, jasmine and the herdsman's evening flute, as his promised return or as an assault on her alone (1-9); then the husband, returning, hurries his chariot to see her waiting (10).
source_issues: Verse 10: show flags that sangamtamil.com's text lacks line 1 (நூல்நின்ற பாக! தேர் நொவ்விதாச் சென்றீக); our text has all four lines.
Verse 1 line 3 எய்தவன தார் and verse 7 line 3 சிறுகுழல ஓசை look like எய்தவன் தார் and சிறுகுழல் ஓசை with the final consonant misprinted; the sense is unaffected.
Bracketed sandhi letters are printed in the text (மற்(று), கொண்(டு), கூர்ந்த(து), அரும்(பு)); words cited from them omit the brackets.
The colophons give no thurai for any verse of this chapter, so thurai_akam speakers are inferred from the verses and occasion words are null.

reading: The prefatory verse says that Maran Poraiyan of generous fame bound together the Ainthinai Aimpathu so that great men of good character might see its worth, and that those who do not recite it with eagerness have not attained pure Tamil.
nuance: It praises a book, not a king, and makes the fifty poems a test of belonging to செந்தமிழ்: the five landscapes are offered as the curriculum of correct Tamil, not only as love poetry.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the poet and his book, the nearest puram class to a eulogy

reading: Good lady, the friend says, see: the rain cloud has gathered, massed and dark like the colour of Mal who overcame the wrestlers, flashing with lightning that is the spear of Murugan who wears the kadamba, making the konrai bloom as the garland of Shiva who shot the moving forts, and it rises turning to the right.
nuance: Three gods each lend the storm one attribute: Mal, god of the mullai, its colour; Murugan, god of the hills, its lightning; Shiva its konrai. The cloud rising on the right (வலன் ஏரும்) is the auspicious omen, so the friend shows the season as a sacred sign of his return rather than only as weather.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain cloud rising on the right fixes the rainy season

comparisons.tenor: the dark massed rain cloud
the lightning, as Murugan's spear
the konrai blossoms, as Shiva's garland

reading: As the beautiful peacock calls, the roaring sky, which has taken on the nature of rain, thunders and hangs low over the sapphire-dark mountain; every time she sees it, the heroine tells her soft-spoken friend, her shoulders take on the yellow of the peerkku flower.
nuance: The two halves are built on the same phrase: the sky takes on the nature of rain (கார்நீர்மை கொண்ட) and her shoulders take on the nature of the peerkku (பீர்நீர்மை கொண்டன), so the season's fulfilment and her pallor arrive as one event. The speaker could also be the friend observing the heroine's shoulders; the vocative பணிமொழி fits either.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-laden roaring sky and the calling peacock fix the rainy season

comparisons.tenor: her shoulders turned the yellow of the peerkku flower, the pallor of separation

reading: Lightning, thunder and the thunderbolt, such killing weapons this rain has spread wide; she asks her friend, whose teeth outshine jasmine buds, whether there is no such rain in the land where their man has gone.
nuance: The question is an accusation turned inside out: if the rain were in his land too, he would have read it and come, so either it is not there or he has not heeded it. The season meant to be his signal falls on her alone as an attacking army.

thinai_evidence.note: the rainy season's lightning and thunder and the jasmine

comparisons.tenor: lightning, thunder and thunderbolt, as an army's killing weapons
the friend's teeth, which surpass jasmine buds in whiteness

reading: Does our lover not think of how it is with us, she asks her bright-bangled friend: this rain, roaring like the voice of a strapped war-drum and appearing so as to seize the hearts of good women, has grown keen as if to kill the soft-spoken one.
nuance: The war-drum makes the thunder a summons to battle aimed at women (நல்லார் மனங்கவர), and the soft-spoken one it would kill is the speaker herself named in the third person; it may instead be the friend speaking of the heroine.

thinai_evidence.note: the roaring rain cloud fixes the rainy season

comparisons.tenor: the thunder of the rain cloud
the rain grown sharp as a weapon meant to kill

reading: Each time she sees the sky, where dark clouds gather on the high-peaked mountain, spread in rows with their heads tangling, run on mingled with the wind and pour down, her eyes fall too, mingled with drops.
nuance: The verbs carry over: what the clouds do in three lines (கலந்து, வந்து உறைக்கும்) her eyes do in one (துளிகலந்து வீழ்தரும்), so the poem never says 'I weep like the rain' but makes her tears another fall of the same storm.

thinai_evidence.note: the massed rain clouds pouring fix the rainy season

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, which pour drops as the clouds do

reading: The dark bee humming after sipping the fragrant jasmine is sweet to those who have someone to lean on, she tells her good friend, but on us, who live with hearts that have no one, the dark evening comes and saws.
nuance: The same hour is sweet or cruel by company alone (செல்சார்வு உடையார்க்கு), so the evening's cruelty is in her solitude. The bee at the jasmine is a near miss for iraicchi: it acts like a lover, but the poem itself states the contrast, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the jasmine and the darkening evening, mullai's flower and hour

comparisons.tenor: the evening that cuts her as a saw cuts

reading: In the dull evening when the sun has hidden behind the hill and the sky holds its red glow, the sound of the fine little flute the herdsman plays in joy once the cattle have fed, she tells her friend of close-set bangles, is to her like a spear thrown at her.
nuance: The herdsman plays because he is glad (உவந்து ஊதும்) and his flute is called fine (சீர்சால்): the music is not harsh, it wounds because it announces a homecoming that is not hers.

thinai_evidence.note: the red evening and the herdsman's flute, mullai's hour and people

comparisons.tenor: the herdsman's flute, which strikes her like a thrown spear

reading: The valli creeper, dull like the bodies of those who are parted, has grown lovely like the bodies of those united; she asks her well-adorned friend whether, even though the sky now pours, the man who crossed the cruel forest will not come.
nuance: The usual direction of the simile is reversed: human bodies are the vehicle and the plant the tenor. The creeper has passed from the parted state to the united one; she has not, so the plant shows her the change the season promised her.

thinai_evidence.note: the pouring rain that revives the creeper fixes the rainy season

comparisons.tenor: the creeper as it was before the rain, dull
the creeper revived by the rain, lovely

reading: He will come, the friend tells the heroine of shining jewels; she need not melt and waste away with her bright sword-like eyes full of tears: if she will look, the green-stemmed jasmine has put forth opening buds, having heard the secret of the new rain.
nuance: The jasmine is said to have heard the secret (மறை) of the coming rain before anyone saw it, so the friend offers it as inside knowledge of the season. It is a near miss for iraicchi: the flower's answering of the season's message suggests the man will answer too, but it is offered as evidence, not as an act a person of the situation does, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the jasmine in bud is mullai's flower and the sign of its season

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, bright and sharp as a sword

reading: Charioteer skilled by the rule, the returning man says, let the chariot go swiftly; looking at the beauty of the forest where bees hum, let us learn the state of her who stands with the bolt of her practised chastity drawn shut and her hand pressed to her cheek.
nuance: Chastity is a door bar she has let fall, so her waiting is a house closed from within; the hand on the cheek is the posture of that waiting. He wants to see her before she sees him, to know her state as it is.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest road home by chariot, the mullai land of the returning husband

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the charioteer (பாக)

comparisons.tenor: her chastity, as a bolt dropped to shut the house

title: குறிஞ்சி 11-20
theme: Kurinji: the secret love of the millet field on the hill, from the sweet days of guarding and the hunter's pretext (11-15) to the end of the guarding and the dangers of his night path, which the friend turns into a plea for marriage (12, 16-19), and the veri rite the mother holds because no one knows the cause (20).
source_issues: 11-20: the colophons give the thinai (குறிஞ்சி) and the poet but no thurai; every speaker and addressee in thurai_akam is inferred from the verse, with occasion words left null.
11 line 1: சவினிய is not a common word; read as 'made lustrous, in bloom' (from சவி), describing the vengai. Line 4 ஏயினார் is read as those who would order or direct the girls.
12 line 3: பூக்கண் கழூஉம் புறவிற்றாய் is hard to construe; read as 'having a slope where the waterfall washes the flowers'.
14 line 2: வினைவாய்த்து does not construe easily with the rest; taken with his coming.
16 line 1: கோட் பட்டு is unclear (seized, or struck); read as the elephant having been caught by the tiger and escaped hurt.
15: whose eyes and to whom the friend speaks are not stated; the verse is marked uncertain.

reading: The friend reminds the soft-breasted girl that the few days they spent hidden in the millet field, while the lord of the good hill dressed her beauty in the flowering grove of gold-clustered vengai, have gone by, sweet because no one was there to give them orders.
nuance: போயின, 'they have gone', makes the memory a farewell: the secret days lasted only while the girls were sent to the field, and ஏயினார் இன்றி, with none to command, names the freedom that the return home will take away. The colophon gives no thurai; the speaker and addressee are inferred from மென்முலையாய் and the shared 'we'.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai grove and the millet field of the good hill

comparisons.tenor: the yellow flower clusters of the vengai

reading: The friend tells the lord of the great hill that their natural task of guarding the bending millet is over, and points him to their home: this village, where the clean waterfall washes the flowers on the slope and gold is found, is where they live.
nuance: With the guarding over, the field can no longer be the meeting place; telling him where the house is, பாக்கம் இது எம் இடம், moves his courting from the field to the family's door, which is where marriage is asked. பாக்கம் and புறவு are usually words of the shore and the woodland; here they only name a hill village and its slope.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill and its millet field

reading: The friend tells the doe-eyed girl not to be bewildered by the thought that the man of the forest country will not come to embrace her shoulders: when they bathe in the white waterfall that comes down the good hill mingled with musk, her loneliness will not stay.
nuance: The bathing place in the falls is a meeting place, so the comfort is practical: the loneliness will leave because he will be there. The water that comes 'mixed with musk' carries the scent of his hill down to her.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest country and the hill waterfall

comparisons.tenor: the girl's eyes

reading: The friend tells the gold-like girl in her leaf skirt that while they were guarding the millet on the slope the man came, like hunters who come asking after a beast, and that there is something else he has come to ask them.
nuance: The friend names the hunter's question about the animal as a manner of coming (போல), so she has already seen through the pretext: his real question, ஒன்றுண்டு, is left unsaid for the girl to guess. வினைவாய்த்து in line 2 is hard to construe; the reading takes it with his coming.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill slope and its millet field

comparisons.tenor: the girl's colour
the man's approach to the millet field

reading: The friend explains that the red-lined eyes of the gentle-spoken girl have reddened because they plucked fragrant vengai flowers on the hill till their mango-shoot bodies sweated and then bathed again and again in the leaping waterfall.
nuance: The poem speaks of the girl in the third person (பணிமொழிக்கு) and offers a cause for her red eyes, which suggests the friend is answering an elder who has noticed them; the bath in the falls is an innocent explanation for eyes reddened by love or weeping. The addressee is inferred: the colophon gives no thurai.

thinai_evidence.note: vengai flowers and a waterfall on the hill

comparisons.tenor: the girls' bodies

reading: Remembering the path where an elephant with folded ears, having escaped the curve-striped tiger, sits down hurt and shrinks aside in fear at the sound of footsteps, the girl with bright bangles cannot sleep through the thick dark.
nuance: வேங்கை here is the tiger, not the tree. The elephant that has survived the tiger and still flinches at a footfall measures the path the man takes at night; a reader may hear the girl's own fear in it, but the beast only shows the danger, so it is scene, not iraicchi. Telling him she lies awake is a way of asking him to stop the night visits and marry.

thinai_evidence.note: tiger and elephant on the night path of the hill

reading: The friend tells the lord of the rich hill with cloud-climbed groves that, thinking he will come without fail and afraid for him, the girl with the honeyed garland loses her bloom and soft grace and her body shrinks as she stands melting within.
nuance: The wasting here comes not from his absence but from his coming: எஞ்சாது நீ வருதி, you come without fail, is what she fears. His faithfulness to the night meetings is itself the harm, so only marriage would end it.

thinai_evidence.note: cloud-wrapped groves of the rich hill

reading: The friend tells the lord of the great hill with roaring falls that now not even the parrot flocks come, even by mistake, to the moist-eared millet that their kin cleared and ploughed, and asks him not to forget, but to keep in his heart, his bond with the gentle-spoken girl.
nuance: மறந்தும், 'even by forgetting', and நீ மறவல், 'do not forget', answer each other across the poem. With no parrots to chase, the girls will not be sent to the field, so the meetings there end; the friend asks that the bond outlast the field.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill millet field and its parrots

iraicchi.act: the parrot flocks stop coming to the field once there is nothing in it for them
iraicchi.sense: the man, whose meetings in the field are ending too, must not stop coming and forget her as the parrots forget the field

reading: The friend tells the lord of the tall hill that when he comes at midnight along the cruel path, with only his long spear for company, swimming across the fierce white waterfall, her heart asks what will become of the girl with the cool garland.
nuance: The friend does not say she fears for him: her heart asks what will become of the girl if harm meets him. His danger is counted as the girl's, which is the friend's way of pressing for marriage without naming it.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill waterfall crossed at midnight

reading: The girl says the man of the fragrant hill has taken her body's true nature, but the velan, not knowing this, declares that a spirit has seized her, drags a kid and scatters its blood, and her mother, having brought him, whirls distraught in the veri rite.
nuance: அறியான் is masculine: the one who does not know is the velan, whose whole office is to know the cause. அணங்கு அணங்கிற்று, 'a spirit has seized her', is true in a way he cannot see: the afflicting beauty is the hill man's. Spoken to the friend, the complaint is meant to reach the man and hurry the marriage, though the colophon gives no thurai to say he overhears.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill man and the velan's veri rite

title: மருதம் 21-30
theme: Marutham: the wife turns away the bard who pleads for her straying husband (21-23), then tells her friend of her anger, her faded beauty, the son his father passed by on the way to a new wedding, and the union she still finds sweet (24-30).
source_issues: 24 line 1: சறுகுருகின் reads as a misprint for சிறுகுருகின், the little heron.
27 line 2: நுண்ணுறல் is not a clear word; the hair thinned 'like fine ...' is uncertain, and the verse is marked uncertain. Line 1 தணவயல் is probably தண்வயல், cool fields.
21 line 1: கொண்டுழிப் பண்டம் விலையொரீஇ is hard to construe (taking goods in exchange instead of a price?); the needle-sellers' simile is clear but this clause is not.
All ten verses: the core record has no thurai, so speaker and addressee are inferred from the vocatives (பாண, பெய்வளைக் கையாய், வாட்கண்ணாய், புனையிழையாய், ஒளியிழாய்) and occasion words are null.

reading: The wife tells the bard that in pressing her to trust the word of the man of the wide town he is no different from those who hawk fine-eyed needles in the smiths' own street, taking any goods offered for them.
nuance: The smiths' street is where needles are made, so selling them there is the proverbial wasted errand: she knows the man's word better than any go-between can describe it. The bard is mocked, not answered.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife turns away the bard who pleads for the man of the town

comparisons.tenor: the bard urging the wife to trust her husband's word

reading: The wife asks the bard who roams as envoy for the man of the watered fields where bees hum at the blossoms what he has come into her house to do, out of his wits, and points him to the road to her 'younger sisters'' houses.
nuance: எங்கையர், 'our younger sisters', is the wife's barbed courtesy for the other women. The bee that moves among blossoms is only the town's scene here; read as the husband moving among women it would make one match, short of a hidden comparison.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife refuses the bard of the man of the watered fields

reading: The wife asks the bard whether the grace of the man of the wide, rich fields needs to be pleaded for, since the bond of those who know what ought to be known will itself show the way.
nuance: The argument turns the bard's office against itself: if the man felt the bond, no envoy would be needed; that an envoy comes proves the bond is missing.

thinai_evidence.note: the bard pleads for the husband and is turned away

reading: For the man of the town where the vaalai fish, afraid of the stab of the handsome little heron, hides among the blue lilies, our shoulders were once sandal paste to lean on; in this season they are hotter than caustic.
nuance: The fish fleeing the heron's beak into the lilies maps onto the husband who, dreading the wife's sharp words, hides in other women's houses; her shoulders, once his cooling sandal, now burn him.

thinai_evidence.note: the pond fish, heron and blue lily of the watered fields

comparisons.tenor: her shoulders, once cool and welcome to him
her shoulders now, burning with anger

ullurai.tenor: the husband who keeps to other women's houses for fear of his wife's anger

pairs.situation: he dreads the wife's sharp reproach
he hides among the other women

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the heron and fish of the pond of her own marutham town (porul 7.26)

reading: Should the pain of longing for the desirable chest of the man of the fine-field town, where lotuses open like flame, come upon her, the wife says it is eased by the earnest prattle of her little son with the curling tuft.
nuance: The sentence leaves its verb unsaid, so the boy's chatter may either console her without the man or soften her toward him; either way the child, not the bard, is the go-between who works.

thinai_evidence.note: the lotus fields and the straying husband's chest

comparisons.tenor: the lotus opening red as flame

reading: The wife tells her bangled friend to see what happened when, as the drums of the man's new wedding, already the town's great joke, were sounding, this little one ran after him mounting his decorated chariot, reached him and came to grief.
nuance: இவன், 'this one', is most naturally the son (as in 28), turned away at the chariot by a father bound for another bride; it could also be the bard, who went to the wedding and was rebuffed.

thinai_evidence.note: the man of the fields takes another bride and his wife is hurt

reading: The wife asks whether she is still the kind the man of the cool fields would quarrel with, now that her five-part hair has thinned like fine grains and her skin has turned pale like the white marul fibre, changed in colour.
nuance: To sulk at someone is to still want her; she says she has faded past even being worth his anger, so his absence is not oodal but neglect.

thinai_evidence.note: the sulk of the man of the cool fields

comparisons.tenor: her hair, grown thin
her complexion, gone pale

reading: The wife tells her sword-eyed friend that her heart has hardened against the man of the town of loud-sounding waters, because, while her son stood there longing, he did not tell the chariot to stop, saw him and drove on without a glance.
nuance: The charge is precise: he saw (கண்டு) and did not look (நோக்கான்). The son's mute yearning (ஏக்கற்று) is the appeal that fails, and her hardening follows from his hardness to the child, not to her.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's anger at the man of the watered town

reading: The wife tells her friend that she would say 'I will not embrace his wide chest', but does the man of the loud waters care at all that she refuses? She will go on doing his bidding.
nuance: The refusal is withdrawn not from desire but because it has no audience: oodal is a weapon only against someone who notices it.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife weighs refusing the husband's embrace

reading: The wife tells her bright-jewelled friend that as the south wind is sweet to the body when it blows even in the cold season, so union with the man's fragrant body is sweet to her even while she sulks.
nuance: The comparison is pointed: the south wind belongs to a warm season, so its sweetness out of season is like a union that pleases against her own quarrel.

thinai_evidence.note: sulking and union with the man of the town

comparisons.vehicle: குளிரும் பருவத்தே யாயினும் தென்றல் வளியெறியின் மெய்யிற்(கு) இனிதாம்
comparisons.tenor: union with the man while she sulks

title: பாலை 31-40
theme: The paalai decade of separation: the woman wasting at the sight of spring (31) and fearing the road of robbers, ghouls and hero-stones (34, 35); the friend's comfort through beasts that care for their mates on that road (32, 36, 38); the mother doubting the eloping girl who has forgotten her toys and faltered at play (33, 37); and the man holding back, telling his heart of her sobs and of tomorrow's lonely bed (39, 40).
source_issues: 31-40: the colophon gives only the thinai (பாலை) and no thurai; every thurai_akam speech situation is inferred from the poem, with occasion words null.
32 line 1: விலங்கல் is hard to construe here (a hill, or 'do not turn aside'), and செல்லாரோ வல்லர் can mean 'is he not able to go' or 'will he not come'; the verse is marked uncertain.
34 line 1: வல்லில் reads as a misprint for வல்வில் (strong bow).
36 line 3: வெடியோடும் is unclear (cracked ground, or bursts of heat); the reading takes it as the cracking heat of the forest.
39 line 2: மாற்றாள் is taken as 'cannot hold back (her grief)'; line 1 மாட்டோ டப் is split oddly and is read as மாட்டு ஓட, 'to run after'.

reading: Each time she sees the early summer, when the murukku puts out buds like a tiger's claws dyed with blood and the cool rains have gone, a season that gives joy to lovers who are together, the woman says her heart, mixed with grief, wastes away.
nuance: The poem names its own contrast: the season brings joy to those who meet (எதிருநர்க்கு), so her grief is measured against the pleasure the same sight gives the united. The blood-dyed claw turns the spring flower into an image of a wound.

thinai_evidence.note: the early summer, the season of paalai

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the woman left behind, seeing the season

comparisons.tenor: the red curved buds of the murukku

reading: The friend tells the bright-jewelled woman that the man is able to go across the wasteland where a handsome tusker takes up in his trunk the little water in the mud of a rock pool and pours it over the head of his mate, worn out by the heat.
nuance: Line 1 is hard to construe, so whether the friend means 'he is strong enough to go' or 'will he not come back?' is open; either way the tusker's care is what she offers as her argument.

thinai_evidence.note: heat and the wasteland

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the friend comforts the waiting woman

iraicchi.act: the tusker carries the little water of a muddy rock pool in his trunk and pours it on the head of his heat-worn mate
iraicchi.sense: the man who passes such care on his road will be moved to the same care for the wife he left

reading: The mother says the girl of chosen words sweet as milk no longer thinks of her doll, her ball, her green parrot with its coral beak or her playmates; will she go after her lover through the forest that the sun's rays scorch?
nuance: The things she forgets are all of childhood, so their being forgotten is the sign that she has left it; the milk of her speech keeps her a child in her mother's words even as she goes.

thinai_evidence.note: a girl going with her lover into the forest

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the mother laments the eloping daughter, to no named hearer

comparisons.tenor: the girl's sweet, chosen speech
the parrot's red beak

reading: The friend asks the man whether he will go, leaving the woman of wide sword-bright eyes, across many wastelands where hard-eyed men with curved strong bows, never parted from killing, harry and rob travellers, to the far place he longs for.
nuance: The danger she names is his, not the woman's: the friend tries to hold him back by the robbers of the road rather than by the grief at home.

thinai_evidence.note: leaving her to cross the wastes

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the friend tries to stop the man's departure

comparisons.tenor: the woman's wide eyes

reading: The woman says that the wasteland the man bent on wealth has gone into is, people say, a hot forest where a ghoul, gorged on the cut fat of men felled by the killing weapons of the curved-bowed Eyinar, sleeps in the wide shade of a hero-stone.
nuance: Everything on that road is at rest, the dead under the stone and the sated ghoul in its shade, while she has only report (என்பர்) to go on and no rest at all.

thinai_evidence.note: the Eyinar of the waste and the hot forest

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the waiting woman's fear for the man on the road

reading: The friend asks the good woman whether he will go to the hot forest of cracking heat, where an elephant takes the swift white mirage for water, runs to it together with his mate and falls with tangled legs, leaving her so that her bangles slip and fall.
nuance: The mirage deceives the pair but does not part them: they run and fall together, which is the reproach the friend leaves unspoken against the man who goes alone.

thinai_evidence.note: mirage and hot forest

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the friend speaks of the man's going

iraicchi.act: the elephant and his mate, deceived by the mirage, run to it together and fall together
iraicchi.sense: even beasts fooled by the waste do not part from their mates, yet the man leaves her

reading: The mother asks whether the girl, who would falter as if about to fall when she played by the ford in front of the house with her friends around her, can now keep pace without lagging behind her lover on the stony paths of the wasteland.

thinai_evidence.note: going behind her lover through the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the mother after the daughter's elopement, to no named hearer

comparisons.tenor: the girl faltering at play

reading: The friend tells the woman that the road the lover's heart has taken is, people say, a wasteland where a stag, judging that the little water in the pool will not be enough, wants the doe to drink her fill and only pretends to drink.
nuance: The stag's love is shown by a deceit (கள்ளத்தின் ஊச்சும்), and the poem sets it on the road the man's heart (உள்ளம்) has gone down, as if his heart had chosen the path where it would be taught tenderness. The words could also be the woman's own, said with the opposite edge.

thinai_evidence.note: the waste and its scant water

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the friend comforts the waiting woman (porul 5.35)

iraicchi.act: the stag, judging the pool's little water too scant for both, pretends to drink so that the doe may drink her fill
iraicchi.sense: the man whose heart has gone that way will see such care and his heart will turn back to the wife he left

reading: The man tells his good heart that it is foolish: when they stir to set out after great wealth, she of bright ornaments cannot hold back, and sobs and sighs with swelling grief; how will she bear it once they have gone from her?
nuance: He argues from what he sees at the moment of setting out to what must follow after, so the sobbing he has watched becomes the measure of a grief he will not be there to see.

thinai_evidence.note: parting for wealth

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the man reasons with his heart against the journey

reading: The man tells his good heart that tonight it slept well in the cool place with the shoulders of her of the cool garland for companion; tomorrow, having crossed the wasteland of hill paths, alone, where will they lie down?
nuance: The cool (ஈர்ம், ஈர்ங்) of tonight is set against a tomorrow that has no place named at all; the question is the whole argument against going.

thinai_evidence.note: crossing the waste alone, away from her

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the man on the eve of going speaks to his heart

title: நெய்தல் 41-50
theme: Neythal: on the sea shore the heroine grieves the shore lord's absence and the doubtful worth of his secret oath and signs (41-45, 49, 50), the friend presses him to marry by appeal to what is fitting and to his name (46, 48), and the hero is struck by the fisher girl guarding the drying catch (47).
source_issues: Verse 41 line 1 prints editorial brackets (புலம்(பு) அடைந்(து)) that restore elided letters; the restored reading was used.

reading: Since the lord of the clear sea's shore has gone away, the heroine tells her bright-jewelled friend that her wide bright eyes, sunk in grief, will not sleep: the flower-crested anril cries out though its mate has come close and rests beside it, so what wonder if she, whose mate is gone, keeps awake?
nuance: The optative துஞ்சற்க can be read as the heroine's vow of wakefulness or as the friend's gentle irony; either way the argument runs from the lesser case to the greater: a bird that cries with its mate beside it licenses a parted woman's sleepless crying.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea-shore lord and the anril of the palmyra shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from ஒள்ளிழாய் and the grief of line 1

iraicchi.act: the anril cries out in the night even while its mate rests close beside it
iraicchi.sense: if a joined bird laments, the heroine parted from her man cannot be asked to sleep

reading: The heroine begs the crooked-legged crab, as a favour, not to walk over and blur the tracks the long chariot of the lord of the ever-roaring shore left behind, so that she may look at the path he took until her eyes are full.
nuance: All she has left of him is the wheel-rut in the sand, and the only creature that can take it from her is the crab, so she pleads with it as with a person (குறையாம் இரப்பேம்).

thinai_evidence.note: the roaring sea's shore and its crab

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses the crab on the shore; the colophon gives no thurai

reading: Climbing the long striped sand where the punnai has put out buds like the eggs of a speckled lizard, the heroine says that if the cool lord of the low-lying sea is to grant her his garlanded chest, she and her friend will surely see it in the circle drawn in the sand.
nuance: ஆழி is taken as the circle a waiting woman draws in the sand to divine whether the lover will come; it can also mean the sea, which would change the last line to seeing him by the sea, so the reading is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai on the dunes and the sea-shore lord

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; the hoped-for gift of his chest points to marriage still to come

comparisons.tenor: the punnai's buds, as if the tree had laid a speckled lizard's eggs

reading: The heroine tells her friend that she wept till her kohl-lined eyes reddened, gazing at the cool flowering grove the shore lord had left, and when her mother saw her face and asked what grieved her, she answered that the sea had come and wrecked her sand-house.
nuance: The lie is also the truth in code: it was the man of the sea, the கொண்கன், who came and broke up her girlhood play, so the excuse names the real cause in terms only the friend can read.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore lord and the sea that comes up the sand

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she reports to the friend how she hid the affair from the mother

reading: The heroine tells her friend, whose body is tender as a mango shoot, that the cool lord of the dark backwater came to her in the moist grove, took her bangled arm and swore his faith, and asks whether the herons of that flowering grove will really let the oath go by.
nuance: The herons are called on as the only witnesses of a secret oath; they are the subject of her question, not a carrier of a further sense, so they are not tagged iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater lord and the herons of the shore grove

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; she recalls the oath given in secret

comparisons.tenor: the friend's body, tender and coloured like a young mango leaf

reading: The friend asks the lord of the seaside grove, where innocent young girls light their sand-houses with cool pearls heaped up by the tide of the roaring sea, whether it befits him to make her friend's shoulders lose their beauty.
nuance: The girls treat the sea's pearls as playthings, which sets the heroine's guarded girlhood against his careless use of her beauty; read as ullurai it gives only that one pair (precious things spent lightly), so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the tide-washed shore and its grove

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; she reproaches him for delaying, as one pressing for marriage

reading: The hero says that the bright-jewelled girl who scares the birds off the fat fish her brothers brought in together, casting their fine nets till the great sea was stirred to its depths, has become a tormenting goddess to him beyond bearing.
nuance: The brothers' nets, cast together, place the girl inside her watchful kin from the first line, which is why the sight of her is fear as much as desire.

thinai_evidence.note: the fishing people's nets and their drying catch

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; he speaks of his own state (எமக்கு), perhaps for the friend to hear

comparisons.tenor: the maiden, who becomes for him an afflicting goddess

reading: The friend asks the cool lord of the long backwater, where pearls brought by the tide onto the heaped sand of the dunes stay and glitter, whether men who do not take up the distress of those who have come to depend on them can carry great renown.
nuance: The pearl the tide leaves on the dune keeps shining where it was set down; the friend wants the girl who has come to him to be kept so. That is one pair only, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the dunes and the long backwater

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; she presses him to marry by appeal to his name

reading: The heroine says that the lord of the clear sea's shore, where the bright flower of the thorny-fronded thaazhai opens among its leaves like a lump of butter and the whole shore round about smells as if a god dwelt there, gave her a sign she cannot trust.
nuance: The place of the tryst is so fragrant it seems holy, while the man's signal there is the one thing on that shore that is not clear (தெளி-கடல் against தெளியாக் குறி).

thinai_evidence.note: the thaazhai of the shore grove and the sea-shore lord

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; the sign (குறி) is the tryst signal

comparisons.tenor: the opened white thaazhai flower among its fronds, like butter

reading: The heroine tells her bright-jewelled friend that she rose and went out, thinking it the sound of the bells on the horses yoked to the chariot of the cool lord of the lovely sea, and turned back, her heart melting within her, when she heard it was only the noise of fruit-seeking birds.
nuance: The birds that crave fruit mirror her own craving: she too goes out at a sound, and both are disappointed waiters.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea-shore lord

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; she waits for his coming

title: குறிஞ்சி 0-14
theme: Kurinji: the invocation to the elephant god (0), then the hill lovers' secret love, the friend's pleas to the man not to forget and to marry (1, 5, 7, 11), the girl's trust in his pledge (2, 4, 8, 9, 14), her care for him on the night path (10), the friend shielding her from the mother and the velan's rite (6, 12), and the coming that ends the mother's harrying (13).
source_issues: No verse in this chapter has a colophon thurai; every thurai_akam speaker and addressee is inferred from the verse.
0: the invocation to the elephant god is in a different style from the kurinji venbas and is probably a later addition to the book.
2 line 2: குன்றன is unclear (குன்று அன்ன, 'like a hill', would need a tenor); line 4 தலையளி ஒன்றுமற்(று) ஒன்றும் அனைத்து does not construe cleanly, and the verse is marked uncertain.
6 line 3: முடைந்தாட is not a usual verb for bathing; perhaps முனைந்து ஆட, bathing with zeal.
7 lines 1 and 3: வெறிகமழ் தண் is repeated (தண்சுனை, தண்சோலை), which may be a copying error in one line.
8 line 4: நேர்வனை reads as a misprint for நேர்வளை, 'friend of fitting bangles'.
10 lines 1-2: whose life is meant by நிறையில்லா மன்னுயிர் (hers, without restraint, or his) is unclear; the verse is marked uncertain.
11 line 1: பிரைசங் is probably பிரசம் (honey or bees).
12 lines 1-2: வளைலாய is probably வளைவாய், curved beak; நீரால் தெளிதிகழ் does not construe clearly; the verse is marked uncertain.

reading: The invocation asks that the elephant born of the god with the eye in his forehead, he of the skull, of the whole universe, of the root of things and of the fair dark throat, bring every purpose we hold sweetly to its end and grant us all the arts.
nuance: The elephant god is never named; he is known only as the offspring (ஈன்ற களிறு) of Siva, who is drawn by four epithets ending in -த்தான். The prayer asks for success in what one intends and for learning, the two things a poet beginning a book needs.

thinai_evidence.note: praise and prayer to a god, the கடவுள் வாழ்த்து placed under paadaan

reading: The friend tells the lord of the forest land, whose spreading slopes see the yak and the gaur graze on the green-eared millet twined with avarai beans, not to forget that she stood as the raft between him and the girl of bright jewels.
nuance: The friend claims her own part: the love was crossed to on her as on a raft, so forgetting the girl would also be forgetting the one who carried him. The beasts eating a guarded millet field invite a hidden reading of the man taking what is watched over, but only one correspondence can be named, so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field of the slopes and its raiding hill beasts

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse

comparisons.tenor: the friend herself, the raft that carried him across to the girl

reading: The girl says that she trusted the assurance given by the lord of the hills, where a troop of black-faced langurs leaps on the boulder of the village common, thought it good and was set at rest; his grace, she says, is one and the same from first to last.
nuance: Three forms of one root, தெளித்த, தெளிவினை, தெளிந்தேன், make the verse a small study of trust: he made her clear, she weighed it (தேறி) and then was clear. The last line is the doubtful one; it is read here as saying his kindness is the same throughout.

thinai_evidence.note: langurs on the boulders of the hill country

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse

reading: The girl says they cannot part from the lord of the lovely mountain, where a female monkey, having eaten the sweet ripe fruit of the jackfruit on the common, strokes the udder of a wild cow, and the cow, as glad as with her own calf, lets her milk flow.
nuance: The milk is not taken but given: the cow lets it down (சுரக்கும்) because the touch feels like her calf's, so tenderness flows across kinds.

thinai_evidence.note: the monkey and the wild cow of the hill slopes

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse; it could also be the friend telling the man that they (the girl and she) will not part from him

iraicchi.act: the wild cow, stroked by the monkey as if by her calf, gladly lets her milk flow to it
iraicchi.sense: a heart once touched with tenderness gives itself and cannot be withdrawn, so the girl cannot part from the man who has won her

reading: The girl says her heart tells her that, as the friendship of the worthy stands firm without decay, grows into strength and keeps yielding good afterwards, so the friendship of the lord of the mountain, with its groves bright with pools, will shine with goodness and never weaken.
nuance: The first two lines are a maxim of the ethics books, set down whole before the love situation; the girl's trust rests on ranking her lover among the சான்றவர், and it is her heart, not her friend, that makes the argument.

thinai_evidence.note: the mountain land and its groves

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse

comparisons.tenor: the mountain lord's bond with her, set beside the friendship of the worthy

reading: The friend tells the lord of the good mountain, whose dense groves smell of the vengai's golden clusters, not to forget that the girl of bright jewels has no medicine but him to keep her sweet life, and asks whether he will not give it out of kindness.
nuance: Line 2 repeats verse 1's மறவல் வயங்கிழைக்கு, so the friend's plea has a refrain. The gift she asks for is named by the Kural's word for regard toward one's own, கண்ணோட்டம், making his return a duty of kindness rather than a favour.

thinai_evidence.note: the flowering vengai of the mountain groves

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse

comparisons.tenor: the man himself, the only medicine that can hold up her life

reading: The friend tells the mother not to rage, since the girl is not at fault: her eyes turned red because she bathed again and again in the waterfall that came down mixed with honey in the red, swollen water of the forest stream.
nuance: The excuse is precise enough to be believed: red flood water, honey in the stream, long bathing. What reddened the eyes is left unsaid, and the friend's defence is itself the sign that the girl has been weeping for her lover.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest stream and hill waterfall

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse

reading: The friend asks the lord of the fragrant cool groves, where the cool water of a fragrant spring brims over and the sweet ripe fruit of the mango on which pepper vine climbs falls into it, whether any folly can stand where knowledge stands.
nuance: The rebuke is a compliment turned against him: he is wise, so his delay must be the one folly wisdom cannot hold. The ripe fruit falling into the brimming spring has been read as the girl ready for marriage; it is one match of mood only, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the spring, pepper vine and mango of the hill groves

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse; the question presses him to act as his knowledge requires, that is, to marry

reading: The girl tells her friend that the lord of the land of falling waterfalls, where in the burnt clearing the boar has ploughed a male monkey buries mature plantains to ripen and then rests, has given her his pledge, and that pledge is the staff her heart leans on.
nuance: The monkey's stored fruit and the girl's stored promise both wait to ripen; the comfort is in having put something by.

thinai_evidence.note: the burnt hill clearing, the boar and the monkey

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse

comparisons.tenor: his pledge, the staff her heart leans on

iraicchi.act: the male monkey buries unripe plantains in the ploughed clearing to let them ripen and then rests at ease
iraicchi.sense: the man has laid his pledge by as the monkey lays by its fruit, so she can rest on it until it ripens into marriage

reading: The bond with the mountain lord of the bee-loud groves, where a great-trunked dark bull elephant eats hill paddy and sleeps in the green-leaved shade of the black-stemmed kadamba grove, gives safety to those who join with it.
nuance: ஏமாப்பு உடைத்து is the didactic books' word for lasting protection; here it is said of a lover's bond.

thinai_evidence.note: the elephant, hill paddy and kadamba grove of the mountain

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse; the general statement could equally be the friend's reassurance to the girl

iraicchi.act: the elephant, fed, lies down to sleep without fear in the shade of the grove
iraicchi.sense: as the elephant sleeps secure in the grove's shade, the woman joined to this man may rest without fear

reading: The girl tells her friend that she has one want: to keep safe a life that is dear to her, so tell the lord of the long groves where snakes move that he must not come to their house by night.
nuance: The refusal is made out of care: the danger is to him on the snake path, and asking him to stop coming is how she protects him. அரா and இரா sit two syllables apart in line 3 and 4, the snake and the night together.

thinai_evidence.note: the snake-haunted grove and the night meeting

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse; she refuses the night meeting (இரவுக்குறி) for fear of the path

reading: The friend tells the lord of the mountain land, where the calf of a wild cow tramples with its hooves a honeycomb of sweet honey that has fallen under its weight, that if he keeps coming without marrying her, the girl of the rows of bangles will not live.
nuance: வரையக நாட and வரையால் play on one sound: lord of the hills (வரை), you who do not wed (வரை). The trampled honeycomb has been read as her ruined sweetness; it gives only one correspondence, a near miss for ullurai, and stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the wild cow's calf and the fallen honeycomb of the hills

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse; she presses him to marry

reading: The girl says she has embraced to the full, with longing, her bond with the lord of the forest land where flocks of curved-beaked parrots carry off the long ears of millet, and now the velan has firmly resolved to cut a goat kid.
nuance: The two halves are set side by side without comment: she knows the cause of her sickness, an embrace she chose, while the diviner the mother called readies a sacrifice for a god's seizure. The irony is all in the juxtaposition.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field raided by parrot flocks

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse

reading: The friend tells the girl that the lord of the mountain land, where swarms of bees hum on the clustered kaanthal in a bower thick with the leaves of cool wild jasmine, has come at last, and their mother's harrying has gone away today.
nuance: அலையும் அலைபோயிற்று: the harrying itself has gone off, a play on அலை. The bees finding the kaanthal mirror his coming, but they carry a mood and are not tested as iraicchi. That he came to ask for her is inferred from the mother's anger ending.

thinai_evidence.note: kaanthal and wild jasmine of the hill bower

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse; his coming is taken as the coming to ask for her in marriage

reading: The girl says that because they say the lord of the land, where a stream carrying eaglewood from the clearing leaps over rocks and the waterfall from the sky brims in beauty, is a man of goodness, her shoulders have forgotten to waste even if he goes away.
nuance: The usual sign of separation, wasting shoulders, is cancelled by reputation: what others say of his goodness (என்பதனால்) is enough to keep her body whole. Her confidence in the bond, not the waiting, is the matter, so uri is taken as punarthal.

thinai_evidence.note: eaglewood and waterfall of the hill clearing

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse

title: முல்லை 15-28
theme: Mullai: the wife waits through the rainy season; the evening, the thunder, the peacocks and the homecoming herdsmen each turn the promised season against her (15-24, 27-28).
source_issues: Verses 25 and 26 are absent from our text, so the chapter has 12 verses for the span 15 to 28.
Verse 27: show flags that sangamtamil.com lacks this verse; its closing line is obscure in our text and the verse is marked uncertain.
Verse 19 line 2 பீவி looks like a misprint for பீலி (peacock plumes).
Verse 24 line 4 முலைவற்று is doubtful in sense; verse 28 line 3 படுமழைகொல looks like படுமழைகொல் with the final consonant misprinted.
The colophons give no thurai for any verse of this chapter, so thurai_akam speakers are inferred from the verses (the friend as addressee where none is named) and occasion words are null.

reading: When the red-rayed sun has put away its heat, the green-stemmed jasmine smells sweet and the bees hum, she says that every time she sees the rain sky tossing with its clouds, her eyes toss with tears.
nuance: The two closing lines repeat one verb, அலமரும், for the sky and the eyes, and only the noun changes (காரோடு, நீரோடு): the sky's clouds and her tears are matched sound for sound rather than through a simile marker. The sun is not set but has 'hidden its anger', the cooling hour of mullai.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain sky at the hour the sun cools, with jasmine in bloom

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, which toss with tears as the sky tosses with clouds

reading: She tells her friend of broad, soft, bamboo-like shoulders that the man who left has not come, though the soft-stepping peacock calls and the lovely sky that drew up the sea has come with its lightning, and there is no one who asks her what is wrong.
nuance: The season has come (வந்தது) and the man has not (வாரார), and the last line turns from him to the household: her worst complaint is that no one even asks, so her grief is also isolation.

thinai_evidence.note: waiting for the man who left while the peacock greets the rains

comparisons.tenor: the friend's shoulders, rounded and smooth as bamboo

reading: As the cool glory lily lifts its spoon-shaped buds to greet the rains and thunder roars in the high sky, the little evening comes like killers, so that those who have no one to hold them close tremble.
nuance: The victims are named as a class, புல்லுநர் இல்லார், 'those without someone to embrace them firmly', so the speaker counts herself among them without saying 'I'. The evening is called small (சிறுமாலை) and still comes as a killer.

thinai_evidence.note: evening at the coming of the rains

comparisons.tenor: the little evening coming upon those with no one to embrace them
the glory lily's buds, shaped like ladles

reading: As the sky scatters its swift rain and the konrai with pollen in its petals blazes like a growing fire, she looks at the lovely sky that seems to thunder as it spreads, and says her life seems to throb.
nuance: The two last lines rhyme இடிப்பது and துடிப்பது, each with போலும்: the thunder's beat outside is matched by the beat of her life inside, the same device as verse 15.

thinai_evidence.note: the konrai's bloom under the first heavy rain

comparisons.tenor: the konrai's golden clusters
her life, which throbs as the sky thunders

reading: As the peacock, longing for the raindrops, calls and spreads its plumes over all the woodland and dances, and this rain cloud thunders as if a pregnant one were bursting, she says her life seems to melt.
nuance: The peacock's joy and the cloud's fullness (சூலி, 'the pregnant one') are both images of fruition, set against her melting. Reading சூலி as the heavy cloud like a woman in labour is our reading of a compressed line.

thinai_evidence.note: the peacock dancing over the woodland at the rains

comparisons.tenor: the rain cloud thundering as it breaks

reading: As the stags coming with their herd leap up, the jasmine twined with the creepers of the clearing puts out shoots, and thunder rolls, the little evening comes together with the storm, so that she and he both suffer.
nuance: யானும் அவரும் வருந்த: she imagines him suffering too, so the poem is not a reproach. The stags arrive (வரும்) with their herd and rejoice at the hour he cannot.

thinai_evidence.note: the herd of deer, the jasmine and the evening storm

iraicchi.act: the stags come in together with their herd at evening and leap for joy
iraicchi.sense: the beasts come home in company at dusk, which the man who left has not done, and so both of them suffer apart

reading: Before even the man who left her, letting her beauty fade, has come, the rain-fed jasmine shows its teeth, and the evening comes with the rain cloud to torment her: no one, she says, lives in such folly as we do.
nuance: The jasmine 'bearing teeth' is the usual figure for its buds, but next to her self-mockery it also grins at her. The closing line can mean that no one is as foolish as she, who still lives, or who let him go; the poem does not choose.

thinai_evidence.note: jasmine in bud and the rainy evening

comparisons.tenor: the jasmine's white buds, shown like teeth

reading: The herdsmen blow their konrai flutes and follow talking behind, the herd with its calves goes into the fold, and today, as she watches, the evening that comes every day has come, and the sky has thundered and drawn its bow.
nuance: Nothing is said of the man or of her pain: the evening is only watched (யாம் காண). The herdsmen and the herd coming home are a near miss for iraicchi; the act fits, but the poem never names the absent man, so the sense it would carry has nothing in the poem to attach to. The sky 'drawing a bow' arms the evening.

thinai_evidence.note: herdsmen bringing the cattle home at evening

comparisons.tenor: the rainbow the sky draws as it thunders

reading: As the frogs' clamouring voices and the bells on the garlands ring out and the roaring sky begins to rain, she asks whether her lover will fail to come today to comfort her when the rains set in, for her bangles will not stay on at all.
nuance: Whose bells ring (தார்மணி) is not said: cattle bells fit the mullai evening, chariot-horse bells would be the sound she hopes for, and either is possible. The slipping bangles are her wasting body's evidence.

thinai_evidence.note: the onset of the rains with frogs calling

reading: On the stony woodland, grown lovely, jasmine opens its buds on the bushes together with the wild jasmine; in the night the sky has stopped its tossing, the friend says, but the water of your kohl-lined eyes has not stopped running down to your breasts.
nuance: The rhyme அலைவற்று / முலைவற்று sets the sky that has ceased against the eyes that have not. The second half is compressed and our reading of முலைவற்று is doubtful.

thinai_evidence.note: the stony woodland in bloom after rain

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, still raining after the sky has stopped

reading: As the paandil of the rains smells sweet and the swarms of bees hum and dance with a din over all the woodland, the little evening torments her without mercy, never relenting, and, fighting it, her tears stand as they have always stood.
nuance: நீர்த்தின்றி, 'without fitness', makes the evening a wrongdoer; the closing line is obscure and we read it as her tears never ceasing.

thinai_evidence.note: evening over the woodland in the rains

reading: She asks her well-jewelled friend whether what has happened to her is like the pouring rain that lingers behind and then moves away, at the hour when the herdsman comes home wearing a fine garland headed with kurunthu flowers while bees hum.
nuance: The herdsman comes home garlanded at the very hour she asks her question, so his return frames her lover's absence. Reading the lingering rain as a figure for the man who stayed and left is ours; the line can also be read of the rain itself.

thinai_evidence.note: the herdsman's homecoming with a kurunthu garland

comparisons.tenor: what has befallen her: the man who stayed a while and went

title: பாலை 29-42
theme: Paalai: the road of separation, tigers, robbers, cairns and hero-stones, seen from home; the mother of an eloped girl (30), the friend before the man leaves (31, 36), the heroine's reproaches and fears (32-40), and omens of his return (41, 42).
source_issues: 29 line 2: அருஞ்சுரம்நரம் is not a word; perhaps அருஞ்சுரம் நாம் ('we, thinking of the hard road'). Lines 2-3 (அறிவிட்(டு), கொடியக) are hard to construe.
35 line 2: இருங்கினை is probably இருங்கிளை ('dark kin').
37 line 2: கடவு தெவுட்டு is obscure and may be corrupt.
38 line 1: நல்வய மரக்குழுமும் is probably a misdivision (நல்வயமாக் குழுமும், 'the strong beast roars').
39 line 3: அருள்நினைந் lacks its final syllable (அருள்நினைந்து).
41 line 2: குன்றனம் may stand for குன்றம்.
42 line 3: மெள்தோள் is a misprint for மென்தோள்; பிணைதீர is uncertain.

reading: The speaker thinks of the hard wasteland whose paths are choked, where a speckled cock pecks at the striped maral, and of the mountain of the land of the one the gossip went out about, which now shows itself rising high on the right.
nuance: A hill seen rising on the right (வலன்) is the auspicious side, so the closing image may be an omen of the man's good journey or return, as in 41 and 42; but line 2 (அருஞ்சுரம்நரம்) and line 3 (அறிவிட்டு, கொடியக) are hard to construe, and the speaker and situation are our guess.

thinai_evidence.note: the hard wasteland the absent man crossed

reading: A mother whose daughter has gone off with a man wonders whether the girl sits pining, sighing that she cannot go on, or whether she walks behind that man like a killer elephant across the stony wasteland, the pebbles in her anklets ringing and her soft toes reddening.
nuance: The anklet is the unmarried girl's ornament (the silambu is removed at the wedding), so its ringing on the desert road says she has gone before her marriage rite. The addressee is no one present: the mother speaks to herself. மெல்விரல் may be fingers or toes; walking makes toes the likelier sense.

thinai_evidence.note: a girl's going with her lover through the wasteland

comparisons.tenor: the man the daughter follows

reading: Under the dappled shade of the rough-barked omai a striped-trunked elephant sleeps with its mate, and when the man speaks of leaving through that fire-hazed forest the tears in the heroine's kohl-lined, red-streaked eyes will not stay.
nuance: The speaker is most likely the friend telling the man what his talk of going has already done: the tears come at the word, before any parting.

thinai_evidence.note: the man speaks of leaving through the burning forest

iraicchi.act: the bull elephant sleeps beside its mate in the thin shade of the burning forest rather than leaving her
iraicchi.sense: even the beasts of the road he means to cross keep to their mates in the heat, so the man should not leave her to cross it

reading: The heroine says that the road is lined with lettered stones where archers with fine arrows harass the lovely way and fill the wasteland, and yet, fitting his labour that wins great things, his longing in love has become longing for hard-won wealth.
nuance: The lettered stones are hero-stones of men killed by the road's archers, so the danger and the motive are set side by side. ஏற்க, 'fitting', may be praise of his effort or a bitter concession; the poem leaves it open. Lines 1 and 2 are hard to divide (வாயில், அம்ஆ(று)), so the scene is read only in outline.

thinai_evidence.note: the road of hero-stones the man takes for wealth

reading: The heroine asks whether the man, whose heart without kindly regard for his soft girl climbs after wealth and will not stay, does not see on the road the men who live by ploughing with the bow, rushing out to harass travellers among the stone-ringed cairns.
nuance: The cairns are the stone heaps over travellers the robbers killed, so 'do they not see?' means: he can see the death on the road and still goes, but cannot see her.

thinai_evidence.note: the man leaves for wealth through the robbers' road

comparisons.tenor: the robbers who live off travellers as farmers live off the field

reading: The heroine asks her friend whether the man will cross the waterless hard road where herds of wild cattle roam, and whether her heart, throwing off shame, will go along with her life and contrive that she see him.
nuance: உயிரோடு உடன்சென்று: the heart will leave with her life, so following him and dying are the same act; shame is the only thing that keeps her body at home.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is to cross the waterless road

reading: The heroine asks whether the man with a heart without moisture does not know the waterless hard road, where the sharp-clawed bear's dark kin settle in an abandoned house overgrown with gourd vine and sleep.
nuance: If இருங்கினை stands for இருங்கிளை (the dark kin), the bears that sleep together in a deserted house are set against a man who leaves his own house: a near miss for iraicchi, kept as scene because the word is in doubt. The 'moistureless heart' answers the waterless road.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's journey over the waterless road

reading: The friend asks whether the man without sense will drive his chariot away through the forest, where squirrels squeal in the cane of the scrub and the village cock fights the quail round the garden plots, rather than ending the gossip the town has raised.
nuance: ஒழித்து can mean that he goes leaving the gossip behind for her to bear, or that he should end it by marrying; either way the journey is set against marriage. The scrub with its village, cock and quail is a mullai woodland on the paalai road. The fighting cock and quail may hint at the town's quarrel, but one match of mood is not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: the man leaves while the town gossips about the secret love

reading: The heroine asks whether the man will cross the tall-hilled road, where a creature that lost its mate to the leaping tiger crowds in fear at the sun-baked rock, the wasteland where the beast of prey watches for its kill.
nuance: துணையிழந்து அஞ்சி, a beast that has lost its mate and fears, is the fate she fears for herself, but the creature only suffers and does nothing a lover does, so it carries a mood, not an iraicchi. Line 2 (கடவு தெவுட்டு) is obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's crossing of the tiger's road

reading: The heroine asks whether he has crossed the forest of cairns and fallen blossom where the strong striped tiger, skilled at the kill, roars, he of a hero's strength who went far to finish his labour and does not understand what is good.
nuance: The praise is barbed: மீளி, the hero's might, and ஆள்வினை, manly labour, are the virtues that make him blind to the good at home. Line 1 (நல்வய மரக்குழுமும்) is probably a misdivision of a line about the tiger's roar.

thinai_evidence.note: he crossed the forest for his labour

reading: The heroine asks her own life whether it will live on, thinking of the grace of the man who went off in unreflecting desire for wealth on the road where a gape-mouthed tiger, having missed its elephant, watches the entrance of the common hall of a ruined village, or whether it will not.
nuance: The addressee is her own life (உயிர்), set apart from her as the heart is in other poems. The tiger that failed with an elephant and now waits at a ruined village for weaker prey makes the road dangerous to the man; the 'grace' she must live on is the very thing his going denies.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has gone for wealth across the ruined road

reading: The heroine says that the road her lover's heart set out on is, people say, a wasteland where robbers roam and where, in the plots ringed by tangled thorny bamboo, the spotted wildcat watches for prey for its kitten.
nuance: She has only heard of the road (என்பர், 'they say'); it is his heart, not his body, she follows along it.

thinai_evidence.note: the road the man took

iraicchi.act: the wildcat goes out on the dangerous ground to watch for prey to feed its young
iraicchi.sense: the man too has gone out on the robbers' road to win what his household needs, so his going is provision as well as desertion

reading: As the owl hoots from the old tree of the village common, bright sneezes come one after another, so the man who went over the hills and past the hill forts seems to be thinking of her in secret.
nuance: A sneeze was taken as a sign that someone far away is thinking of you; repeated sneezes mean steady thought. கள்ளிய தன்மையர், 'of a stealing nature', suggests he thinks of her secretly or is stealing back unannounced; the owl's cry is a second omen whose sense the poem does not spell out.

thinai_evidence.note: the heroine waits for the man who crossed the hills

reading: Her flower-like left eye throbs, her dreams have turned good, her swollen soft shoulders grow lovely again as she thinks of the man who crossed the high hills, and the lizard chirps at the favourable side.
nuance: Four omens are heaped up: the throbbing left eye (good for a woman), dreams that come right, the body's own return to beauty, and the lizard's chirp from the proper quarter. The body recovers before the man arrives. பிணைதீர and மெள்தோள் (for மென்தோள்) are uncertain in the text.

thinai_evidence.note: the heroine waits for the man who crossed the hills

title: மருதம் 43-56
theme: Marutham: the wife refuses the husband's bard and his excuses, mocking the man who comes in behind their son and sending the go-between back to the other women's street (45, 47-51, 56), laments his false oath (44), and the friend and wife lay the blame on him for his straying, his withheld regard and the 'manliness' he claims (46, 52-55).

source_issues.issue: மாண்ழாய் is probably a misprint for மாணிழாய் (vocative).
மார்(பு)யுஅறிம் is garbled; the line's sense cannot be fixed.
அகன்பனை may stand for அகன்பணை (wide fields); read so here.
மேற்றுச் சிறுதாய காய்வஞ்சி போற்றுருவி is obscure and possibly corrupt.
வளைகிய is unusual (வளைந்த?); lines 2 and 3 cannot be construed with confidence.

reading: The woman tells her fair-jewelled friend that those who scold their own kin as simpletons still sit with sealed lips once they have looked the lord of the lotus town in the face; why then should she grieve, when today his chest is known for what it is?
nuance: The point seems to be that even the sharp-tongued, who call others fools, fall silent before him, so his charm is no proof against what he does; but lines 3 and 4 are corrupt and the last clause is a guess.

thinai_evidence.note: a lotus-pond town and a quarrel with its lord

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; addressee inferred from the vocative ஏர் மாண்ழாய் (for மாணிழாய்), speaker from the complaint

reading: The woman asks her bright-jewelled friend to whom she can say that the lord of the town where bright-petalled lotus buds crowd took her heart and now gives her no thought; long ago she drank in his soft humble words, not knowing they were a false oath.
nuance: The complaint looks back from married neglect to the oath of courtship: what betrays her now is not a new act but the discovery that the first words were already false. அச்சுப் பணிமொழி is obscure; 'humble, trembling words' is a guess.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord of the lotus town and the broken oath, a marutham complaint

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; addressee from the vocative ஒள்ளிழாய்

reading: The speaker says with irony that the lord of the good town is a man of great resource: he comes home carrying their son on his chest, the boy's pearl-strung ornaments crushing the frontlet he wears.
nuance: ஆற்றல் உடையன் is praise turned to mockery: his 'strength' is the cunning of coming in behind the child, whom no one can turn away. Line 2 (மேற்றுச் சிறுதாய காய்வஞ்சி போற்றுருவி) is obscure and is not construed here.

thinai_evidence.note: the father uses the son to win entry, the marutham husband's device

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; speaker and addressee inferred: the wife comments to her friend on the husband's arrival

reading: The woman says she will sit counting it an offence that the lord of the town of wide fields is bound by a garland, but asks why those who have watched his folly should blame the stranger women who show them no friendly face.
nuance: She turns the blame from the rival women back on the man: the garland that binds him is his own choosing. The construal of the last two lines is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband bound by other women, a marutham quarrel

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; speaker inferred from இருப்பன், the addressee from the general question

reading: The wife tells the bard, his mouth greasy with meat, that the son has been fed at her breast and she has grown old, so let him go and speak in the street of the women whose breasts are just rising, and eat there, even if he must dance for his meal.
nuance: She sets her own body, aged by nursing (மூத்தேம்), against the budding breasts of the street women, and makes the bard a hired dancer who eats where he performs. The opening words போத்தில் கழுத்தில் are hard to construe.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife turns away the husband's bard, the marutham refusal

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; the vocative பாண names the addressee

reading: The wife tells her bard to leave off speaking of the ways of the lord of the rich good town: let that man of shame keep all that has befallen him, and let the great bard tell what has befallen himself, if anything has.
nuance: நாணுடையான், 'the man of shame', is pure irony: the man without shame is given the virtue he lacks, and the bard is invited to talk about anything but his master.

thinai_evidence.note: the bard sent by the husband is told to drop his errand

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; the vocatives என்னுடை பாண and இரும்பாண name the addressee

reading: The wife tells the bard to lead his master off and tell the flower-like women of the other street what he is: the lord of the cool-ford town, where the red-eyed buffalo that broke its wooden clog sinks into the field pond, gorges on the crop and lies at ease in the shade.
nuance: The flower-like women are meant to hear in the buffalo a portrait of the man they are getting.

thinai_evidence.note: the field buffalo and the cool ford

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; the vocative பாண names the addressee

comparisons.tenor: the women of the other street
the husband

ullurai.tenor: the husband who has left home for the other women

pairs.situation: he breaks the restraint of his own household
he feeds on what is not his own, the other women
he settles at ease in their houses

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the buffalo of her own town's fields, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

reading: The wife says it is folly for him to seek entry with the son as his backing: what can they do for the lord of loud revels? Let the bard go on without pause to the street of the gold-like women with flower-filled hair.
nuance: ஓவாது செல், 'go without ceasing', tells the bard where his real work lies: he is as much a regular of that street as his master. Line 1 (பேதை புகலை புதல்வன் துணைச்சான்றோன்) is hard to construe.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord of revels and the street of other women, a marutham refusal

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; the vocative பாண names the addressee

comparisons.tenor: the women of the other street

reading: The wife tells the bard to get up and go, though to speak of the lord of the good pond-town is her own grief: she has as her companion her little son, who every day waves his flawless gold bangles and cries.
nuance: துணை closes the poem: the son, not the husband, is named her partner, so the bard's plea has nothing to fill.

thinai_evidence.note: the pond town and the wife who refuses the go-between

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; the bard is inferred as addressee from எழுந்தீக and the errand of speaking of the husband

reading: The friend asks the lord of the cool-ford town, where the shoal of varaal fish scatters in the drinking pond, whether it is fitting to pass by the bright-bangled wife without a look, leave the house for that street, and call it manliness before the town.
nuance: The fleeing fish may hint at the household scattered by his going, as in the long marutham buffalo scenes, but the poem gives only one such match, so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the cool ford and the husband's straying

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; the vocative ஊர names the hero, the third-person ஒண்டொடி the wife

reading: The speaker sets the woman's bewilderment at the deluding words of the lord of the fertile-field town against a pledge: if he comes back having won, as the wheel's rim never misses, she will be one with him through all his days.
nuance: Lines 2 and 3 (the bent wheel and its unerring rim) are obscure, and the poem's situation cannot be fixed with confidence.

thinai_evidence.note: fertile fields, marutham land

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; speaker and addressee are guesses from நின் வாழ்நாட்கள் and உளேன்

reading: The friend tells the lord of the strong-field town, who accepts the wife's devoted service, that if he thinks her merely the gift of the wise elders' wish and resolves to withhold kindly regard from those who do not reckon with him, the blame of it falls on him.
nuance: The wife's வழிபாடு (worshipful service) is set against his கண்ணோட்டம் withheld: the poem turns an ethical term into the measure of a husband. The construal of lines 1 and 2 is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: field town, and the husband's withdrawn regard

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; the second person நின்மேலது names the hero

reading: The wife tells the other women not to embrace the lord of the town of loud waters, where the flood crowds in, to the full end of love, nor to pine for him in folly; let them too speak so that their endless longing may leave them.
nuance: நீயிரும், 'you too', puts the rivals in the wife's own case: they will be left as she was, so her warning is half scorn and half fellow-feeling.

thinai_evidence.note: the river town and the husband's other women

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; the plural imperatives (முயங்கல்மின், ஏங்கல்மின்) and நீயிரும் address the other women

reading: The wife says the lord of the town of honey-scented ponds among the fields, letting their flower-eyed son trample and kick him here, praises her slackened breast, while he is the one who presses the budding breasts of his young 'doll'.
nuance: தளர்முலை against வளர்முலை: the nursing mother's breast and the girl's rising breast meet in one line, and the domestic scene with the son is exposed as half of a double life. Reading பாவை as the young rival is a guess.

thinai_evidence.note: the field town and the husband's double life

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; speaker and addressee inferred

title: நெய்தல் 57-68
theme: Neythal: on the sea shore the heroine grieves the shore lord's absence and coldness, turning to the sea, the heron, the stork and the anril as fellow sufferers, witnesses or messengers (57, 60, 62-66), presses through her friend for marriage as her mother grows suspicious (58), waits for his chariot (59), is overwhelmed at the sight of him (67), and the friend reassures her of his love (61) and reproaches him with the paired crab (68).
source_issues: Verses 57 (இனி(து)), 58 (நின்னல்ல(து), இல்லென்(று)), 65 (துறைவற்(கு)) and 68 (நீக்கியிட்(டு)) print editorial brackets that restore elided letters; the restored readings were used.
Verse 62 line 2 reads ஏறிதிரைச் where the sense needs எறிதிரைச் (leaping waves); and the line break splits கொடுமை யறியாகொல் with a dash.
Verse 68 line 2 reads தனபெடை, likely தன் பெடை, and the clause of the crab has no finite verb; the sense 'with its mate' was taken.
