reading: The speaker says that the heart which has come to know the shore lord, of the bank where the roaming cold wind lifts the down of the white herons ranged along it, for a simple fool is itself a sweet thing, for is not the truth a gain to one's life?
nuance: The down that the wind picks up and carries off is the lightest thing on the shore, and the poem sets it beside a man the heart now judges light; only one correspondence can be named, so it is scene, not ullurai. The bitterness is turned into consolation: knowing the truth, however hard, is a gain.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore lord and the herons of the bank

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the speaker is taken to be the heroine, disillusioned with the man, and no addressee is named

reading: The heroine asks her friend what is to be done, since there is no kindness even in his eyes and her mother's face has turned the same way, and bids her tell the lord of the shore grove of golden-flowered punnai whether this is fitting, saying she has no one but him.
nuance: The mother's face has 'become that too' (அதுவாகும்): the secret is close to discovery at home just as the lover cools, so the plea that she has none but him is a push toward marriage.

reading: Taking the noise of birds for the bells of the swift horses of the shore lord, of the wide grove with its heaped sand dunes, the girl of the curved earrings rose and then turned back when she heard what it was, afraid that the people of the little hamlet would make talk of her.
nuance: Her turning back has two causes folded together: the sound was only birds, and going out to meet a chariot would give the hamlet its gossip; the waiting girl is caught between longing and the town's eyes.

reading: The friend tells the jewelled girl that the cool lord of the curved backwater, fragrant with neythal that meets the eye, is no longer his own master: holding it manliness to have been caught by her lovely smile, he comes on his well-made chariot.
nuance: கண்ணுறு நெய்தல் can be the neythal that meets the eye or the neythal like eyes; and the joke is that his manliness consists in being captured, so the friend reassures the girl by mocking him gently.

nuance: The heron was the one witness of the secret union, and her question accuses it of keeping silent; the waves that throw the sharks into confusion carry the cruelty she names, but only one correspondence is stated, so it is not ullurai.

nuance: The catch the fishermen laboured for is snatched while it dries, as her colour, won from her, was taken; only this one correspondence holds, so it stays scene, a near miss on ullurai condition 3.

nuance: மீன்தபு நீ turns the praise into reproach: the devoted parent is also a killer, as the man who seemed gentle proved cruel.

title: குறிஞ்சி 1-12
theme: Kurinji in the secret love: the girl's pallor, slipping bangles and wasting shoulders tell of the hill lord (1, 5, 7), her heart goes to him or pines bound by longing (3, 6), she wonders whether he will come or has turned from her (2, 9) and is sure he will come at midnight (10), while the friend comforts her (4), names him as the only cure (8), notes the house that keeps her (11) and warns of an angry kinsman's spear (12).
source_issues: 1-12: the core records carry no colophon thurai, so thurai_akam speaker, addressee and stage are inferred from the poems and occasion.words is null throughout.
1 line 2: எரியும் ('burns') makes poor sense of the doe on the slope; a form such as வெரூஉம் ('fears') or a verb of roaming may lie behind it.
3 line 1: அழிமுதுநீர் is obscure; line 3 பாசம்பட் டோ டும் has a stray space splitting டோ, read பாசம்பட்டோடும்.
8 line 2: largely lost (கி...க்...கொண்...கரும்); the description of the elephant and snake cannot be recovered and no comparison is read from it.
9 line 1: காந்தள ரும்புகை may divide as காந்தள் அரும்பு புகை (the bud as smoke) or அரும்பு உகை; the reading taken is the first.
11 line 4: அரிதுரைத்திவ் is hard to divide (அரிது உரைத்து இவ்); the sense that his coming to this house is hard is a guess.

reading: The friend says that on the slope by the millet field where parrots eager to feed are driven off and the matchless young doe moves, the girl's body wastes and turns pale, as if announcing that the lord of the forest land is the one who joined with her.
nuance: The pallor does the talking: the secret union is written on her body in a way the field-watch was meant to prevent, so the line works as a push toward marriage. இவன், 'this man', may point at the hero standing there, which is why the friend is taken as the speaker; the girl herself could equally be saying it.

thinai_evidence.note: the guarded millet field and the hill slope are kurinji ground

reading: The girl asks her friend whether the deceitful hill lord, from whose hill the waterfall carries sandalwood down so that the burnt clearing grows fragrant, will not come, for her heart comes trembling.
nuance: வஞ்ச, deceitful, sits right against the stream's kindness: the water brings sweetness to scorched ground unasked, while he, who scorched her, does not come.

thinai_evidence.note: sandal, the hill stream and the burnt millet clearing are kurinji things

iraicchi.act: the waterfall bears sandalwood down to the burnt clearing and makes it fragrant
iraicchi.sense: the hill's own stream heals the scorched field as the hero ought to come and soothe the girl he has left burning, so his absence is the deceit

reading: The girl says that her heart pines with longing for the lord of the hill of trap-stones, where by the green moss-grown spring the fierce female monkey, used to the place, tastes the fruit and, caught in the noose, runs.
nuance: பாசம் is both the hunter's noose and attachment, so the snared monkey and the 'bond' of love are one word. The subject of the running in line 3 is not certain; if it is not the monkey, the hidden comparison weakens to a mood.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill monkey, the mountain spring and the hill lord fix kurinji

ullurai.tenor: the girl herself, who tasted union and is now bound by longing

pairs.situation: she has tasted the sweetness of union with him
she is now caught in the bond of desire and cannot free herself

ullurai.speaker_fit: the girl uses a monkey of her own hill, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

reading: The friend asks the jewelled girl whether the hill lord, from whose hill the langur leaps off the sweet-fruited mango to take the pleasure of the tall jackfruit, is a man to join with her and then forget, he who assured her with words mixed with honey.
nuance: The friend's comfort carries a shadow: the langur that leaves one sweet tree for a sweeter one is the very fickleness she says he lacks. It is a single mood with no second pair and no stated situation, so it is not tagged as ullurai.

thinai_evidence.note: jackfruit and the langur of the hill trees are kurinji things

comparisons.tenor: his words of assurance

reading: The girl says that for the lord of the hill where the waterfall roars like a drum and the dark she-elephant comes tending a honeycomb loud with bees and full of sweet honey, her shoulders lie as though in hell.
nuance: Hell is a startling vehicle in a love quatrain and belongs to the later moral vocabulary of the didactic books. குரல் in line 1 may be the bees' hum or a millet ear, and the first two lines do not settle what the elephant carries.

thinai_evidence.note: the she-elephant, honey and the hill falls are kurinji things

comparisons.tenor: the roaring waterfall
the wasting of her shoulders

reading: The girl says that, unspoken, her heart goes to the jewelled broad chest of the faultless hill lord, from whose grove thick with trees the wild cow leaps and the famed young female monkey runs and leaps.
nuance: உகளும் is repeated for the wild cow and the monkey, and the heart's going is the third leap; the creatures carry a mood of unchecked movement only, so they are scene. உரையா, without telling, makes the heart a secret traveller, which is the whole of kalavu.

thinai_evidence.note: the wild cow, the monkey and the hill grove are kurinji things

reading: The girl says that when the friendship of the hill lord is spoken of, her bangles slip off: in his land the male monkey climbs the rock, stuffs the sweet ripe banana into its cheek in the daylight and runs off with a rush.
nuance: கேண்மை, friendship, is ironic after the picture of the monkey that grabs and bolts.

thinai_evidence.note: the male monkey, the plantain and the rock cliff are kurinji things

iraicchi.act: the male monkey takes the sweet fruit in its cheek and runs away at once
iraicchi.sense: the hero, like the monkey, took his pleasure and made off, which is why the mere mention of his friendship loosens her bangles

reading: The friend says that if the lord of the great rocky hill, where the black-trunked angry elephant and the dark snake are named in a line now partly lost, comes caring for the girl, the sickness she suffers will shrink.
nuance: The cure named is the man, not a rite: பேணி வரினே, if he comes cherishing her, reads as coming to wed. The addressee may be the hero, urged to marry, or the foster mother, told the true cause of the illness; the poem does not decide.

thinai_evidence.note: the angry elephant and the great rock hill are kurinji

reading: The girl asks her friend whether the lord of the good fruitful hill, where the angry elephant, taking the kaanthal's bud for smoke, lays its trunk between its raised tusks, looks to its herd and leaps up and flees, has grown averse to union with them.
nuance: The word division of line 1 is unsure (அரும்பு புகை, the bud as smoke, or அரும்பு உகை, the bud rising); the elephant's flight from a harmless flower is what the hidden comparison rests on.

thinai_evidence.note: the kaanthal and the hill elephant are kurinji things

comparisons.tenor: the red kaanthal bud, mistaken for fire

pairs.situation: he takes a harmless thing for a danger
he has fled from their union and stays away

ullurai.speaker_fit: the girl uses an elephant of her own hill, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

reading: The girl tells her friend that the lord of the hill whose millet fields are ringed by vengai with golden clusters will come right now at midnight, bearing a spear like lightning, so how could her eyelids close.
nuance: இமைபொரு, eyelids meeting, may mean she lies sleepless waiting or that only his coming lets her sleep; either way the midnight tryst is fixed in her mind before it happens.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill and the midnight tryst are kurinji's land and hour

comparisons.tenor: the vengai's flower clusters
his spear

reading: The friend asks whether the lord of the good hill bright with tender leaves, where the spotted peacock delights in scratching the ground a fierce boar has dug up, will come, since coming is hard for him to this house of theirs.
nuance: The peacock that takes its pleasure in ground the boar has turned is a picture of one creature enjoying another's labour; it has no single act a person of the situation does, so it stays scene. The house in line 4 suggests the girl is now kept indoors.

thinai_evidence.note: the boar, the peacock and the young leaves are kurinji things

reading: The friend warns that a man, angry, comes with a sharp spear in hand, asking whether the chest of that bright handsome one who wears fragrant naagam flowers mixed with fresh vengai blossoms in his hair can be ended.
nuance: Who the angry spearman is the poem does not say; he is most simply one of the girl's kin who has learned of the visits, and the warning is the friend's way of shutting the night path.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai and naagam flowers worn in the hair are the kurinji hero's

title: பாலை 13-24
theme: Paalai: the man's journey through the hot wasteland seen from home; the report of his going melts her eyes (13, 14), the road's killers and beasts make her fear for him (16, 23), omens of lizard and forehead promise his return (18, 19), and her heart follows him while the friend turns its swimming into his homecoming (21, 22). Five verses (14 to 17, 20) survive only in pieces.
source_issues: Verses 14, 15, 16, 17 and 20 have lost most of their lines (dotted gaps in the source); they are marked from what survives and flagged uncertain.
Verse 15: show flags that sangamtamil.com's text lacks lines 1 and 2, which are blank in ours too.
The colophons give no thurai for any verse of this chapter, so thurai_akam speakers are inferred from the verses and occasion words are null.

Verse 15 line 3 பல்லாருட்கண் divides two ways (பல்லார் உட்கு / பல்லார் உள் கண்); verse 18 line 2 ஏமாண் சிலையார்க்கும் is read as ஏ மாண் சிலை ஆர்க்கும் (the bow with fine arrows twangs), not as 'bowmen'; verse 23 line 4 தொலைவிலர் is ambiguous between unharmed and not far.

reading: The friend tells the man that when she heard him speak of leaving by the long wasteland, where travellers hurry among stone-ringed cairns and run at the whistle of the Eyinar loosing their bows, her eyes, shaped like split tender mango, went soft with tears.
nuance: Nothing has happened yet except talk: the eyes give way at செலவுரைப்ப, the telling of the journey, so the poem shows the parting doing its harm before the man has moved. The first line is hard to construe (who hurries and harries the path), and the speaker is not named; the friend reporting to the man is the likeliest frame.

thinai_evidence.note: the eyes melt at the mere report of a journey through the wasteland

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, long and pointed like a split tender mango

reading: Only fragments survive: fierce dogs give chase, something blossoms, and when the journey through the hot forest where the bushes have withered is spoken of, something will not stay; the end is lost.
nuance: போக்குரைப்ப repeats the situation of verse 13 (செலவுரைப்ப), so the poem probably turned on her response to the news of his going; நில்லா may have described her tears or her strength failing, but the lines that would say so are lost. The speaker is a guess from verse 13.

thinai_evidence.note: the report of a going through the hot forest

reading: Only the last lines survive: the one who went has crossed the hot forest of fierce sunrays, a place many dread (or: in a company of many), and a hill of crooked rocks is named before the text breaks off.
nuance: பல்லாருட்கண் can be divided as பல்லார் உட்கு (what many fear) or பல்லார் உள் கண் (among many), and the choice decides whether the line is about danger or company. The speaker is a guess.

thinai_evidence.note: the sun-scorched forest the man has crossed

reading: Of a damaged verse, what remains says that in the wasteland the fierce tiger brings down the charging elephant, and that 'our man' is somewhere in the lost close.
nuance: The tiger felling the elephant is the danger of the road at its most extreme: even the strongest beast is prey there, which is what makes the absent man's safety a question. Whether the lost close feared for him or promised his return cannot be told.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's road through a wasteland of killing beasts

reading: The stony wasteland where the wild gaur flee is named, with a young dark she-elephant and a tusker, and then the tears within kohl-lined eyes; the rest is lost.
nuance: A she-elephant and a tusker named together is where Sangam paalai often places a pair of creatures acting for each other, the textbook iraicchi; here the line breaks at மரு.... and no act survives, so the pair stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the stony wasteland and the eyes' tears

reading: The friend tells the woman that in the hard way among lovely hills, where wild cattle low and herds of beasts flee when the bow with its fine arrows twangs, the truthful-mouthed lizard has chirped as if it has seen the one who went through that graceless hot waste coming home.
nuance: வாய்மாண்ட praises the lizard's mouth as truthful, so the chirp is offered as testimony rather than hope; the verb கண்டு even gives the lizard eyes, as though it had seen the return before anyone at home. The hill with its lowing wild cattle is a kurinji scene set on the paalai road.

thinai_evidence.note: the man away on the hot waste and the omen of his return

reading: The friend tells the woman that the man who went for much wealth through the gravel forest, where the fierce proud tusker goes to stand asleep in the thin, broken shade of the lac-laden omai tree, will come back: the brightness climbing again onto her forehead says so.
nuance: The proof is in her own body: the pallor is receding before he arrives, and the friend reads the returning light (இவர்ந்து ஏறும், climbing up) as a sign, not as an effect of his coming. The tusker sleeping upright in shade too broken to cool it is how the forest's heat is shown; it does nothing a lover does, so it is scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the man gone through the gravel forest for wealth

reading: A damaged verse: something is made to fall, the one who went has crossed the ceaseless hot forest, and the surviving close says that our man will come.
nuance: வருவார் நமர் closes the verse with the promise verse 19 makes (வருவர்), so the speaker is probably the comforting friend, but the lost lines may have held the reason she gives.

thinai_evidence.note: the man crossing the hot forest, and the promise of his coming

reading: The woman tells her friend of young lifted breasts and moist teeth that, as the owl begins its short hooting and our man has crossed the forest where the rays burn and scorch, her heart goes after him, swimming the long way.
nuance: The dry forest is crossed by swimming: the heart moves through the scorched land as if through water, so the metaphor carries the effort and the danger of drowning into a waterless place. The owl's short cry marks the night falling as she speaks.

thinai_evidence.note: her heart following the man across the burning forest

comparisons.tenor: her heart crossing the long distance to him, as one swims a flood

reading: The friend asks the woman of bright jewels whether she really thinks the heart of the man who crossed the forest where robbers roam has parted from her, and says that he will cross back over the old mountain clefts and they will soon see him come.
nuance: Line 2 can also be read as a statement, 'you know he parted from you in mind (by his own resolve)', which would make the comfort harder; the question reading fits the confident close. The friend uses the same verb of swimming that the woman used of her heart in verse 21, now for the man's crossing home.

thinai_evidence.note: the man gone through the robber-haunted forest

comparisons.tenor: the man crossing the mountain clefts on his way home

reading: The woman asks her friend whether the man who went in this very season, through the hot forest of rustling leaves where men with cruel arrows and twanging bows, their hearts empty of thought, run like Death with bows bent on killing, has come to no harm.
nuance: தொலைவிலர்கொல் turns on தொலைவு: as ruin it asks whether he is unharmed; as distance it asks whether he is not far away now, i.e. near home. The fear of the archers favours the first. சிந்தியா நெஞ்சு, hearts that do not think, makes the killers' danger their thoughtlessness rather than malice.

thinai_evidence.note: the man gone this season through the killers' forest

comparisons.tenor: the archers who run with killing bows

reading: The woman tells her friend of chosen bangles that the road taken by the loveless one is, they say, the graceless, hard waste where, on the burning track as the mirage runs, the deer of the wilderness, craving, takes it in its mind for water and runs on without end.
nuance: The deer that runs forever after false water is close to the man who left for gain, but the poem draws no second correspondence and does not apply it, so it fails the two-pair condition of ullurai and stays scene; a reader may still hear it. பண்பில் (graceless) of the road and நண்பிலார் (loveless) of the man are set in one rhyme, so the land's want of kindness becomes his. The speaker could also be the friend, since ஆய்தொடி usually addresses the heroine.

thinai_evidence.note: the hard waste the loveless man took

title: முல்லை 25-36
theme: The mullai section of the Kainnilai (25-36, Pullankadanar), much of it lost in the manuscripts: in the rains the friend shows the waiting heroine the mullai's teeth, the red thonri, the stag with his doe and the plumed horses he will yoke as proof he will come; the heroine's evening, with the cowherds entering the common and blowing their pipes, brings pallor; in 34 he has come.
source_issues: Kainnilai 26-35 are damaged in the source: 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32 and 35 have whole lines with no Tamil letters, and 26, 33, 34 and 35 have broken lines; readings cover only what survives and every damaged verse is marked uncertain.
Kainnilai 32 line 3: 'லக மெழுநெஞ்சே' begins mid-word; the vocative may be 'எழு நெஞ்சே' (rise, heart), which would change the speaker.
Kainnilai 35: the site's text lacks lines 1 and 2 (flag site_diff); line 4 ends after அரித.
Kainnilai 36 line 4: இடபம் is obscure in sense.

reading: The friend tells the heroine of wide sword-bright eyes that in the woodland the rains have made, the creeping mullai has grown lovely and put out sharp teeth as its shoots bud, so their lover will surely come: let her not take on this grieving, pallid sickness.
nuance: The buds are the creeper's teeth, so the woodland already smiles; the friend's argument is that the season has kept its side of the promise and the sickness (பைதல்நோய்) has no ground left. ஓரும் is an expletive of assurance, not a verb.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-made woodland and the mullai in bud

comparisons.tenor: the pointed white mullai buds, as sharp teeth
the heroine's eyes, bright and long as a sword

reading: The friend tells the heroine of gold-like colour that, now the blood-red thonri puts out its sharp buds, so red that a bird climbing the pidavam shies from them as from blazing fire, it is unlikely he will fail to come.
nuance: Line 2 opens with a gap, so who takes the buds for what is partly guessed: சேவல் என may mean the creature takes the red bud for a cock's comb before shying from it as fire. அரிது ... வாரா விடல் is a double negative: his not coming is the hard thing.

thinai_evidence.note: the thonri and pidavam bloom in the rains

comparisons.tenor: the thonri flower, red as blood
the red thonri buds, which a bird shies from as from fire
the heroine's colour

reading: In the evening the rains bring, when something now lost comes in swaying, pallor spreads over her body as she thinks of the coming of the man who was one with her.

theme: The marutham decade of the wife against the bard: she bars the go-between and the man (37, 38, 46, 47), mocks the husband as a dancer worked by others (42), sets the son as her own against the bard's praise and against the man's use of the boy to gain entry (39, 41), weighs her age against his old promises (45, 48), and hears the other women's boasts and the town's gossip of his affair (40, 43, 44).

title: நெய்தல் 49-60
theme: Neythal on the Pandya's shore: the heroine wastes in the shore lord's absence (49, 53, 58), turns from him to the stork that saw his oath (50), sends his envoy-bird away (51), recalls the drying-ground where he lied and took her beauty (54, 56), faces the mother's confinement that ends the night meetings (52, 59), is warned her bangles will slip if he leaves unembraced (55), and sees her pallor lift as his chariot comes (60).
source_issues: 49-60: the source heads these verses பாலை; the work's order and the shore scenes make them நெய்தல், as the colophon field already gives.
49 line 3: பாவாரம் சேர்ப்பதற்கு is likely corrupt; the sense wants சேர்ப்பற்கு, 'to the shore lord'.
51 line 2: part of the line is lost (dots in the source), between உண்டிறந்து and ம்மருளோ.
57: the four lines have no finite verb; a line may be missing or the verse is a fragment.

reading: The heroine bids someone go and tell the lord of the cool sea, where ships ply over the great waves and heaps of prawns lie noisily piled, how she has wasted away with love-sickness, and not to spare him the telling.
nuance: Line 3's பாவாரம் சேர்ப்பதற்கு is obscure; the sense needs சேர்ப்பற்கு, 'to the shore lord', as in 51 and 52, and ஓவா கலந்தார்க்கு (to the one who joined without ceasing) is read with it. The ships that never stop plying are set beside a man who has stopped coming.

title: களவழி நாற்பது 1-20
theme: The first twenty stanzas of Poigaiyar's Kalavazhi Narpathu: each paints one sight of the field where the Chola Sengan killed his enemies, elephants, blood, broken drums and scavengers, each in a single simile drawn mostly from hills, sea, rain and the farmer's tank, and each closes on the same refrain of the field where he killed.
source_issues: 1-20: the core record gives no thinai or thurai for any verse; all are marked vaakai here (Tholkappiyam places களவழி among the thurais of vaakai), and puram_thurai is empty.
1 line 3: முன்பசு லெல்லாம் is a misprint for முன்பகல் எல்லாம் (the variant reads முற்பகல்); the line is otherwise clear.
9 line 3: சுறபிறழ்வ is a misprint for சுறாப் பிறழ்வ; the printed variant runs the words together (இருங்கடலுணீலச்சுறாப்பிறழ்வ).
12 line 3: போன்றவெ for போன்றவே, as the misprint_candidate flag notes (tamilvu: போன்றனவே).
15 line 3: பள்ளிறிய் றோன்றும் is garbled; read as பள்ளியிற் றோன்றும்.
17: only four lines; tamilvu has five, and the missing line is most likely the one naming the king (its line 4 repeats verse 2's last line).
18 line 3: தார்ச்சே(ய்) carries the editor's bracketed letter; the variant தடற்றிலங்கொள்வாள் changes the sword phrase.
19 line 1: printed without word spaces (இடைமருப்பின்விட்டெறிந்தவெஃகங்கான் மூழ்திக்); மூழ்திக் is a misprint for மூழ்கிக், and the variant gives காழ் for கான்.

reading: On the field where the lord of the river country killed those who had wronged him, the blood of the fallen, deep enough to swallow swords, is churned by elephants until feet sink in it, lies as mud through the morning of the battle that met the rising sun, and by afternoon rises as dust red as coral.
nuance: The poem measures the slaughter by a single day: the same blood is mud in the forenoon and coral-coloured dust after noon, so the field's horror is shown through time rather than numbers. Line 3's முன்பசுல் is a misprint; the printed variant reads முற்பகல்.

nuance: The vehicle comes from the farmer's year, the full tank after the rains and its sluice, the same world that gives the genre its name of the threshing floor; the burst drum becomes the sluice pipe and the heaped elephants the bund.

nuance: The dead elephant becomes a staff for the living: the tusk that killed is now what a slipping soldier leans on to stand. The printed variant in line 2 reads எழூஉம் for எழுவர்.

title: களவழி நாற்பது 21-41
theme: Poykaiyar's battlefield of the Chola Senganan, the red-eyed wrathful Maal, lord of the Kaveri's watered land: each poem fixes one sight of the field in a simile, mostly of falling elephants (sinking mountains, snakes struck by thunder, a god's ploughing), with severed limbs, umbrellas and drums, the wailing kin, the taking of Kalumalam and the killing of the Vanji king, and each ends on the field where he killed his foes.
source_issues: 21-41: the core records carry no colophon thinai or thurai; every poem is marked vaakai here as a kalavazhi (the battlefield sung after victory), so puram_thurai is empty throughout.
22 line 4: நக்கும்பரம் பொக்குமே does not parse; read as நக்கும் பாம்பு ஒக்குமே (a snake licking the moon).
24 line 3: our text புக்கேற்ற has no comparison marker; tamilvu reads புக்கற்றே, which supplies one. Marked as juxtaposition and uncertain.
28: the creature that carries off the severed hand (இகலன், line 4) is not identified with confidence; Project Madurai's variant keys give ஓரி and other readings.
40 line 3: போர்த்தானைடச் carries a stray ட; read போர்த்தானைச்.
41: printed without a number and numbered 41 by its place; the site lacks it, and its lines 4-5 repeat 22 lines 5-6 (பாய்ப்புன / பாய்புன).
25 line 4 repeats 27 line 4 and 36 line 5 (புனனாடன் மேவாரை யட்ட களத்து), the book's refrain.
21 line 1 (மருமத்து), 27 line 3 (பூநீர் வியன்றமிடா), 30 line 3 (மடங்கா), 32 lines 1-2: the flags and variants show competing readings; the sense marked does not turn on them except at 27.

reading: Elephants with paired spears sunk in their chests and their wounds deepening, swaying under the arrows, with nothing to lean on and their old strength gone, stagger slowly like mountains whose footing the ground swallows, on the field where the red-eyed, wrathful Maal fought.
nuance: The mountain does not fall; the ground takes its foot (நிலம் கால் கவரும்), so the image is of slow subsidence, not collapse: the elephant goes down by degrees. செங்கண் சினமால், 'the red-eyed wrathful Maal', is the king's epithet that recurs through the book.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the field where the king killed his foes, the victory the kalavazhi celebrates

reading: Under umbrellas fallen to the ground, the trunks of the stately elephants with lined brows, cut through by the flashing swords of warriors who do not flee, lie across the umbrellas like a snake licking the bright crescent moon, on the field where the lord of the land of rushing water, with his thunderous drum, killed those who would not join him.
nuance: The white umbrella is the moon and the cut trunk the snake that swallows it at an eclipse, so the fallen umbrella, the sign of a king, is shown eclipsed. The snake rests on an emendation: the line prints நக்கும்பரம் பொக்குமே, read here as நக்கும் பாம்பு ஒக்குமே.

reading: Like vaalai fish leaping here and there among the water-lilies wherever the water rushes from a burst tank, the bright swords with their fine shining blades flash and spread, on the field where Chempiyan, of the horses with trimmed manes and the strong flagged chariots, killed his enemies.

title: முல்லை 1-20 (1/2)
theme: The friend shows the waiting wife the rainy season he promised to return by, reading cloud, lightning, thunder and the flowers of the mullai woodland as proof that he will come (1-18); then the man, his king's work done, turns home (19-20).
source_issues: 19, 20: the colophon reads வினைமுற்றிய தலைமகள் பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது, but both verses are the returning man's speech to his charioteer (19: his heart goes to the woman with bangles; 20: the king's work is done); தலைமகன் is meant.
1 line 2: தீம்பொழல் is not a known word; தீம்பெயல், sweet rain, fits the sense (the variant gives வீழ for தாழ).
8 line 2: வால்கூறும் reads as a misprint for வரல்கூறும் (compare 9 line 3 and 11 line 2); line 4 நுண்ணுரும் பூழ்த்த is probably நுண்ணரும்பு ஊழ்த்த, fine buds opened.
9 line 1: உருவினை names no clear flower; the flower likened to eyes may be கருவிளை; the verse is marked uncertain.
13 line 2: கூந்தல வனப்பின் is hard to construe with காதலர் in line 1 (whose hair is meant is unclear); the variant ஏமாந்த for ஏமார்ந்த changes the lover's epithet.
15 line 3: திருந்தின் repeats line 1's திருந்தி and does not parse; the sense is taken from இளிவண்டு பாட.
16 line 4: பழங்கூண் is unclear (perhaps பழங்கண்); the sense that the pallor will fade is a guess, and the verse is marked uncertain.

reading: The friend says that the man who promised 'we will come' when the rainbow lay across the sky like the garland on the chest of Mal, the god coloured like the warring sea, and sweet rain hung low, can hardly fail to come now that the sky, its clouds massed, roars and pours.
nuance: The question வாரார்கொல் ('will he not come?') is reassurance put as a doubt, and the promise is quoted in his own word, வருதும். The mullai god Mal lends the rainbow his garland, so the season he swore by arrives with a sacred sign.

title: முல்லை 21-40 (2/2)
theme: The second half of the rains: the man, his work done, tells his charioteer and his heart that the flowering woodland calls him home (21, 22, 24, 28-33, 36), while the friend alternately shows the waiting wife the season as proof he will come and lets her own distress, or his broken word, show (23, 25-27, 34, 35, 37-40).
source_issues: 21, 22, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33 (and 24, 36): the colophons read வினைமுற்றிய தலைமகள் (36: வினைமுற்றி மீளுந் தலைமகள்), but each verse is the returning man speaking to his charioteer or his heart; தலைமகன் is meant.
21 line 3: மழைந்தடங்கட் reads as a misprint for மழைத்தடங்கட், cool wide eyes (compare 36 line 3, மழைமதர்க்கட்).
24 line 3: பணிநோனாள் is taken as பனி நோனாள் (cannot bear the cold); the sense is unsure and the verse is marked uncertain. Line 1 கிடப்ப sits uneasily with the colophon's வினைமுற்றிய.
29 line 4: கரம் reads as a misprint for சுரம், the road (compare 28 line 3, சுரநெஞ்சே); பகைகொண்டல் is split across lines 2 and 3.
30: the verse ends on the participle உரைத்து and its construction is incomplete; marked uncertain.
32 line 4: பிடாஅப் பெருந்தகை நற்கு is hard to construe (whether பெருந்தகை is the man or the woman is unclear); marked uncertain.
33 line 2: பிறைக்கும் is not clear (the variant gives பிறக்கும்); marked uncertain.
37 line 2: இயுர்க்கும் is not a known form; the sense 'pours' is taken from context.
39 line 3: மேர்க்கடி is read as ஏர்க்கடி, the start of ploughing; the line's sense is uncertain.
40 line 3: இந்தின் (of the indu) is a rare plant name; the variant களிவண்ணம் changes the colour word.

nuance: The usual simile runs from woman to flower (teeth like jasmine buds); here it runs from flower to woman, so every bud on the road home already shows him her mouth.

reading: The friend says that now the men wearing the green leaves of the dark-clustered nochchi, whose buds have opened like crabs' eyes, have begun ploughing the wide dry fields, he has become the great talk of our town.
nuance: கௌவை, the town's talk, is turned on him rather than on her: it is he who has become the byword for a broken promise. The crab is a shore creature borrowed as an image for a mullai bush.

reading: The friend says that for the woman who grieved that the signs he set had come but he had not, the lovely sky has taken on the dark colour of the indu and become the medicine to end her sickness: the brow of my simple girl will regain its brightness.
nuance: The sky does not bring him; it is itself the cure, because its dark colour proves the season and so his return. The first line repeats verse 25's despairing thought word for word, now as the thing the sky answers.

title: குறிஞ்சி 1-16 (1/2)
theme: Kurinji of the secret love in Kanimedaviyar's quatrains: the hunter's pretext question at the millet field and his confession of it (1, 8, 9), the girl seen on the platform (3, 4), the friend forbidding the night path for its elephants, tigers, snakes and gods (6, 7, 10, 11, 13), the ripening millet that ends the meetings (5), the friend's disclosure of the elephant and flood rescues to the household (2, 12, 14), her plea against a bride price (15), and the lover's madal (16).
source_issues: 1-16: the core records carry no colophon thurai, so thurai_akam speaker, addressee and stage are inferred from the poems and occasion.words is null throughout.

reading: The man asks the long-haired girls, whose bright faces are like lotuses facing the crescent moon, whether they have not seen an arrow-struck deer come this way into the millet field sown in good time with the first rain on a slope cleared of fragrant sandal.
nuance: The question about the wounded deer is the conventional pretext of the hunter who comes to the field; the praise packed into the address (crescent brow over lotus face) shows that the real question is not about the deer. The plural address (தாழ்குழலீர்) takes in the heroine and her friend together.

thinai_evidence.note: a millet field cut out of sandal forest is the kurinji clearing

comparisons.tenor: the girls' faces under brows like the crescent

reading: The friend says there is a man who gathered sulli, pool lilies, sobhalika and asoka flowers, sorted them and set them on the girl's hair, and who with a blunt arrow drove off the wet-musth elephant that the shouts from the platform could not turn away.
nuance: Two acts make the claim: he dressed her hair, which only a husband or one who means to be one does, and he saved her from the elephant. Said to the household, it is the friend's disclosure of the secret love (அறத்தொடு நிற்றல்), and the bare 'there is one' (உளன்) leaves the elders to ask who.

thinai_evidence.note: pool lilies, the field platform and the wild elephant are kurinji things

reading: On the slope where sandal trees were cut down and the ground ploughed for small millet, on the platform built of the cut sandal, the girl like a dark peacock, fragrant with sandal paste, scares off the parrots, and her shouts ring until the parrots cry out.
nuance: The word சாந்தம் comes three times with three senses: the felled tree, the platform built from it, and the paste on her body, so the field's whole history is carried on her skin. Line 4 is hard: whether the parrots cry out or the girl's cry is meant is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet slope and the parrot-scaring girl are kurinji

comparisons.tenor: the girl on the platform

reading: The man says he cannot see her, who is like the Koodal of Maran of unswerving fame, even among the greens of the field, and wonders whether the hair of her with a waist like a slender branch has gone into the vessels of kings whose dark killing spears never fail in battle.
nuance: The kings of line 3 may be rival suitors who have come with gifts for her, so that her not being seen means she is being given elsewhere; the Pandya's city as the measure of her beauty brings puram fame into the field.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem gives no land beyond the field greens; the book's heading places it in kurinji

comparisons.tenor: the girl
her slender waist

reading: The friend tells the peacock-like girl of dark wide eyes that the millet in the plots has ripened before long, as wealth ripens when deeds ripen, and bids her see how this parts them as a hand jerks back from fire.
nuance: Comparing the ripening millet to the ripening of past deeds into wealth makes the harvest a fate no one can hurry or delay: the end of the field-watch, and so of the meetings, arrives on its own schedule. Line 2 (பனைவிளைவு) and the fire image of line 4 are hard to fix.

thinai_evidence.note: the ripening millet in its plots is the kurinji field's clock

comparisons.tenor: the millet ripening in its plots
the girl
the lovers parted by the harvest

reading: The friend bids the lord of the great dark hill, where the waterfall looks like the hill spitting out a fine blue cloth, to listen and judge for himself whether she of spear-sharp eyes that put the blue lily to shame can be at ease while he comes through the thick dark.
nuance: The friend puts the judgement on him (நீ ஆய்): the danger of the dark path is argued through her fear for him, not his own. The repeated மானீல / மாநீலம் plays the blue of the hill against the blue of the lily her eyes outdo. ஆயுமோ is read as 'will she be at ease'.

thinai_evidence.note: the great hill and the night visit mark kurinji's midnight tryst

comparisons.tenor: the waterfall on the hill
her eyes

reading: The friend tells the lord of the good hill, on whose flowered pepper slopes the long tiger prowls the path watching the elephant, that if he comes by night the daughter of the lord of the good hill will not live.
nuance: The same phrase நன்மலை நாட(ன்) names the lover in line 3 and the girl's father in line 4, setting the two men side by side as equals: the night visit endangers a match that could be made openly. The tiger lying in wait on the path carries the danger as a mood; it does no act of a person of the love, so it is scene, not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: pepper slopes, tiger and elephant are kurinji things

reading: Looking at the girls at the fields, the man says that one guards the mountain rice and this one the red millet, and wonders whether the love god has given this one his five arrows twice over: what else could it be, when Kaman's arrows are in her eyes.
nuance: The count is the joke: Kaman has five arrows, and she, with two eyes, seems to carry ten. Line 3 is obscure and the sense of 'five twice' is a reading.

thinai_evidence.note: mountain rice and red millet fields are kurinji

comparisons.tenor: her two eyes

reading: The man says he went alone and unprotected, asking after a beast in a way that was nothing but a ruse, and the girl of flowered hair who took his heart with her beauty, that day among her good companions, took his strength and took its place.
nuance: The hero names his own pretext as deceit (வஞ்சமே), and the trickster is the one caught: he went to take and was taken. Line 4 (வலங்கொண்டாள் கொண்டாள் இடம்) may also be a play on right and left, she who went round him to the right took the left, his heart's side.

thinai_evidence.note: the hunter's pretext at the field belongs to kurinji's first meeting

reading: The friend tells the lord of the hill, where the pregnant female monkey with black fingers, red face and white teeth scatters the green pool's water with her thick fingers and reaches for the honey dripping on the great rock, not to come by the path where the sky gods roam.
nuance: The monkey's sprinkling of water and raising of hands toward the honey look like worship at a sacred hill, which prepares the closing danger of divine beings on the path. A pregnant creature craving honey may hint at the household he should give her, but it fails the act condition for iraicchi, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill monkey, the pool and the rock honey are kurinji

reading: The friend tells the lord of the rich, open hill of rocky falls that, strong as he is with his mighty bow and coming alone, the paths by night are very hard to travel, and he must not come where the musth-streaming elephant meets him.
nuance: She grants his strength before refusing him: the bow does not answer the danger, because he comes alone (ஒரு நீ). கரவில் 'without hiding' may glance at the secrecy he keeps, set against his open hill.

thinai_evidence.note: rocky falls, night paths and the wild elephant are kurinji

reading: The friend says: let the diviner go, set the kid free, give the toddy to the children; by her nature the blameless girl will not offer her shoulders, round as the tall palm, to anyone but the man who swam the fierce flood and set her on the bank.
nuance: The friend stops the rite by naming its true cause: the girl is not possessed but promised, by her own choice, to the man who saved her from the flood. The rescue gives the claim its warrant before the household. பனை is probably பணை (bamboo), the usual vehicle for shoulders.

thinai_evidence.note: the diviner's rite with the kid is kurinji's veri

comparisons.tenor: her shoulders

reading: The friend tells the man that their little village lies inside the hills that crowd round it on every side as if they were one hill, and that within those hills are five-hooded snakes and, all around, a forest where elephants gather.
nuance: Read as 'snake' and 'elephant' (ஐவாய் நாகம், கைவாய் நாகம்), the two closing lines set a creature that strikes inside the hills against one that roams outside them, so every way in is guarded. The reading depends on emending நாதும் to நாகும்.

thinai_evidence.note: a hill-ringed village in the forest is kurinji

comparisons.tenor: the many hills ringing the village

reading: The friend says that when the girl and she were sitting high on the platform in the rich hill of jackfruit and a huge musth elephant came, a man drove it off, and no one but him shall touch her friend's shoulders.
nuance: The friend puts herself in the scene (மாதரும் யானும்), so she speaks as witness to the rescue: her testimony is what makes the claim binding on the household. பருக்கை in line 2 is uncertain; the sense does not turn on it.

thinai_evidence.note: jackfruit hill, field platform and elephant are kurinji

reading: The friend tells the girl's kin that unless they receive the steadfast elders when they come and give her without wavering, not even the whole sea-girt world would be price enough for her unfailing beauty and her breasts.
nuance: The argument turns the bride price inside out: since nothing could buy her, she can only be given, and the giving is the rite with the suitor's elders (சான்றோர்) received at the door. கோடா / கோடாது is played twice, the kin must not swerve, and her beauty does not.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem has no landscape; its pressure for the wedding follows the kurinji sequence

reading: The man says he will not go until she of the wet hair fragrant with fresh naagam flowers grants him her ornamented breast; he has said 'her ornamented breast': is there a second way? And he has taken his stand on the palmyra horse in the middle of the street.
nuance: The repeated பூண் ஆகம் makes his demand a single, fixed word that he will not trade; 'is there a second?' closes off any other remedy, so mounting the madal in the street is the only one left.

thinai_evidence.note: the madal threat belongs to the kurinji lover refused

title: குறிஞ்சி 17-31 (2/2)
theme: The kurinji courtship's second half: the man's pleas, in which the girl's eyes are spears and arrows and her family hunters and clearers of the hill (17, 19, 21-23, 30); the friend's refusals and warnings, of leaf-garment and night visit, with the vengai that is both gold-flowered tree and tiger (20, 24-26, 28); and the end of the field-watch, the harvest, the mother's guard and the push to marry (18, 27, 29, 31).

reading: The man tells the friend that he knows the girl with the slender waist, fears it will snap if she walks even a little, and, finding no moment when she grants him even a little kindness, his heart melts and sways wherever she sways.
nuance: The verse turns on ஒல்கு: she sways as she walks, and his heart sways with her, so his surrender copies her gait. Her fragility is praise, and the fear that her waist will break is his own helplessness projected onto her.

thinai_evidence.note: a man pleading for a girl's favour before any union is the kurinji situation of courtship

reading: The speaker asks what will become of it: the peerless young vengai, turning gold, has announced the day, the spear-bearing kin have settled on what they will do, and now the millet field will be stubble, and with it the bond with the hill lord.
nuance: The vengai's flowering was the sign for the harvest, and once the millet is cut the girl no longer goes out to guard it; so the young tree 'announcing the day' is the clock that ends the secret meetings. மருவியா மாலை may be 'the evening not shared' or 'the garland not worn'.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai's bloom and the millet field fix the field-watch of kurinji

comparisons.tenor: the vengai in bloom

reading: The man says that the eyes of the girl who, after leaping and bathing in a white fall like milk, guards the mountain rice that looks strewn with many flowers, entered his heart like a spear; will they ever let it go? He aches for the gentle one who will not let herself be seen.
nuance: Three likenesses with the same marker build the scene from the outside in: the fall, the field, and then the eye, which ends inside him. The girl is busy guarding a field, yet it is he who is overrun.

thinai_evidence.note: the waterfall and the mountain rice the girl watches are kurinji things

comparisons.tenor: the white waterfall
the field of mountain rice
her eyes entering his heart

reading: The friend tells the lord of the good hill, where the vengai yields gold on its day, that her brothers are cruel like killing tigers and the mother too is a tiger, so they cannot take his rare leaf-garment; what excuse will come easy tomorrow?
nuance: The verse plays on வேங்கை, the gold-flowering kino tree of line 1 and the killing tiger of lines 2 and 3: the same word that gives the hill its beauty gives the family its menace. Refusing the leaf-garment is refusing the suit for now; 'tomorrow' hints that refusal cannot go on.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai, the hill and the leaf-garment offered are the kurinji courtship

comparisons.tenor: her brothers
the mother
the vengai blossoms

reading: The girl whose body puts gold to shame has soft breasts with flower-like spots that swelled as he wasted, the man complains, calling it a wrong; since she does not fade at his fading he cannot bear it, while the kohl-eyed girl, though vexed, does not fade.
nuance: The symmetry is the point: her body grows as his shrinks, so her ripening looks to him like a theft from his own body. Who speaks lines 3 and 4 is unclear; read as the friend reporting his complaint, the last line turns it gently against the girl.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover wasting while the girl ripens belongs to courtship before union

comparisons.tenor: her body

reading: The man tells the girl that her rich brothers gather the white tusks of killing elephants and the skins of strong killing tigers, bringing each beast down with a single arrow, but she today has shot him with two arrows so that he cannot leave.
nuance: One arrow against two: the brothers' skill is real, but she needs twice their shots to bring him down and still he does not go. ஈரம்பு can also be heard as 'a moist arrow', the wet bright eye.

thinai_evidence.note: the elephant and tiger hunted by her hill kin place it in kurinji

comparisons.tenor: her two eyes

reading: The man says that for the lovely breasts of the sister of men who search the great hills, take their fill of honey and then carelessly ruin what was hard to reach, he is one fit to lose his shame, his good looks and his standing, melting away.
nuance: The brothers take the honey and destroy what held it; the poem sets that beside the man's own ruin by their sister, so he feels himself used and spent the same way. அருமலை is hard: 'the hard-to-reach hill' or the hive on it.

thinai_evidence.note: honey-gathering on the great hills is the hill people's work

comparisons.tenor: the girl's undoing of the man

reading: The friend tells the man to consider whether the sister of men who, wanting only what they want, cut down fragrant cool thakaram and vakulam as if they were worthless bush and plough the ground to sow red millet could ever grieve and pine for another's pain.
nuance: The friend turns the family's farming into a character sketch: people who fell fragrance for grain do not keep pity for an outsider's pain. Read as the man's own complaint, the verse would be a lover's bitterness rather than a refusal; the speaker is inferred.

thinai_evidence.note: clearing the slope for red millet is the hill farmers' work of kurinji

comparisons.tenor: the fragrant trees they fell

reading: The friend tells the man that the gentle girl with eyes like dread spears trembles, like an elephant of killing nature that has escaped the grip of the curve-striped tiger and goes looking for its own good herd; let him not come by night bearing his guarding spear.
nuance: The simile gives the girl the elephant's state after danger, still shaking as it looks for safety: her fear outlasts each of his visits. His spear, ஏமவேல், is meant to protect, but it cannot protect her from fearing for him.

thinai_evidence.note: the elephant and the tiger of the slope are kurinji beasts

comparisons.tenor: the girl trembling for the night visitor
the girl's eyes

reading: The friend tells the man that on the cloud-fed slope the flowers the dark-trunked young vengai has dropped look like a big-pawed strong tiger, and if he comes by night she whose soft grace is set off by her jewels will not live.
nuance: Again the two வேங்கை: the tree's spotted heap of flowers looks like the tiger of the same name, so even a false tiger is enough to kill the girl with fear for him. The danger is in her mind, not on the path, and that is the friend's argument.

thinai_evidence.note: the slope and the night visit are kurinji's place and hour

comparisons.tenor: the fallen vengai flowers

reading: The friend tells the lord of the good fruitful hill with tall vengai on its misty peaks that she speaks to urge him to marry now: when he came, relying on one who stood in the hill, mother saw him, and, displeased, she has angrily set a watch on the girl.
nuance: The friend's 'now' (இனி) has a cause: the secret is out to the mother and the girl is kept in, so the only way left to meet her is marriage. முனிவரையுள் நின்றான் is obscure: a god of the hill whom he trusted, or a man who stood guard.

thinai_evidence.note: the misty peak and fruitful hill are the kurinji land

reading: Having seen the great wide eyes of the sister of men who cut down cloud-touching sandal, thimisu, hard-cored agil and the sky-high naagam and plough the ground, would any man who knew wander about this hill, the friend asks.
nuance: The list of precious trees felled without regret is a portrait of the brothers: what they do to sandal and agil they would do to a stranger. The question can also be heard as wonder at the man's daring, since he does wander the hill though he knows.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill trees felled for millet ploughing belong to kurinji

reading: The speaker points out the place: by the bed of milky varukkai jackfruit trees a long stretch of sand white as risen moonlight, and where the forest stream, swirling up, has cut a channel, a cool thicket of glory lilies hangs low and fills it with scent.
nuance: The verse is only a place, with no person named: read as the friend telling the man where to meet, every detail is a sign of shelter (low branches, scent, soft sand). The site's text lacks the first line, so this reading rests on our text alone.

thinai_evidence.note: jackfruit, forest stream and glory lily are kurinji things

comparisons.tenor: the white sand

reading: The man says that her kin, drawing a bow upon the moon and holding back the spear without thought, and holding her cheaply as one of their own, set the flower-haired girl here to guard the millet field, and so, without knowing it, set her to guard his heart.
nuance: The wit is in the double posting: the family sends her out to keep birds from the millet, and in doing so posts her over his heart, which she now holds. Line 1 is dense; the bow on the moon is most easily her brows on her face and the spear held back her eyes.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl set to guard the millet field is the kurinji field-watch

comparisons.tenor: her brows on her moon-like face

reading: The friend tells the girl that the lord of the cool slope brings leaves, never saying it is his own need but thinking only of hers; yet he does not come into the shade of the vengai whose gold is now thinning; what can he mean, this man like a killing tiger?
nuance: The friend praises his tact (he brings the gift as if it were her need, not his) and in the same breath worries: the vengai's blossoms are falling, the season of meeting is passing, and he keeps away. Calling him a tiger is praise of his strength and a hint that he is hard to read.

thinai_evidence.note: the leaf-garment and the vengai of the slope are kurinji courtship

comparisons.tenor: the man
