reading: The man says that the girl set to guard the drying fish that her brothers, knowing the fishing grounds of the cool backwater of blue lilies, scooped up with nets of fine thread, turns on him the look of her long, weapon-like eyes: the guarding is cruel, and it is he, not the fish, whom she holds.
nuance: The verb காப்பு plays on her task: she is set to guard the fish from birds, and the guard her eyes keep falls on the onlooker instead, so the shore chore becomes the first-sight scene. கடிபொல்லா is hard; 'the guarding is cruel' is the reading taken here.

thinai_evidence.note: the netted fish drying on the shore grove and the fishing kin are neythal things

comparisons.tenor: her long eyes, whose look wounds like a weapon

reading: The man says that seeing the white smile, like the pearls of the dark sea, of the sister of those who dive into the vast sea for the white conch without a thought for themselves, his heart has become like theirs, melting and wasting away.
nuance: The brothers neglect their lives diving for the sea's white conch; the speaker, drawn by the sea's other white thing in her smile, says he has become one of those who melt and waste, so the kin's trade and the lover's ruin are set side by side without a marker.

thinai_evidence.note: the conch-divers of the great sea are neythal people and things

comparisons.tenor: her white smile

reading: The friend tells the lord of the cool expanse, whose backwater sleeps with the lotus for its face and the great blue lily among cool leaves for its lovely eyes, that if he comes in the spreading dark he will find the girl of the hanging garland melting in tears, her eyes stretched wide along the way.
nuance: The backwater, given a lotus face and lily eyes, sleeps; the girl, whose own face and eyes those flowers stand for, does not. காணீர் can be read as 'you will see' or 'you will not see', which turns the line into a warning or a reproach.

thinai_evidence.note: the cool sea expanse and the night of waiting fix the shore

comparisons.tenor: the lotus of the backwater
the blue lily among the leaves

reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore of swelling water, where the flowering punnai drives off the smell of fish and the white sand of the cool grove outshines the moon, not to come in the night, and warns that if he comes by day there will be talk by the white waves in the mist, so that neither way is left open to him.
nuance: Shutting both the night tryst and the day tryst is the friend's way of leaving marriage as the only road; the poem does not say so, and the closing lines are obscure (சுலா அகற்றி, மார்க்).

thinai_evidence.note: the flowering punnai and the shore grove are neythal things

reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore, where a heron, taking the long bud of the fragrant thorny screwpine for its chick, puts food to it, and when it will not eat, melts and shades it with its wings from the cruel sun, to give up these coming-and-going visits.
nuance: மன்னா வரவு, a coming that does not stay, is the point of the image: the bird gives unbroken care even to what only looks like its young, while the hero comes and goes.

thinai_evidence.note: the screwpine and the shore heron are neythal things

iraicchi.act: the heron feeds what it takes for its chick and shades it from the sun with its wings
iraicchi.sense: even a bird keeps steady, self-forgetting care for what it holds as its own, so the hero should stop coming and going and marry her

reading: The friend tells the hero that the people of the tide-fenced hamlet, who never hold back their talk, keep their eyes on his comings for love, and only the tide knew of that first day; so, rather than coming in secret, let him marry her for the common square to know, and the gossip will end.
nuance: The tide appears twice, once as the fence of the gossiping hamlet and once as the only witness of the secret union; the friend sets the witness that cannot speak against the town that will not stop speaking, and asks for the square (மன்று) to become the witness instead.

thinai_evidence.note: a hamlet fenced by the tide is the neythal shore

reading: The girl, kept awake because the breast of the lord of the cool expanse has afflicted her, asks the great sea, which like her does not sleep, who has done this to it, and whether it too suffers a grief like hers.
nuance: The addressee is the sea. The question 'who did this to you' answers itself in the first two lines, which name who did it to her: she reads her own cause into the sea's restlessness.

thinai_evidence.note: the sleepless lament addressed to the sea is neythal's irangal

comparisons.tenor: the sea that does not sleep

reading: The friend says the broad soft shoulders belong only to the one who gave himself to her, and she will see whether those who say they will go to whoever comes asking on such a day are speaking true; for the one who came, there is the young njaazhal of the cool backwater grove, unguarded and not yet in flower.
nuance: The unguarded, unopened njaazhal bud, kept for the one who came, may stand for the girl already promised to her lover; it gives only one pair, so it is not tagged as ullurai. The verse reads like the friend's disclosure to the household when another suitor is spoken of, but the addressee is a guess.

thinai_evidence.note: the njaazhal of the backwater grove is a neythal tree

reading: The girl says that, watching the crab play with its mate, she asked whether she might play with her own sweet companion; and he said, 'if you have played with your sweet companion, why grieve over that ache?', and went away, set on going.
nuance: His reply turns her own word இன்துணை back on her: the pleasure is already had, so the ache is not his to answer for. Who speaks the second half is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore crab with its mate is a neythal creature

iraicchi.act: the crab plays with its mate
iraicchi.sense: even the crab keeps its partner at play beside it, while the man who should have stayed has gone

reading: The girl says her heart melts, and not for one day only, while the talk about them swells, and she loosens like the cloud that draws close, gathered with lightning and thunder, and pours.
nuance: The rain-cloud carries both halves of the first two lines: the heart that melts and the talk that swells (பெருகுமால்) gather together in one storm. பேண and பெருகா ஒருங்குவால் are uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: melting under the town's talk is the lament of irangal; nothing in the verse names a shore

comparisons.tenor: her melting heart and the swelling talk

reading: Like the great elephant, heavy with its mouthfuls, that cannot hold its ground when a young aali crawls near, her bangles will not stay on her arms each time she sees pearls set among the coral beads, and pearl-like tears gather in her hands.
nuance: The elephant and the aali belong to the hills; the poet borrows them for a sea-shore girl. The line division is unsure: முத்தம் in line 4 may be the pearls of her ornament or her tears, and the speaker is not named.

thinai_evidence.note: coral and pearl are things of the sea shore

comparisons.tenor: her bangles, which will not stay on her thinning arms
the tears gathering in her hands

reading: The friend tells the lord of the long shore, where the waves become a fierce tusked elephant, with the sea's two horns for tusks and the wind for its mahout, and rage and leap upon the bank, not to come in the thick dark, but to come as one who will marry her.
nuance: The danger of the night shore is drawn as a war elephant under a mahout; the wind drives the waves as the mahout drives the beast, so the image says the danger is steered, not random. கடற்கோடு, 'the sea's horns', is unclear: it may be the conch or the crests.

thinai_evidence.note: the wave-beaten shore at night is the neythal setting

comparisons.tenor: the waves that the wind drives against the shore

reading: The friend tells the lord of the ford, where the punnai drives off the strong fish smell, that the place of the simple doe-eyed girl, who went in to chase the birds from the drying fish, is the broad grove grown thick and tall with screwpine and njaazhal.
nuance: Naming the grove where the girl does her daily task is how the friend fixes a day meeting without saying so.

thinai_evidence.note: punnai, drying fish, screwpine and njaazhal are neythal things

comparisons.tenor: the girl's shy, startled look

reading: The friend says that, having seen the large broad eyes, matchless though one searched every land, of the simple young daughter of the fisherfolk on the cool grove of white sand where the screwpine creeps, he sought her as his partner, and is without fault.
nuance: துணை நாடினன் may be a plea for the hero: he wants her as a wife, not a passing love. The speaker and addressee are inferred, and மாழை and தோம் இலன் can be read otherwise.

thinai_evidence.note: the screwpine and the fisherfolk are neythal things

reading: The friend tells the hero that there is no need to bring gifts and search: if he asks for her one day and comes without delay, he will win her by word alone; but, my lord, the girl of the long makara earrings will not live if he comes in the night when the striking shark circles, so let him not come.
nuance: The same word மகரம் is the ornament on her ear and the beast in the sea: what adorns her is what threatens him, and the friend's fear is for both. தந்து ஆயல் is unsure.

thinai_evidence.note: the shark of the night sea is a neythal creature

reading: The man says that in the backwater grove where bees sing tunes nobody set, she is a beauty that strikes like a goddess those who look without thinking, and her kin, whose courage never flags though they die without a thought, do not guard her: they have slipped the rope and let her loose.
nuance: Her kin let her roam like a beast untied, which is a complaint about the danger she poses, not about her safety. Whether the 'courage that does not flag though dying' belongs to the kin or to the lovesick onlookers is unclear.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater grove is the neythal setting

comparisons.tenor: her beauty, which seizes the onlooker
the kin leaving her unguarded

title: நெய்தல் 48-62 (2/2)
theme: The second half of the neythal section: the friend refuses the shore lord's night visits because the pearls light the village, the tide rises and both day and night carry danger (48, 49, 55, 59), turns the shore into a marshalled royal army to press for a fixed wedding day (50, 52-54), points out the grove and the house where they may meet (56, 58, 61), while the hero names the fisher girl who has maddened him (60), the heroine refuses him (57) and the friend praises the man who once helped them (62).
source_issues: 48-62: the core records carry no colophon thurai, so thurai_akam speaker, addressee and stage are inferred from the poems, and occasion.words is null throughout.
49 line 3: நரன்யியிர்த்த is corrupt; நரல் உயிர்த்த (breathed out by the sounding conch) fits the sense. Line 4 வரன்றுயிர்த்த is unclear.
51 line 4: பாலிகை is unclear here (a pot of sprouted seed is its usual sense); read as a flower of the shore.
53 line 1: நீள்திமிலாத்தேறு joins நீள்திமிலா(த்) and தேறு, which begins the next phrase (தேறு திரைபறையா); a spacing error.
56 line 2: அடற்கானல் is odd; அடர் கானல் (dense grove) may be meant.
60 line 2: காலினாற் கானாக் is unclear; a verb for the crab marking or scratching the sand with its legs is expected.
62 line 3: ஒரோஉதவி may be ஒரோஉ உதவி (a single help) or ஓர் உதவி; the sense, one past act of help, holds either way.

reading: Where the waves have come up and drawn back from the clear backwater grove, the fragrant fishing village has for its lamp the pearls that open-mouthed, green-backed oysters cast on the shore, which drive off the dark as the sun goes down.
nuance: The verse names no speaker or hearer; read beside 49, which turns the same pearl-light into a question to the shore lord, the lit village is a reason he cannot come unseen by night. The praise of the shore's riches is also a warning.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater grove and the fishing village at nightfall

comparisons.tenor: the pearls on the shore, which serve the village as its lamp

reading: The friend asks the lord of the cool, broad backwater where he thinks he will come, into a village where pearls breathed out by conches that the surging waves have kicked ashore sweep away even the midnight dark.
nuance: The objection to the night visit is not the usual dark and its beasts but light: the shore is so rich that its pearls undo the midnight that should hide him. எங்கு வருதி is a refusal shaped as a question.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater, the shore lord and the fishing village

reading: With boats for elephants, waves for drums and the many birds that rise and break the sleep of the shore for an army, the lord of the lovely sea is asked to give up coming without a set tryst, like sleep, and to take her by the proper way.
nuance: The two images pull against each other: the shore is arrayed like a royal army that marches in order, while he comes like sleep, by stealth and without a tryst. The friend asks him to match the order of his own shore (நெறியால் நீ கொள்வது).

thinai_evidence.note: the sea lord and the fishing boats

comparisons.vehicle: திமில்களி றாகத் திரைபறையாப் பல்புள் துயில்கெடத் தோன்றும் படையா
comparisons.tenor: the shore at daybreak, its boats, waves and birds marshalled like a king's elephants, drums and troops
his coming unannounced, unbidden as sleep

reading: On the white sand of the grove that reeks of fish, we watch the catch and sell it, and over all the adumbu creepers nets like coats of mail lie drying while the flowers bloom thick about them.
nuance: The speaker counts herself among the fish-sellers (பகர்தும், we sell): naming the smell and the trade is how the neythal friend reminds a well-born suitor of the distance between them, though the same chore can also mark the place where she may be met by day.

thinai_evidence.note: fish, nets and adumbu creeper of the shore

comparisons.tenor: the fishing nets spread on the creepers, meshed like chain mail

reading: Lord of the sea shore, where with the waves for mahouts, the boats for elephants and the grove on the bank for troops the scene stands like a king roused but unhurried: to choose a day and marry her is right.
nuance: விரையாது carries the argument: a king does not rush to war but rises in order, and so the lord of such a shore should not rush to the grove at night but fix a day (நாள் ஆய்ந்து). Marriage is called அறம், a duty and not only a kindness.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea lord and the shore grove

comparisons.vehicle: திரைபாக னாகத் திமில்களி றாகக் கரைசேர்ந்த கானல் படையா
comparisons.tenor: the shore's waves, boats and grove marshalled as a king's force
the whole shore, risen in order like a king who musters without haste

reading: Lord of the sea shore, where with ships for horses, long boats for many elephants, clear waves for drums and birds for troops the scene is like a restless king risen to war: make sure you come forward before our kin rise first.
nuance: எமர் முன்கிளர்ந்து may mean that he should rise before our kin do (to give her elsewhere, or against him), or that he should come forward before our kin to ask for her; either way the restless king of the image is a pressure, not the calm one of 52.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea lord and the long fishing boats

comparisons.vehicle: பாறு புரவியாப் பல்களிறு நீள்திமிலாத்தேறு திரைபறையாப் புட்படையாத்
comparisons.tenor: the shore's ships, boats, waves and birds marshalled as a king's horse, elephants, drums and troops
the whole shore, astir like a king who has risen and will not settle

reading: You come, but on the fine sand of the backwater grove the legs of your chariot horses sink, which is a harm; on reflection you need seek no other plan: call those who read omens, choose a day and give yourself to her, which is good.
nuance: The friend turns a fact of the shore (horses sink in the sand) into a reason for a public road to her: the secret way is literally unsound under his chariot, and the sound way is the diviners' fixed day. கொண்டோர் is hard to place; it may name the kin who take the bride.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater grove and its fine sand

reading: Look about you: the cold dew is harsh, and the great dark spreads over the land; do not come in your swift chariot when the water floods the ways, for if you come she will not bear it, facing the rising tide.
nuance: The danger is put in her, not in him: வரின் ஆற்றாள், if you come she will not endure it. The friend forbids the night visit by making the heroine's fear for him the cost of his coming.

thinai_evidence.note: the rising tide on the shore at night

reading: Lord of the sea grove, where the punnai of the grove that stretches along the backwater bends low and shades, and the anril calls from the lovely tall palmyras of the frond-thick grove crowding the young sand of our front yard.
nuance: The friend gives the shore lord the marks of their house (எம் முன்றில்): the drooping punnai and the palmyras where the anril calls. The anril, the bird that cannot bear parting from its mate, is the traditional sign of her nights; it only calls here and does nothing a lover does, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: punnai, anril and palmyra of the shore

reading: Lord of the roaring sea, whose long-sanded grove the coming waves roam and whose plenty no single wave runs off from, where two waves at once fall before the grove: you need not desire me any more.
nuance: The waves that come and fall, two at a time, may hint at a man whose comings are divided; the poem does not say so, and the image gives only one match of mood, so it is not tagged as ullurai. The last line is a refusal in the heroine's own voice (என்), not the friend's.

thinai_evidence.note: the long sand of the grove and the sea lord

reading: Do you not see the rolling sea and the white sand that lies against the grove, together like Mayavan and his elder brother, and the grove filled through its middle with njazhal and screw-pine and all round with punnai, flowering gladly?
nuance: The dark god and his white elder brother give the shore its two colours, dark sea and white sand, joined as brothers are. Mayavan is the god of the mullai land, so the simile brings a mullai deity onto the neythal shore. காணாயோ invites the hearer into the grove, which reads as pointing out a meeting place.

thinai_evidence.note: njazhal, screw-pine and punnai of the shore grove

comparisons.tenor: the dark sea and the white sand lying side by side

reading: If you come by day the gossip will be great, and if you come by night without care the dangers are as great; the home of the poor fisherfolk is on the wave-beaten shore where the screw-pine, hard to pass through, sways.
nuance: Both trysts are refused at once, day for the gossip and night for the danger, which leaves only marriage open, though the friend never names it. ஏழை நுளையர், the poor fisherfolk, adds the modesty of class to the refusal.

thinai_evidence.note: the screw-pine shore and the fisher folk

reading: Where the waves cry out and will not leave but shout and wander, and the shore crab marks the sand with its legs, the long-eyed girl plucking neythal flowers near the shore is the fisherman's daughter who has made me mad with love.
nuance: The waves that cry, will not go and wander are the hero's own state set out before he names its cause; the closing word மையல் (madness of love) is placed on the girl, not on himself. She is identified by her people, நுளையர் மகள், which is all the lover knows of her.

thinai_evidence.note: neythal flower, crab and fisher folk

reading: Lord of the sounding sea, it is hard for anyone to know of it, for no one strays along that path: there is nothing there but the backwater ringed by kandal with turning shoots and cool thillai mingled, and the dense cool screw-pine joined among them.
nuance: Read as the friend naming a meeting place, the thicket of kandal, thillai and screw-pine is safe because no one walks there; the same words could be a warning that the way is pathless. இல்லை in line 2 has no stated subject.

thinai_evidence.note: kandal, thillai and screw-pine of the backwater

reading: Neither at the bowmen's festivals nor at the festivals of fine people in this sea-girt world have we seen his like; good girl, if there are any in heaven to match the shore lord who once helped us in the salt land, consider it.
nuance: The help (உதவி) is the founding act of the love, the once-only service in the salt pans; the praise ranks him above earth and sets heaven as the only place left to search, which makes a debt of gratitude into the measure of a lover.

thinai_evidence.note: the salt land and the shore lord

title: பாலை 63-92
theme: Paalai: the dry spring of murukku, kongam and pungu that marks the season of return (63-67, 79-80); the man who cannot leave for her glance (68); the friend's and the heroine's arguments for and against going for wealth, from manly duty to youth that will not come back (82-87, 91-92); and the eloped girl seen on the road by villagers and travellers, and mourned and sought by her mother among trees and diviners (65, 69-73, 75, 81, 88-90).

source_issues.issue: Line 2 is a repaired line (the old encoding '·' for ஃ in வெஃகா) and its reading differs from sangamtamil.com; the sense of விரிந்து விடுகூந்தல் வெஃகா is uncertain.
Line 1 splits தாமரை across a space (முகந்தா மரைமுறுவல்), apparently for the metre; read as முகம் தாமரை.
Lines 1 and 2 (அல்லாத என்னையும் தீரமற்று ஐயன்மார் பொல்லாதது) do not construe cleanly; the text may be corrupt.
நற்றியவேய் (line 2) and நாரில்பூ (line 1) are obscure; the text may be corrupt.

reading: The friend asks the heroine, whose paired breasts are like kongam buds dressed in gold, why, now that striped bees sing over every fire-red cluster of the asoka, her shoulders with their flower bangles wear this matchless pallor.
nuance: The question answers itself: the asoka in flower is the season he named, so her pallor marks that he has not come. என்னணிந்த makes the pallor something she has put on, set against the gold the kongam wears.

thinai_evidence.note: the asoka and kongam in flower, the trees of the dry spring

comparisons.tenor: her paired breasts with their golden spots, seen as gold-decked kongam buds

reading: Though she is told to keep herself in hand she will not, so the friend bids the girl of modest, fine bangles look at the shamelessness of the season: the moist murukku blazing as if fire had been scattered, the pungu white as if puffed rice had been strewn.
nuance: நாணிண்மை is read as நாண் இன்மை; whether the shamelessness is the trees' open display or the girl's open grieving turns on that reading. Either way it is set against her own modesty in நாணாய நல்வளையாய்.

thinai_evidence.note: murukku and pungu in bloom, the flowers of the paalai spring

comparisons.tenor: the murukku's red blossom, as if fire were scattered
the pungu's white blossom, as if puffed rice were strewn

reading: The mother searching for her eloped daughter speaks to the dark kuravam: you bore your doll-flowers while the kongam, sagging, gave them the breast as foster mother; though you will not speak to me as one mother to another, come and show me the way my sharp-toothed girl went.
nuance: The kuravam's flower was called பாவை, doll, so the speaker sees a tree that bore a child and had another nurse it, which is the household's own arrangement of mother and foster mother; she asks the tree for ஈன்றாள் மொழி, the word a mother owes a mother. The addressee is the tree.

thinai_evidence.note: a mother asking the way her daughter took with her lover

comparisons.tenor: a foster mother nursing a child, the kongam bud as the breast
the kuravam's flower as a daughter it has borne

reading: The friend tells the heroine he will come soon: look, all the murukku trees, shining, have chosen and set gold talis over fine coral shoots, like goldsmiths making ornaments for rich men's children.
nuance: The goldsmith simile makes the season a craftsman delivering on time (தேர்ந்து, choosing carefully), so the trees' punctuality stands surety for the man's.

thinai_evidence.note: the murukku in bloom, the season of his promised return

comparisons.tenor: the murukku trees, working their blossoms like goldsmiths making ornaments to order
the red shoots and golden buds of the murukku

reading: The heroine tells her friend that the man who went for wealth has not appeared; if she is told to bear it, can it be borne? The paired murukku blossoms, like coral set in gold, seem to punish her, and the sickness within her is great.
nuance: வெறுக்கை, wealth, is the word the verse opens on, and நோய் the word it ends on: the trade of one for the other is the whole complaint.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has gone for wealth and she waits

comparisons.tenor: the murukku blossom, red set in gold
the flowering murukku as one who punishes her

reading: The man asks his heart what way there is to go when, as he stands in the great wasteland, the meaning in the glance of the young girl who loves her jewels, her eyes reaching to her earrings, stays and will not let him go.
nuance: A செலவழுங்குதல் poem: the journey is undone not by her words but by the குறிப்பு of a glance, which he reads only once he is already on the road. ஒளிவிடா (does not let go, or does not cease to shine) is read loosely.

thinai_evidence.note: the man weighing a journey across the waste

reading: Villagers tell the eloping man that the road is long and the fiery sun has already sunk half his red disc behind the western hill, so it would be fitting for him to stay the night in their small village with this jewelled girl and go on tomorrow in proper order.
nuance: அத்தம் is used twice in one line with two senses, the road and the hill of sunset, so a single word names both the danger and the hour; the offer is shelter for a couple who have left their kin.

thinai_evidence.note: the long road at sunset

reading: On the road the man tells the girl to see the deer with her look resting in the cool kuravam shade and the flowering kongam with the look of gold, and calls her, a slender branch with soft breasts decked in golden spots, to come and play at sand houses on the sand.
nuance: வண்டல் அயர் is the girls' game of sand houses she has left at home; he offers her the wasteland as that playground, so the comfort is for the life she gave up.

thinai_evidence.note: kuravam and kongam of the dry spring

comparisons.tenor: the deer whose eyes have the girl's look
the kongam flower with the colour of gold
the girl, slender as a branch

reading: Seeing the jewelled girl, her face bright as the midnight moon, and the man of the long spear, hot-bright as the sun, walking along together, onlookers cried out in fear that both lights had come down and the world, left with neither, would lie desolate.
nuance: The hyperbole puts sun and moon on one road, which the sky never allows; the onlookers' fear is praise. மாநிலா in line 2 is hard to place and is read with the man's sun-image only loosely.

thinai_evidence.note: onlookers watching an eloping couple pass

comparisons.tenor: the couple as moon and sun

reading: Taking her face for a lotus, her smile for an ambal, her eyes for blue lilies and her fingers for kaanthal, the bees gather over her in delight and make a shade, so the simple girl goes on her way pleasantly, without suffering.
nuance: The bees' mistake turns her beauty into shelter: the four flowers belong to the watered fields and the hills, not the waste, so she carries a cooler land with her and is shaded by it. The speaker is not named; onlookers reassuring the foster mother fits the closing line.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl going on the road with her lover

comparisons.tenor: her face as a lotus
her smile as the white ambal
her eyes as blue lilies
her fingers as kaanthal

reading: The mother laments that her simple girl, with red mouth and dark eyes, has gone off and given up the garlanded parrot of her playmates, whose speech was like hers, and the blue lily of the cool pond, which was like her eyes, unable to bear the town's gossip.
nuance: The parrot and the lily are the things her mouth and eyes were praised by; the mother counts it a loss that the girl no longer needs her likenesses. The run of negatives in lines 1 and 2 (கேளாதும், காணாதும், ஆற்றாதும்) is read only loosely.

thinai_evidence.note: the mother of a girl who has left home

comparisons.tenor: the girl's speech, matched with the parrot's
the girl's dark eyes, matched with the blue lily

reading: The heroine tells a small dove not to sulk with its mate, since sulking is no matter even between those bound in love: he hardened and left, and she bids it look at the road he went by and at her own colour, now turned to gold from watching it.
nuance: The warning may carry a confession: her own sulking came before his going. The dove pair is addressed and the moral is spoken aloud, so it is neither ullurai (the tenor is stated) nor iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: watching the road he left by

comparisons.tenor: the pallor that has covered her like gold

reading: The mother says the road her girl took behind the man of slaying strength is the long wasteland where the sun burns with matchless rays, not sparing her loosened hair, and where the python lies dying, limp as a twisted rope let go.
nuance: The heat kills even the python that lies in wait for travellers, so the mother's fear passes from the beast to the sun. Line 2 (விரிந்து விடுகூந்தல் வெஃகா) is a repaired line whose reading differs from the web witness, and its sense is guessed.

thinai_evidence.note: the long waste under the burning sun

comparisons.tenor: the python lying limp, like a rope let go

reading: The friend tells the man that, on the long waste where paddy would pop into puffed rice at the mere thought of it, she was afraid of the road even when told not to fear, and tears filled her long spear-like eyes, slit wide to her ears.
nuance: The hyperbole (grain pops at a thought) puts the heat in the mind before the body; whose fear அஞ்சிற்று names, and whether the speaker is the friend, is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the waste so hot that grain would pop

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, long and sharp as weapons

reading: The heroine asks her slender-waisted friend whether, when he comes, she cannot go with him across the long bamboo waste that looks burnt by the sun's long rays, and recalls the look given as she set out, her fragrant hair tumbling, her trailing robe gathered in her hand, her makara earring turned back.
nuance: Who gave the look of lines 3 and 4 (தந்தார்) and to whom is not clear; the reading takes it as the picture of a girl setting out with her lover.

thinai_evidence.note: the sun-scorched bamboo waste

comparisons.tenor: the bamboo waste, looking as if burnt

reading: The heroine prays that the man who went into the hill waste, where even the great elephant with one trunk, two tusks and three musth streams finds no water to drink in the green spring, turns off the path and falls, may come to no harm.
nuance: The counting conceit (one, two, three) builds the elephant up only to fell it, so the wish அழிவிலர் ஆக asks for more than the land allows. Not iraicchi: the elephant is alone and does nothing a lover does.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill waste whose springs are dry

reading: The friend tells the tight-bangled heroine, who will not trust those who stand by her, that the return of the man who went is not far off: let her see, without delay, the hill country where the shining waterfall shows like the banner raised by victors.
nuance: The victors' banner makes the waterfall announce his success before he arrives; the falls run full only when the rains he promised to return by have come.

thinai_evidence.note: waiting for the man's return from his journey

comparisons.tenor: the waterfall, white and streaming as a victors' banner

reading: The friend tells the heroine of spear-fine eyes that the man who went far to bring wealth will come today in honour across the long waste where things have shrivelled and dropped in dread of the lord of the one-wheeled chariot, for this is the hour her left eye throbs.
nuance: இடம் closes the verse in two senses, place and the left side: the throbbing of a woman's left eye is the good omen, so the poem ends on the sign, not the road.

thinai_evidence.note: the long waste under the sun

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, sharp and bright as a spear
the sun, lord of the one-wheeled chariot

reading: The mother of the girl who has gone speaks to the konrai, the kuruntham and the mullai creeper: you have withered; I stand here and I know; what did you say to the long-eyed girl as she went, and what did she say to you, leaving with her lightning-bright ornaments glittering?
nuance: The stammered question of line 3 (என்னுரைத்தீர்க்கு என்னுரைத்தாட்கு...) puts the grief into the syntax. The withered mullai plants may be read as having withered at the girl's going.

thinai_evidence.note: the mother of a girl who has eloped

comparisons.tenor: her ornaments, flashing like lightning

reading: The friend tells the soft-spoken heroine that men, weighing the way that is a man's duty, have taken it up and cherished it as a duty they must bear, and so will go to make wealth; it is good that she not go even a little into wasting grief.
nuance: கடன் is said three times (ஆண்கடன், பூண்கடன் twice): the comfort is an argument from obligation, which casts the heroine's grief as a lapse from her own duty to bear it.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's going for wealth

reading: The heroine asks whether he would really go: even the thought is unbearable and her heart burns; will he who went win and finish his work? She bids her friend hear the cicadas that wander and shrill like a doe crying at a beast of stone.
nuance: The simile of lines 3 and 4 is obscure (இதடி, கல் மா); the reading follows the plain words, a doe calling at something that will never answer, which fits a voice crying to an absent man.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's going on his work

comparisons.tenor: the cicadas' shrilling, like a doe crying at a beast of stone

reading: The heroine asks whether men with someone of their own would thrust her aside and go by the track of graceless warriors, who rush out and shoot travellers even when they carry no wealth to take, in the cactus scrub where the wild bison flees.
nuance: அருளில் sets the robbers' lack of grace beside the man's own: he goes for wealth by a road where others kill those who have none, and the parallel is left for the hearer.

thinai_evidence.note: the cactus scrub of the waste

reading: The man who keeps saying 'wealth, wealth' has treasured those words like gold until grace counts for nothing; since he has a way to bring wealth back, let him agree to bring back youth as well.
nuance: The taunt rests on what it leaves unsaid: wealth can be fetched again, youth cannot, so his own reasoning about wealth refutes his going.

thinai_evidence.note: the man resolved on going for wealth

comparisons.tenor: his talk of wealth, held as precious as gold

reading: The heroine tells her friend, who said he would surely go, to name anyone who could bear it, and calls her excellent indeed, when he would hurry across the waste where a worn-out elephant that can go no farther eyes men in its hunger and eats.
nuance: சிறந்தாயே is irony. ஆள் பார்த்து மிசைந்தொழியும் is read literally, though an elephant eating men is odd; the sense may be that it waits by the path for travellers.

thinai_evidence.note: the waste of the starving elephant

reading: The friend asks whether they can say even one word against the going of the man who guards his fame and never turns back: the far waste is hard to cross even as companion to that unconquerable young spearman, skilled with the bow.
nuance: The repeated பின்றா (not turning back) is made his virtue and the reason no one can hold him; whether the heroine is being told she could not go with him is not clear.

thinai_evidence.note: the far waste he will cross

reading: Speaking of her elder brothers' disapproval, which the heroine of long sword-like eyes will not accept, the friend seems to warn her that if she holds back now he will embrace her once and go away offended.
nuance: The first two lines are hard to construe; the reading rests on ஐயன்மார் (elder brothers), வல்லி ஒழியின் (if you fail to be firm) and புல்லி ஒழிவான் புலந்து (he will embrace and leave, sulking).

thinai_evidence.note: the brothers' opposition and the lover's possible leaving

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, long and sharp as a sword

reading: Travellers answer the searching mother: go on close behind them, for if they are your people your purpose will not come easily; I saw the man like the hot sun, and she saw the girl like the cool moon.
nuance: The sighting is divided by sex: the man saw the man and his woman companion saw the girl, a propriety of the road; sun and moon make the couple a matched pair. Line 2's எண்ணிய எண்ணம் எளிதரா is read only tentatively.

thinai_evidence.note: travellers who have seen the eloping pair

comparisons.tenor: the man, bright and hot as the sun
the girl, bright and cool as the moon

reading: The mother asks the diviner apart, by his god, to tell her, since telling is his gift: will the youth bring the girl of victorious bangles first up to her house, or take her straight to his own?
nuance: வேறாக, said twice, frames the question as private: the mother asks apart because the answer (his house, not hers) would shame her before others. The addressee is the diviner.

thinai_evidence.note: the mother of an eloped girl asking where the wedding will be

reading: The heroine asks whether men who mean to live would go near a place of cactus, dark omai, long murungai with fibreless flowers and bamboo, where the spotted kite and the vulture watch for travellers and sit there sleeping till they die.
nuance: The birds' patience is the horror: they sit and doze because the travellers will die without their help. நற்றிய and நாரில்பூ are uncertain words, and வாழ்பவர் may mean those who wish to live or those who live well.

thinai_evidence.note: cactus, omai and carrion birds of the waste

reading: The heroine asks whether a man would go, ruining the well-being of those who depend on him, by the road where cicadas crowd and shrill as if to kill under the hot sun, the dust swells and burns, the sky scorches from above and from below the feet burn and the eyes smart.
nuance: தம்மடைந்தார் (those who have come to him for refuge) makes the wife a dependant, so his going is a breach of the protector's duty, not only of love; the heat is mapped above, below and in the eyes.

thinai_evidence.note: the road under the burning sun

comparisons.tenor: the cicadas' shrilling, as if they were killing

title: முல்லை 93-108 (1/2)
theme: The first half of Kanimethaviyar's mullai: the rains and the evening come and the man does not. Clouds that drank the sea, the konrai and the kodal announce the season (93, 98, 104, 107), the evening and moonlight wound (94, 96, 97), the woman counters her friend's counsel that the season is false or that she should bear it (99, 103, 106), and the paired deer and clinging creepers set off her loneliness (102, 105).
source_issues: 95 lines 1 to 4: the run of நோக்கு words (மேல்நோக்கி, கீழ் நோக்கி, கால்நோக்கம்) and போதாரி are hard to construe; the reading is tentative and the verse is marked uncertain.
97 line 2: வாழிபோல் is read as ஆழி போல் (the discus) with a glide after எறிந்த; பாழிபோல் in line 1 is not fixed.
99 line 3: வனம்பிழந்த is very likely a misprint for வனப்பிழந்த, 'lost their beauty'.
104 line 2: இந்துருவின் is obscure (the moon's form, or a misprint); the verse is marked uncertain.
105 line 4: ஒடுங்கழுத்தம் is obscure; the reading is tentative.
106 line 3: வந்(து)ஆரம் தேங்கா is hard to construe.
107 line 1: கணமயிலென்று றஞ்சி has a doubled ற and should read கணமயில் என்று அஞ்சி.
108: lines 1 and 3 (முலையல்லை, நோய்மொழிச்சார்) are very likely corrupt; the reading is a guess and the verse is marked uncertain.

reading: The white-topped cloud that drank the dark sea flashes lightning like the spear of the god who killed the beast in the great sea and roars as the great sea roars, while the thalavam and the kurunthu flower together; the woman asks how she is to bear it.
nuance: The cloud drank the sea and now roars like it: the sea comes back as sound. Murugan, god of the hills, is borrowed only for his spear's flash, so the mullai scene carries a kurinji god (mixed). குருந்தனைய may be read குருந்து அணைய, the thalavam creeper embracing the kurunthu, which would set joined plants against her loneliness; read as அனைய ('such'), it is a list of the season's flowers, so the plants stay scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-season flowers of the scrub

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the closing question is the waiting woman's own

comparisons.tenor: the lightning
the thunder of the cloud

reading: As the many-rayed sun, having drunk up the day, reaches the hill and the moon, as if picking a quarrel, pours white moonlight to bring day back over the dark, the woman tells her bamboo-shouldered friend that in this bewildering evening her life will not stay within her but rides away.
nuance: The sky is a battle (இகல்) between sun and moon in which neither side is hers; the moon's false day is no comfort. ஊர்ந்து makes her life a thing that rides off. மருள்மாலை is the Kural's word for the same hour.

thinai_evidence.note: the evening hour of waiting

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): a woman speaks of her own life leaving to a bamboo-shouldered listener, most likely the friend

comparisons.tenor: the friend's shoulders
the moonlight

reading: The speaker bids the simple, doe-eyed woman look: the hot sun has turned upward, the gathered water comes down, the wind has taken on beauty, and the bees that fill every flower hum the saadhaari mode on long-drawn notes.
nuance: The verse plays on looking: the sun looks up (மேல்நோக்கி), the water looks down (கீழ் நோக்கி), the wind takes on a look (நோக்கம்), and the woman addressed is herself 'doe-look' (மானோக்கி). நெட்டெழுத்தின் மேல் puts the bees' hum on long syllables, as a singer holds a note.

thinai_evidence.note: the bees hum saadhaari, a mode tied to the mullai land

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the speaker points out the signs of the rains (காண்) to a doe-eyed simple woman, most likely the friend showing the heroine the season; the heroine speaking is possible

comparisons.tenor: the woman's eyes

reading: The dark spreads like the colour of the discus-bearer and the moonlight like the pale colour of his gracious elder brother, white as milk and bewildering; the speaker tells the woman of the serpent-hood waist that it falls like a spear on those who have lost their partner.
nuance: Both halves of the night are coloured by the mullai god and his brother, the dark one and the white one, so the land's own divine pair makes the night; the night of the two brothers is a spear to one who has no partner.

thinai_evidence.note: Maayon, the god of the mullai land, colours the night

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the speaker generalises her own pain (துணை இலார்க்கு) to a woman she addresses, most likely the friend

comparisons.tenor: the spreading dark
the moonlight
the white moonlight
the moonlit night, to the parted
the woman's waist

reading: As the sun reaches the hill like the discus Maayavan hurled at his foes' elephant, and the moon sprouts in the dusky evening with the colour of his elder brother, the woman tells her friend she cannot bear the evening as she thinks of him.
nuance: வாழி in line 2 is read as ஆழி, the discus, with a glide after எறிந்த; பாழிபோல் in line 1 (like a stronghold, or like a field of war) is not fixed. The setting sun is a weapon still red from killing, the evening a battle that ends in her defeat.

thinai_evidence.note: Maayon, the mullai god, supplies both images of the evening

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the woman names her friend (தோழி) and speaks of herself (யான்)

comparisons.tenor: the red setting sun
the rising moon

reading: With the drops falling over the wondrous scrubland the great konrai bursts into flower, and the speaker bids her friend look at it at once, with the others too: its blossoms sharpen into anklet, golden coin, garland, sheath, curl and twisted rod.
nuance: The list of ornaments is a timeline: the konrai passes from bud to full cluster through six shapes, and to watch it is to watch the season he named ripen. Calling on others as witnesses makes the flowering evidence, not scenery.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain on the scrubland and the konrai of the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the speaker calls on a listener and the others to witness the konrai now (நீயும் பிறரொடும்காண் நீடாதே), most likely the heroine proving to her friend that the rains he named have come; the friend showing her the season is possible

comparisons.tenor: the konrai flowers at each stage of opening

reading: Though golden blades of lightning cloak the dark hill of the forest, you say 'idly', bright-toothed friend; yet, like my own lustre, my eyes have lost their light, my shoulders their beauty, and my soft fingers are worn out with counting the days that have gone.
nuance: The verse turns on வாள்: the golden blades over the hill, the friend's வாளா ('for nothing'), and வாள் as lustre, which her eyes have lost. Counting days on the fingers until they wear thin is the Kural's image, here put in an answer to the friend.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest hill under the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): she answers a bright-toothed listener who has called her grief idle (வாளா)

comparisons.tenor: the lightning (or the konrai) over the hill

reading: Because the word he once spoke to win her has proved false, the cloud has seen the great sea, drunk its fill, let down its rain and darkened; the rains appear in all eight quarters but the lover's chariot does not, so pallor appears, and tears appear in her eyes.
nuance: Four 'appearings' carry the poem: the rains appear, the chariot does not, the pallor appears, the tears appear. The blame is laid on his word (சொல்பழுதால்), as if the broken promise had itself called up the rain.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains have come and he has not

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the woman speaks of her own eyes and pallor at the coming of the rains

reading: The water-lily the bees do not plunder, the evening in which the swarms do not drop into the mouths of the long-petalled flowers: since the man of the decorated chariot, whose flower garland the bees never tire of, went away, only the days on which he does not come keep coming.
nuance: Bees run through all three lines: they leave the lily and the evening flowers alone but never tire of his garland. One may hear in it her untouched beauty against his crowded garland, but only one pair can be named, so the bees stay scene (a near miss on the ullurai test). The last line makes the calendar itself the injury: every day that comes is one on which he does not.

thinai_evidence.note: the evening of waiting for the chariot

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the woman counts the days of his absence

reading: With deer everywhere playing with their does and fawns leaping, the sky everywhere giving its plenty and bees all over the forest that have stored their honey, the woman says that she, who did not judge his going a harm, has paid her life for this season.
nuance: எங்கும் is repeated three times (deer, sky, forest): the plenty is everywhere except in her house. தீதா எனத்தேராது turns the reproach on herself: she did not see his leaving as the harm it was.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest and the sky of the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the woman blames herself (யான்) for letting him go

iraicchi.act: the stags play everywhere with their does in the rains
iraicchi.sense: even the beasts of the scrub keep their mates by them in this season, while the man who should be with her is away

reading: To the friend who says it is not certain, that this water of unripened rain may mean his task has met ruin and that the season has not truly come, the woman answers that she has already boiled her life away in tears over it.
nuance: The friend's comfort is the old one, that this is not the true season; the woman does not argue the weather but answers with what the waiting has already cost (அட்டினேன் ஆவி, 'I have cooked my life').

thinai_evidence.note: she waits on the season he named

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): she quotes the friend's words (என்றி) and answers them

reading: As the five-coloured bow is drawn and the great cloud, having drunk the sea of the four quarters, gathers into one with thunder as if about to pour, the woman tells the konrai that, by flowering at that word, it has killed her and wilted her.
nuance: கொன்றாய்கொன் றாய் is a pun: 'O konrai' and 'you have killed'. The tree is blamed for believing the cloud's show, and its flowering kills her because it announces a season in which he has not come. இந்துருவின் in line 2 is obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: the konrai that flowers at the first rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the woman addresses the konrai itself, in the hearing of her friend

comparisons.tenor: the rainbow
the cloud that only seems about to rain

reading: The speaker bids the listener see how the rain-cloud, born after drinking the rays of the sun that sets the day's bound, makes the creepers climb in the fields, and how the mullai, with the great cool thalavam, clings close about the kurunthu like kinsfolk.
nuance: The simile runs backward: plants are likened to kin, not people to plants. Their embrace is the subject of the whole poem, so it fails the deletion test and is not tagged iraicchi. The last line (ஒடுங்கழுத்தம்) is obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: the mullai, thalavam and kurunthu of the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the speaker points to the season's signs (காண், காணாய்), most likely the friend to the heroine; the returning man speaking is possible

comparisons.tenor: the creepers clinging round the kurunthu

reading: Who are they, those who tell a woman parted from her chosen partner to bear it? They speak so only for themselves; for already, before he comes, the bees that settle on the unceasing mullai sing the gandhaaram mode in their joy.
nuance: The bees' gladness is the evidence against the counsel: the season of joy is already here, before him (முன்னரே). Line 3 (வந்(து)ஆரம் தேங்கா) is hard to construe.

thinai_evidence.note: the mullai in flower

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): she rejects the counsel to bear up (ஆற்று), which in these poems comes from the friend

reading: Fearing the budding kaayaa to be a flock of peacocks, the thunder-struck glory lily has shrunk away, and the gem-dark rain-cloud, like a five-headed cobra in the thunder, has now come down upon my head.
nuance: A chain of fears: the glory lily, shaped like a snake's hood, fears the kaayaa it takes for peacocks; the cloud is itself a snake in the thunder; and the woman is the one it falls on. The lily's fear carries a mood but is not an act of a person of the situation, so it is not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: the kaayaa and the glory lily of the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the woman speaks of the season falling on her own head

comparisons.tenor: the budding blue kaayaa
the dark rain-cloud

reading: Very obscurely, the woman seems to say that the thundering sky, if it had eyes, could see her, and if it had thought, she would not be dying; lacking both, it has made her sick in the one way it could.
nuance: The verse runs on two conditionals (கண்ணுள வாயின், எண்ணுள வாயின்) and seems to charge the sky with blindness and thoughtlessness rather than cruelty.

thinai_evidence.note: the thundering sky of the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the speaker is the sick woman, but the addressee cannot be fixed

title: முல்லை 109-123 (2/2)
theme: Mullai in the rains, second half: the wife waits as the konrai, kodal, kurundham and jasmine bloom and the thunder rolls, refuses the friend's plea that it is not yet the season (118), counts the kodal's whole life passing (119), finds every sight and sound an enemy (121, 122), while the friend urges readiness and reproaches the flowers (112, 116); the last poem turns to the rival women, burned in this life for scorning her (123).

source_issues.issue: Line 3 reads வண்துடுப்பாயப் where the run of -ஆய் forms (பாம்பாய் விரலாய் வளைமுறியாய்) suggests வண்துடுப்பாய்ப்; probably a misprint.
Filed under முல்லை, but the poem has no mullai thing, season or hour; its matter is the rival women, so the inferred thinai is marutham.

reading: The heroine tells her friend, a woman in her own plight, that the clouds which drank the dark sea have come and the konrai has hung out its gold-like strings; the man who left his partner, precious as gold, will not appear, and from now on the two will live apart.
nuance: தோன்றுவர் தோன்றார் sets 'he will appear' against 'he will not' in one breath, so line 3 may be her doubt swinging both ways rather than a verdict; என்போல் இகுளை makes the friend another woman left alone.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-clouds and the konrai in bloom fix the rainy season of mullai

comparisons.tenor: the konrai's hanging flower strings
the partner he left, as precious as gold

reading: The heroine says that the greatness of the great is great indeed: when the cool wild jasmine laughed in bloom at her as she grieved with bowed head, the hills, lofty and hard to reach, were moved to pity for one so low and wept in streams, deeply troubled.
nuance: Nature splits into mockers and mourners: the small flower laughs, the great hills weep, and that is the 'greatness of the great' of line 1. Line 2 (அரியார் எளியரென்று) is hard; it may instead say that those hard to reach (the hills) came down to her level.

thinai_evidence.note: the wild jasmine in flower is the mullai blossom of the rains

comparisons.tenor: the wild jasmine's opening, taken as laughter at her grief
the streams running down the hills, taken as tears

reading: The heroine tells her friend that the forest has become a festival stage, the glory lilies beckoning like hands, the full sky calling, the bees playing the lute and the peacock that starved through the summer dancing, and asks her to say how one is to stay alive through it.
nuance: The whole festival is staged for a return that has not happened, so its gaiety is the threat: உளராகி உய்யும் வகை asks not how to be happy but how to survive.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest and the calling sky of the rains are mullai's land and season

comparisons.tenor: the forest in the rains
the glory lily's opening petals
the humming of the bees

reading: The friend tells the heroine that as the sun goes behind the hill and the sweet flute burns in the ear, the man will not leave his word unkept: the kurundham and the mullai have flowered together in the rains, and it is their part now to stand ready to welcome him as a guest.
nuance: விதி may be fate as much as duty, so 'our lot is to stand with the guest-feast' can be weary (they wait, ready, once more) rather than confident. The kurundham joined by the mullai is a pair the season shows while the couple are apart, but the poem draws nothing from it, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: sunset, the herdsman's flute and the mullai in the rains

reading: The heroine tells her friend that even at midnight, when the herdsmen, turning their leaf baskets upside down, call out and drive the herd and the jackal howls, the man who mounted the chariot of spread-maned horses has not appeared.
nuance: The herdsmen settle and call at night, the jackal is awake, and only the man with the fast chariot, who could most easily come, does not.

thinai_evidence.note: the herdsmen and their calls belong to the pasture land

reading: The heroine speaks to the kurundham: before the many clouds that drank the deep sea could let fall their heavy drops, it blossomed, marked out the season, and so decreed that she should grieve with her bangles slipping.
nuance: She blames a tree for the timetable the man set: the blossom is the sign he named, so its coming before him turns his promise into her sentence. The first line (பாத்து, காத்து) is hard, and if வருந்தே is read as a prohibition the tree tells her instead not to grieve. The addressee is the tree.

thinai_evidence.note: the kurundham in flower and the rain-clouds are mullai things

reading: With the sky roaring like many wide-faced drums and the lightning above like Death with cruel wide eyes, the speaker asks why, for the girl whose long wide eyes stand full of tears and whose soft shoulders are like long bamboo, the chariot has stopped and turned away.
nuance: தடங்கண் comes three times: the drum's broad face, Death's eye in the lightning, and her own eye full of tears, so the storm's eyes are set against hers; பணை is drum in line 1 and bamboo in line 3. The speaker is not stated; the third person for the girl suggests the friend speaking to the man or his charioteer.

thinai_evidence.note: the thunder and lightning of the rains, when the chariot should come

comparisons.tenor: the thunder of the sky
the lightning
her soft shoulders

reading: The friend reproaches the kurundham, the mullai creeper, the konrai and the wild jasmine: by staying here and putting out flowers and buds white as peacock-quill teeth, they have spread a great pallor, like the ridge-gourd flower, over the bamboo shoulders of the girl with budding breasts and decked, falling hair.
nuance: கொன்றாய் is the vocative of konrai and also 'you have killed', so of the four flowers hailed, one is hailed as a killer. இருந்தே, 'staying', sets the plants that stay against the man who went. The addressees are the flowers.

thinai_evidence.note: the four flowers of the rainy forest are addressed

comparisons.tenor: the white buds, like teeth white as peacock quill
her shoulders
the pallor on her shoulders

reading: The heroine tells her flower-garlanded friend that now, when the angry cobra shrinks into its anthill as the rain's thunder rages, the rutting elephant trumpets back at it, and the naagam in the thicket bears its gold beside silver, her soft shoulders have turned pale.
nuance: நாகம் is cobra, elephant and the naagam tree in three successive half-lines: the creatures answer the thunder by hiding or by roaring back, while she can only pale. The gold and silver of line 3 (flowers, or the colours of the tree) are unclear.

thinai_evidence.note: the thunder of the rains marks mullai's season

reading: The heroine answers her friend: the rains have appeared, the glory-lily buds have opened like the soft finger of a woman, pale herself, trimming a lamp, water has come and the forest has kept its season, so how can she say today that it is not the season.
nuance: The friend's consolation, that this rain is not the season he named, is quoted only to be refused. The pallor (பீர்) is put on the lamp-trimmer's finger inside the simile, so the heroine's own paling slips into the flower.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains have come to the forest

comparisons.tenor: the glory-lily buds opening in the rain

reading: The heroine says the townsfolk talk and she cannot settle whether what they say is fitting; is it fitting, she asks, that the cool white kodal has passed through all its shapes, a ladle, a snake's hood, a finger, a broken bangle, a white parasol, and has withered.
nuance: The flower's life is a calendar: from bud to wilting, the whole season the man named has passed while she watched. The first line (உகவும்கள் அன்று) is obscure, so what the townsfolk say is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the white glory lily of the rains runs through its season

comparisons.tenor: the kodal's closed bud
the bud lifting like a hood

reading: The heroine asks whether those who say she has lost her dignity cannot see that the hot sun has turned every branch of the lush konrai to gold, and that before the sun sets on the hill the bees and honey-bees hum the thuttham note without pause.
nuance: பீடிலார் may be aimed at her (she has lost her composure) or at the man (he has broken his word); on either reading the bloom and the evening hum are her defence, the season's evidence that excuses grief.

thinai_evidence.note: the konrai in bloom and the hour before sunset

comparisons.tenor: the konrai branches yellowed with flowers

reading: The heroine says she is one woman, and not one but many foes have taken her for their living, each apart: the anril on the palmyra frond, the evening, the falling rain, the ambal flute, the sea, and, beyond the sea, the dark cloud that rides in blackening.
nuance: The list of foes runs across landscapes, the anril and the sea from the shore, the evening, the flute and the cloud from the pasture, so the separation draws enemies from every land. ஆம்பல் may be the evening flute tune or the water lily, and பொருத்தில் is unclear.

thinai_evidence.note: evening and the dark rain-cloud are mullai's hour and season

reading: The heroine says that as the forest flourishes and the herders' flutes sound, while lightning plays over the gems the boar has dug up as though the sky were laughing, her shameless life seems to break and slip away.
nuance: She calls her own life நாண் இல், shameless, because it clings on after the season he named has come; the boar turning up gems is a hill image set in the pasture forest.

thinai_evidence.note: the herders' flute in the flourishing forest

comparisons.tenor: the lightning flashing across the sky

reading: The heroine tells her friend that what is done in this life seems to bear its fruit in this life, and those who say it comes in the next do not understand: see how the women with moist hair, who tormented the two of them thinking them weak, have now plainly been burned.
nuance: Filed under mullai, the poem has no rain, flower or evening; its matter is the rival women. If 'burned' means their own lovers are now away and the rains scorch them as they scorched her, it stays mullai waiting. Either way a doctrine of deeds and their fruit is turned into a wife's satisfaction.

thinai_evidence.note: the rival women who scorned the wife are marutham's quarrel, not mullai's waiting

title: மருதம் 124-139 (1/2)
theme: The first half of the marutham section: the wife refusing the bard who comes as the straying man's go-between (124 to 127, 131 to 133, 136), mocking his lute, his modes and his lies; the man's field town, its paddy and lotus likened to a dancing or bathing woman's jewels, as the place she will not enter (128, 129); her doubt at his return (134) and wonder at his servitude to another woman (135); and the field town described as the father's town of a little boy with a toy chariot (124, 125, 137 to 139).
source_issues: 124-139: the colophon gives only the thinai (மருதம்) and no thurai; every thurai_akam speech situation is inferred from the poem, with occasion words null.
127 line 3: the bracket in என்(று(அணுகான் is misprinted (read என்று அணுகான்), and குலம்காரம் is obscure; the verse is marked uncertain.
130 line 1: என்செய் திரம்நின் றவரை is split oddly and hard to construe; the reading is a guess.
132 lines 3-4: the sense of இறவாது and பின்னாரில் அந்தி முடிவு is unclear.
135: the printed number 35 is a misprint for 135 (flag), and the site lacks this verse; lines 3-4 are hard to construe.
136 line 1: the site's text lacks this line; பண்மகனே may be a misprint for பாண்மகனே; lines 3-4 are obscure.
138 line 1: the site's text lacks this line; வன்றுள்ளி is read as வன் துள்ளி, 'spurting hard'.
139 line 3: தாராத்தோ(று) ஆய்ந்தெடுப்பும் is obscure; the reading takes it as herons picking along the field.

reading: The wife tells the bard of the sevvazhi lute that, before his little son could even appear drawing his fine toy chariot along this way by hand, the lord of the town of fine fields had bathed in this stream, embraced the shoulders of her 'younger sisters', and grown keener for them after.
nuance: The son with his toy chariot is used as a clock: the man went to the other women 'before the boy appears', so the claim the child should make on him came too late. எங்கையர், 'my younger sisters', is the wife's barbed name for the other women.

reading: The wife tells the bard, whose lute is curved like a bent prawn and who has no good nature, that he need not fashion words to open a reconciliation: she was roused for good on the day she heard the lies of the lord of the flowered pond, where bent prawns look like strung bows.
nuance: The two similes are chained: the bard's lute is like the prawn, and the prawn of the man's pond is like a strung bow, so the instrument that comes to make peace is lined up with a weapon drawn. The bard's lute and the man's lie (பொய், inside பொய்கை) meet in one line.
