title: மருதம் 140-payiram (2/2)
theme: Marutham, the close of the book (140-153) and its preface: the husband's straying and the wife's sulk, told through the field buffalo raiding the pond, the bard turned away, the son carried home as a passport, and the eyes that never see him in any phase of the quarrel.
source_issues: The colophons give no thurai for any verse of this chapter, so thurai_akam speakers and addressees are inferred from the verses, with occasion words null.
Verse 140 line 4 'மயல் ஊ ரரவர்' is broken in spacing and probably corrupt (perhaps மயலூரவர்); who 'strings' and what is unclear.
Verse 141 line 4 'யாட்டை இருந்துறையும்' is obscure.
Verse 142 line 2 'புண்கயத் துள்ளும்' is doubtful in sense; a verb of clinging or embracing is expected.
Verse 146 line 3 'மூலையினாள்' looks like a misprint for முலையினாள் (of the breasts).
Verse 149 line 1 'புள்மனுநுன்' is corrupt, and the sense of line 3 'பண்கிடந்து செய்யாத மாத்திரையே' is uncertain.
Verse 150 line 2 has unbalanced editorial brackets ('மற்(று(இன்(று)'), and line 3 'கல் பெயர் சேராள்' is obscure.
Verse 153 line 1 'நோக்கு(எ)ன்' carries an editor's inserted letter; the reading takes it as நோக்கு என்.

reading: The bee that will not drink even in the lotus flower, holding that the honey laid up inside the earth-rooted banana cluster is its own, has its likeness in the lord of the eye-filling field town, and the daughter of that bewitched town, knowing his nature, strings her garland to suit it.
nuance: A hidden comparison is near: the bee that scorns the lotus for honey it calls its own is like the lord who leaves the wife for another house. It is left untagged because the pairs cannot be fixed on this text: who 'strings' (தொடுப்பாள்) and what, and who the 'daughter of the bewitched town' is, turn on a broken last line. தேன் is read as the bee, as often in this book.

thinai_evidence.note: banana, lotus and the field town of the marutham lord

reading: When he said he had sported in the water with fair women of lovely voice, the lady with a voice like a bell sulked; such is the town of fields fed by running water where the blue kingfisher sits and wearies by the path.
nuance: He reports the sulk with his own boast in it (ஆடினேன், 'I sported'), so the offence and the account of it come from one mouth. The two voices are matched, அணிக்குரல் for the other women and மணிக்குரல் for the wife.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's sulk over his water-play with other women

comparisons.tenor: the wife's voice, clear as a bell

reading: The friend tells the lord of the field town, where in the cool pond the stooping hen keeps to her tall cock among the lotus, that his chest is like a rich pool, and that the wife, with a single craving like a pregnant woman's for sour things, wants it as the only cure for the longing that will not leave her.
nuance: The hen keeping to her mate could be read as iraicchi (as she clings, so the wife wants only him), and the deletion test would pass; it is left as scene because the verb of line 2 (புண்கயத்துள்ளும்) is doubtful, so the act cannot be fixed. The pond of line 1 returns in line 2 as the simile for his chest (வண்கயம்), so the scene and the comparison share one word.

thinai_evidence.note: the lotus pond of the field town

comparisons.tenor: his chest, cool and refreshing as a rich pool
her single longing for him, as fixed as a pregnant woman's craving for sour food
his chest as the medicine for her love-sickness

reading: No sooner had she embraced the sandal-smeared chest of the lord of the good field town, before she had even turned on her side, than the cock that lives at the foot of the poor folk's huts woke the sleepers and the dawn tune began to hum.
nuance: The night is measured in a single gesture: புடைபெயரா மாத்திரைக்கண், 'in the time it takes not even to turn aside'. That the cock lives among the huts of the poor (புல்லியார் கூட்டு) sets the lovers' brief night against the town's working day that the bird begins.

thinai_evidence.note: the field town at cock-crow, marutham's dawn

reading: The courtesan, wrapped in red cloth, smeared with paste that yellows her jewels and wearing red water-lilies with care, sends him off towards his house in style, coaching him: 'even if she looks at you and speaks, do not answer'.
nuance: Read with பரத்தை as the subject of all three participles and of விடும், the verse turns the wife's complaint into a report of the rival's stage-management: she dresses him off, even scripts his silence. Read otherwise (the warning as the wife's), the sense changes, so the verse is marked uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the courtesan sends the husband home to face his wife

reading: With the noise of songs, of tunes and of the unbending horns all crowding together, rising like a hooded serpent that rears at a charm, he came carrying his son to our place like Indra.
nuance: கோட்டரவம் is used twice with two senses: in line 2 the sound of horns (கோடு, horn), in line 3 the serpent with a curved hood. Indra is marutham's god (porul 1.5), so the simile places the husband's return in his own landscape. The pomp may be mocking: he needs a procession and a child to get through the door.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband comes back bringing his son, under marutham's god

comparisons.tenor: the husband arriving with his son amid music
his proud bearing as he enters

reading: Though the great of this earth-bound world went on slighting her for days past counting, she of the pearl-strung breasts, letting go the reserve that is a woman's nature, made herself wholly gentle.
nuance: The verse repeats கிடந்த three times (மண்கிடந்த, எண்கிடந்த, பெண்கிடந்த): the earth that lies there, the days that lie uncounted, the nature that lies in a woman, and only the last is undone.

thinai_evidence.note: no native thing; the colophon's marutham and the sulk given up decide it

reading: The red-eyed, black-horned buffalo, with a little lowing, plunges into the field pond of the lovely fields and comes back crowned with blue lilies and red kayal fish, carrying frogs on its back as well.
nuance: This is the classic marutham ullurai vehicle (the buffalo that raids the pond and comes home wearing its flowers, as the husband comes home with other women's marks), but nothing in the verse or its colophon states the situation, so condition 4 fails and the buffalo is scene. The frog riding home on its back is a comic touch no Sangam buffalo has.

thinai_evidence.note: the field buffalo in the lily pond

comparisons.tenor: the buffalo decked with the pond's spoils like a reveller with a garland

reading: The dark-horned buffalo, like darkness walking, having grazed the great field pond where all is confusion, with horns that could shift stones, lows remembering its calf and comes home wearing a cover of paddy straw.
nuance: Unlike verse 147, this buffalo's raid ends with a return, and the cause given is the calf (தன் கன்றுள்ளி). Read as iraicchi it would say the husband should come home for his son, but the verse has no other sense to survive the deletion test, so the buffalo is the subject, not a carrier.

thinai_evidence.note: the buffalo, the field pond and the paddy stack

comparisons.tenor: the black buffalo, dark as walking night

reading: Even if you leave her and live apart, a woman's nature is something else: see how she of eyes like red kayal fish, not wasting away, only feels shame, before even a tune has been played.
nuance: Line 2 repeats the phrase of verse 146, பெண்கிடந்த தன்மை, and here the woman's nature holds where there it gave way: shame (நாணும்) instead of pining (நையாது).

thinai_evidence.note: only the colophon's marutham places it; the line naming the land is corrupt

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, long and red-edged like the kayal fish

tamil: கடல் வட்டத்(து) இல்லையால் கல் பெயர் சேராள்
reading: O bard of the lute of mingled strings, what of it when one looks closely? Reckoned up, there is none today in the sea-ringed world equal to her; if there were any in the circle of the mighty, so be it.
nuance: Turning the bard away by praising the wife's worth rather than blaming the husband leaves the bard nothing to argue with. Line 3's கல் பெயர் சேராள் is obscure in our text.

thinai_evidence.note: the bard as go-between belongs to the marutham quarrel; no native thing of the land

reading: The wife tells the bard of the great-stemmed lute that her son, with anklet bells on his mud-splashed feet and a red-gold plate on his brow, plays in the dust before this house and will not play as other women's do; today his father may go and play with 'our younger sisters'.
nuance: எங்கையர், 'our younger sisters', is the wife's ironic courtesy for her rivals. The verb ஆடு runs through the verse in three senses: the son plays in mud and dust, the other women 'play', and the husband may go and sport.

thinai_evidence.note: the bard and the courtesans of the marutham quarrel; the mud is the only sign of the land

reading: The wife tells her husband not to embrace her: the marks printed on his chest by another woman's breasts, jewels and leaf-paintings would be wiped away by their son's wet mouth, and her breast milk would spoil his garland.
nuance: The refusal is phrased as care for his finery: what the son's mouth and her milk would 'spoil' is the evidence of the other woman (இட்ட குறி), so her concern is the accusation. உலையாது, 'without fail', makes the spoiling certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife refuses the embrace of a husband marked by another woman

reading: Neither in the look of sulk, quarrel and pique she kept up, nor in the love of the ripe union that followed, has she seen him; and if he goes off angry her eyes tremble without shame: her eyes never once see the lord of the dense field town.
nuance: The three grades of the quarrel are named in a row (துனி, புலவி, ஊடல்) and then union is called 'ripe' (கனி), the vocabulary the Kural uses in its chapter on புலவி. The paradox is that every stage of the cycle hides him from her eyes.

thinai_evidence.note: the cycle of sulk and union with the lord of the field town

reading: The prefatory verse says that the poet, ripe in the doctrine of secret love, bound the Thinaimalai, a garland of paired landscapes, in matchless sweet Tamil, so that the displeasure of the critical might cease and the book come easily to the hand of those who study it.
nuance: கணிந்தார் in line 2 seems to play on the poet's name, Kanimethaviyar, and the book is offered as a garland (மாலை) twice over: இணைமாலை and திணைமாலை.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the poet and his book, the nearest puram class to a eulogy

title: குறிஞ்சி 1-10
theme: Kurinji in the time of the secret love: the friend forbids the night path and the field, naming the elephants, the armed kin and the town's gossip (1, 5-8), while the heroine, pale and with loosening bangles, waits for the hill lord to come, until the harvest ends and her mother keeps her from the field (2-4, 9, 10).
source_issues: 1-10: the core records carry no colophon thurai, so thurai_akam speaker, addressee and stage are inferred from the poems and occasion.words is null throughout.

1 line 4: கரம் is obscure at the close; it may be the elephant's trunk or a word for hidden places, and the sense of the line (the night way holds elephants) does not turn on it. Line 2 புலவோர் is read as the celestials who receive the smoke.
2 line 3: வரிஅரிதாங் is unclear; வரவு அரிது ஆம் ('will coming be hard?') fits the sense and the closing of the field-watch.
7 line 4: flagged as differing from the site, and ௌ repaired from the split encoding; ஊரறி கௌவை reads well as it stands.
9 line 2: தோழ is a masculine vocative in a heroine's speech to her friend; தோழி is probably meant.

reading: The friend tells the lord of the sky-high hill, where sandal burnt with a grass fire sends up its smoke as an offering and dust rains down, that he must not come by night, since the dark ways hold elephants.
nuance: The opening may make the hill a place of worship: புலவோர் 'who are given smoke' reads most easily as the celestials receiving burnt sandal, so the hill he comes from is sacred and fragrant, and the warning that closes the poem turns that grandeur into danger. The last word கரம் is hard; 'hidden ways' or 'trunks' are both possible.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill and the night visit forbidden fix kurinji and its midnight tryst

reading: The friend asks the lord of the mighty hill, where the kaanthal's clustered buds bloom like hands and the female monkey, taking them for fragrant buds, plays with them, whether his coming will now be hard, since the guarding of the millet fields has ended.
nuance: The end of the field-watch is the end of the girl's licensed days outdoors, so the question about his coming is a push toward marriage. The monkey's delight in the hand-like buds is an image of the hill's ease set against the closing of their meetings; its exact sense (மணமுகை, fragrant bud or wedding bud) is open.

thinai_evidence.note: the kaanthal, the hill monkey and the millet field are kurinji things

comparisons.tenor: the clustered buds of the kaanthal, shaped like hands

reading: The heroine says that the bangles that slipped here are not as they were on the day she joined the lord of the flowered hill, where on the high steep slope the kaanthal blooms and thunder, taking it for a snake, rushes and strikes and roars.
nuance: Thunder that kills snakes is a stock hill image; here it falls on a flower that only looks like a snake's hood, so the violence lands on something harmless. Set beside the loosened bangles it reads as the hurt that has come to her though she did no wrong, but there is no act of a person in it and it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the kaanthal on the hill slope and the hill lord

comparisons.tenor: the kaanthal blossom, which the thunder takes for a snake's hood

reading: The heroine asks her friend whether the lord of the sky-high hill will come, so that the pallor of her body may leave, in his hill where the hunters' children pick up the wet gems lying in the millet field and warm their hands at them by night as if at embers.
nuance: Gems so common that children use them as a fire make the hill rich beyond need, which sharpens the one thing she lacks: his coming, the only cure she names for her pallor.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field and the hill hunters' children

comparisons.tenor: the glowing gems, at which the children warm their hands as at embers

reading: The friend tells the man not to come among the hills, for those who guard the ripening fields on the fragrant slope are her kin, harsh of word, with bows, spears and swift arrows, living among the rocks.
nuance: The threat is built as a list of weapons, and the last word, எமர் 'our people', is held back to the end, so the danger is named as kinship: the men he would face are the girl's own family, whose consent marriage would need.

thinai_evidence.note: the field-guards and bowmen of the rocky hill are kurinji people

reading: The friend tells the man that they are daughters of the hill folk who live in the forest of the long gem-bright hill where elephants roam, and asks why he comes into the millet field, since their kin would rage even to see him.
nuance: The friend's 'we' names the two girls by their tribe, so the refusal speaks in the voice of the family; it is the same self-naming the friend uses in verse 8 to turn aside his pretext.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill folk's daughters in the millet field of the elephant hill

reading: The friend tells the lord of the good land of the mighty hill, whose falling cascades sound as lute, flute and drum together, that the girl with a young deer's glance cannot bear his absence, but that if he comes by night it will bring gossip the whole town knows.
nuance: The waterfall as an orchestra makes the hill a stage, and the warning follows from it: what happens on a stage is heard, and the night visit will become the town's talk. The girl's distress is set against the danger, which leaves marriage as the only way out.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill cascade and the night visit

comparisons.tenor: the sound of the falling cascade, like lute, flute and drum in concert
the girl, whose glance is a young deer's

reading: The friend answers the man who asks after a wounded elephant: we are girls of the hill folk with soft shoulders like bending bamboo, on this cool slope fragrant with blooming vengai, and no tusker came this way, sir, flagging and streaming blood.
nuance: His question is the hunter's pretext for speaking to the girls, and the friend answers it literally, which is a way of showing she sees through it; she also names who they are, the hill folk's daughters, as in verse 6.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai slope, the hill girls and the hunted tusker

comparisons.tenor: the girls' soft shoulders, like bending bamboo

reading: The heroine asks her friend whether the lord of the gem hill will come, so that her sickly colour leaves and her broad bamboo shoulders fill out again, in this lovely evening when the vengai, the tree that tells the season, is in full flower and bees hum.
nuance: கணி, 'the reckoner', is a name of the vengai, whose flowering marks the season of the millet harvest and of weddings; so the evening she describes is a sign that the time for his coming to marry her is here.

thinai_evidence.note: the flowering vengai and the hill lord

reading: The heroine asks her friend whether the lord of the rock-ringed hill, where the green-eyed male monkey that has got a jackfruit calls its mate with 'ela!', will be vexed, now that mother, learning of their union, has forbidden her to go to the millet field.
nuance: The confinement (இற்செறிப்பு) ends the field meetings; the question whether he will be vexed is put so that he, or the friend for him, will see that only marriage can bring them together again.

thinai_evidence.note: the jackfruit, the hill monkey and the millet field

iraicchi.act: the male monkey that has got a jackfruit calls its mate to share it
iraicchi.sense: the hill lord, who has the means, should likewise call her to him openly, now that the field where they met is closed to her

title: பாலை 11-20
theme: The paalai decade of Kannan Senthanar: the man leaves for wealth across a waste of fire, stone, bowmen and vultures (11, 12, 15, 17, 18, 19), the woman watches her bangles and colour fail while the season he swore by comes (13, 14), and the lovers elope, the man praising the road and the mother fearing it (16, 20).
source_issues: 11 line 1: repaired from ெ + ள to ௌ (கௌவையோ); the sangamtamil.com text lacks line 1.
11 line 3: அழிநீர் வாகி reads as அழிநீர ஆகி (compare 12 line 1, முரிபரல வாகி); the line's sense (water perished, heat rising) is uncertain, and the verse is marked uncertain.
17 line 3: எல்வனை is very likely a misprint for எல்வளை, bright bangle (compare Akananuru 185 line 1, எல்வளை ஞெகிழ).
18 line 3: எதிர்வன போல்இலவே is hard to construe; it is taken as 'they do not look like bangles that will meet his return', and the verse is marked uncertain.
13 line 4: whether the koel proves his words false or is itself false (calling before the season) cannot be fixed; the verse is marked uncertain.

reading: Gossip aside, the speaker tells the woman with eyes like washed blue lilies that her lover, whose nature is set on wealth, broke his word and left for a wasteland where the waters have perished, the heat rises shimmering, and the water along the way is cut off.
nuance: பொய்த்தனர் and நீத்தார் stand side by side: the lie and the leaving are one act. The water named three times (அழிநீர, வழிநீர் and the lily of கழுநீர்) sets her watered eyes against the land that has lost its water.

thinai_evidence.note: the waterless wasteland he crossed for wealth

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): a woman is addressed by her eyes, most likely by the friend; the heroine speaking to the friend is possible

comparisons.tenor: the woman's eyes

reading: To the man setting out for the wealth he hopes to gain across a forest where fire has spread and the land, strewn with broken pebbles, has lost its nature, the speaker says that when it comes to weighing it, no one can know better than he the helplessness of the woman whose kohl-dark eyes are streaked with red.
nuance: The closing question flatters and accuses at once: he, her intimate, knows her grief best, so if he goes he goes knowing. The ruined land (முரண் அழிந்து, its strength or nature destroyed) foreshadows what his going will do to her.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is about to leave for wealth through the burnt forest

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred: the friend speaks to the departing man of the heroine's ஆற்றாமை, to hold him back

reading: The tall kurunthu has budded, beside it the maraa has bloomed, and glory lilies have come out among them; now, O you with golden bangles, the koel has turned into a lie every word he swore when he joined us and went.
nuance: The season of the flowers is the season he named, so the koel's call is the proof that his oath failed; the poem blames the bird for making the words false, a displacement that spares the man's name. Read the other way, the koel's call is itself false, a season come too soon, and the line consoles; the verse is marked uncertain for that reason.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits at home past the season he swore to return by, which is the situation of irutthal

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred: the woman whose man has not come in the promised season speaks to her gold-bangled friend

reading: Even after seeing the season when the red-eyed koel calls through every cool flowering grove where the punnai opens its puffed-rice blossoms, he left her, driven by his heart's craving for wealth; yet her heart keeps watching for his coming.
nuance: Two cravings are set in the same word: his நசை for wealth that drove him off and her heart's நசை for his return. கண்டும், 'even seeing', makes his leaving a choice made against the season of love.

thinai_evidence.note: he left for wealth in spring, and she bears the parting

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred: the woman speaks of her own heart; the friend is the likely hearer

comparisons.tenor: the punnai's white blossoms

reading: The woman asks her friend whether the man, who gave up grace for the craving of hard-won wealth while her body, lovely as tender leaves, grows pale, is now halting somewhere on the long wasteland of hard paths, where the little hawk rages at the small dull dove.
nuance: Reproach and worry share one sentence: he abandoned grace (அருள் ஒழிந்து), yet she wonders where he lodges tonight. The hawk at the dove is the road's violence; it could be read as his harshness to the meek, but no act of a lover is in it and the deletion of line 1 takes nothing she says, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: he is away on the long waste for wealth while she pales

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the vocative தோழி

comparisons.tenor: the beauty of her body before the pallor

reading: The man tells the shy girl with sweet speech and newly budded sharp teeth that the place they are going to is one to be wished for, now that the dark-trunked maraa blooms together with the nuna and swarms of broad-winged bees hum the paalai melody.
nuance: The bees hum பாலை, the music named for the very land the lovers must cross, so the man turns the dreaded landscape into a song to lead her on. The verse never names the road's hardship; its comfort is all in what it leaves out.

thinai_evidence.note: the lovers set out together, leaving her home

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: inferred: the man reassures the girl as they set out together (உடன்போக்கு)

comparisons.tenor: her small new teeth, like buds

reading: The woman wonders whether our man, who left without grace for love of wealth while her soft shoulders with their bright bangles grew slack, will pass even through the hamlets of those who live by ploughing with the bow, where at the mouth of the stony track the black thudi drum sounds and toddy flows.
nuance: வில்லுழுது வாழ்நர், 'those who live by ploughing with the bow', is the bandit's livelihood named as a farmer's, which makes the threat sound settled and ordinary. நமர், 'our man', keeps him hers even in the sentence that calls him graceless.

thinai_evidence.note: the stony track and the bow-living hamlets of the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred: the woman speaks of 'our man' (நமர்), so to her friend

reading: For the man going to the wide forest where tangled bamboo, its nodes split by the scorching sun, sheds pearls, the speaker's bangles do not look like ones that will meet his return; every one of them seems ready to fall, for nothing.
nuance: The bamboo sheds its pearls in the heat as her bangles are about to fall from her thinning arms: the land drops its treasure on the road he takes for wealth while she loses her ornaments uselessly (கொன்னே). Line 3 is hard to construe, so the verse is marked uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the sun-scorched wide forest he travels

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred: the woman speaks of her own bangles

comparisons.tenor: her bangles ready to fall

reading: The woman asks her friend whether he, afraid of the stony desert track where the doe cries out with the stag, will halt somewhere in the long wasteland; alas, the gold colour that wilts down over her breasts, and her shoulders, slip away together with her bangles.
nuance: Three things droop together, the pallor with the breasts and the shoulders with the bangles, matching the pair of deer that suffer together on his road: in the waste even the beasts keep each other company, while he and she wilt apart.

thinai_evidence.note: the stony desert road he is on

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the vocative தோழி

comparisons.tenor: the pallor spreading over her breasts

iraicchi.act: the doe and the stag cry out together in the parched track, sharing its hardship instead of parting
iraicchi.sense: even the deer of the waste keep together in distress, while he faces the road alone and she wilts alone at home

reading: The mother asks a passing man whether her daughter can bear to walk, beside the young man with a strong bow fierce as Death, across the harsh wasteland of the Eyinar with their strung bows, where flocks of vultures gather and she will shrink in fear from the shadows they cast.
nuance: The youth she went with is himself likened to Death (கூற்றின), so the mother finds no safety even in the girl's protector; the question is whether the girl can bear it (ஆற்றுங்கொல்), not whether she will come back.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter has gone off with the youth across the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: inferred: the mother (என்மகள்) asks a man met on the road (ஐய) after her eloped daughter; she may be the foster mother

comparisons.tenor: the young man with the strong bow

title: முல்லை 21-30
theme: The mullai decade of the Thinaimozhi Aimpathu (21-30, Kannan Chenthanar): in the rainy season the friend points the waiting heroine to the season's signs (the kaayaa, kodal and mullai in bloom, the thunder like kings' drums, the cloud drinking the sea, the deer with his doe, the herds dripping milk) as the token the absent man set for his return, and promises that her pallor will go; in 21 he has already come.
source_issues: 21-30: the colophon gives the thinai (முல்லை) but no thurai; the speaker (thozhi) and addressee (thalaivi) are inferred from the verses' vocatives, so occasion words are null.
27 line 1: ஆம்பல் அடைதாய் is hard to construe (the ambal flute tune of the herdsmen, or the water-lily leaf?); line 4 செயவர் is probably சேயவர், the one far away. The verse is marked uncertain.
28 line 4: கணங்கு reads as a misprint for சுணங்கு, the beauty spots (compare 24 line 1, செஞ்சுணங்கின்). The verse is marked uncertain.
30 line 3: வரிவனைத் is a misprint for வரிவளைத், striped bangles; line 1 அருளி and line 2 தெரிஆ are unclear, and the verse is marked uncertain.
26 line 2: சுருங்கொடி may be சுரும்கொடி or a curling creeper; taken as the mullai creeper.

reading: The friend tells the heroine that her lover has come and her shoulders shine: the collyrium-dark kaayaa has bloomed, the kurukilai buds have taken the beauty of the smile of women with bright bangles, and the cool kodal has put out its ladle-shaped spathes.
nuance: Unlike the verses around it, this one reports the arrival as done (வந்தார், past), so the season's flowers are no longer a promise but the frame of the return; her shining shoulders are the pallor's undoing, said without naming the pallor. The women's smile is set inside the flower, so the woodland already smiles the smile the heroine will now smile.

thinai_evidence.note: the kaayaa and kodal in flower are the rain-season blossoms of the woodland

comparisons.tenor: the kaayaa blossom, dark as collyrium
the white kurukilai buds, given the beauty of women's smiles
the kodal spathe, shaped like a ladle

reading: The friend asks the heroine of the fine brow what will become now of the pallor that crept over her soft breasts, for here, she says, our man will come: this rain-cloud has made the season, with mullai of many colours in bud, and taken on its sweet colour.
nuance: The pallor is spoken of as a creeping thing (ஊர்ந்த) whose fate is now in question, so the friend's 'what will become of it' is a playful threat against the pallor rather than a question to the girl. The cloud is said to 'make' the season (பருவஞ்செய்து), as if keeping the man's appointment for him.

thinai_evidence.note: mullai in bud and the rain-cloud making the season

comparisons.tenor: the pallor as a thing that crawls over her breasts

reading: The friend tells the heroine of close-set bangles that he who went will come: here is the rain, thundering and roaring like the drums of fiercely angry kings, having drunk the flood of the cool sea and come to its height, and tomorrow it will be greater than today.
nuance: 'Tomorrow more than today' turns the friend's proof into a rising scale: each day's heavier rain is a nearer return. The kings' drum keeps the reason for his absence, the king's war or work, inside the sound that promises his coming.

thinai_evidence.note: the thundering rain-cloud that has drunk the sea

comparisons.tenor: the thunder of the rain-cloud
the cloud as a drinker of the sea

reading: The friend tells the heroine, whose soft breasts bear red beauty spots, to let the pallor that has settled on her go: here is the woodland where the rain-sky, swelling with fierce anger, thundering and roaring, has poured its cool rain as the sign of the return of him who swore his oath and held to his resolve.
nuance: Two kinds of சினம் face each other: his வஞ்சினம், the sworn vow he made when he left, and the sky's வெஞ்சினம், fierce anger, so the storm reads as the vow made audible. The sign (குறி) is his, not the sky's: the rain is the token he named.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-sky pouring on the woodland

comparisons.tenor: the rain-sky, swelling with anger as it thunders

reading: As the massed dark rain-clouds, mingling with the wind, rise up, and the tender young buck leaps with his doe, the friend tells the heroine of lovely breasts that our lover will come right now, at the time he resolved on.
nuance: Strike line 2 and the friend's word stands: the rains have come and he will come now, at the time he set. The buck with his doe is the one thing in the verse that acts as a lover should, which is why it can comfort.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-clouds and the deer at play with his doe in the woodland

iraicchi.act: the young buck leaps and plays together with his doe in the first rains
iraicchi.sense: the creatures keep their mates beside them in this season, so the man who fixed this time will be beside her now

reading: The friend says this is the time he told us of, fittingly, when he made the sign of his return: the beautiful cloud that drank the dark sea has thundered so that the curling mullai creeper grows lovely, and the great rain hangs low.
nuance: பொருந்த, 'fittingly', says the season and his word now match: the friend's proof is the agreement of the two, not the rain alone. The poem names the moment of his speaking (நமக்குரைத்த போழ்து), so the friend counts herself among those he promised.

reading: The friend points to the bewildering evening, when the herdsmen move their herds home, the cloud, having scooped water from the deep sea, thunders to spread far, and the vast dark world fills with darkness, as the sign that he who went on his work set for his return.
nuance: The mullai evening, which elsewhere torments the waiting woman, is here turned by the friend into his appointed token. The verse gives no vocative, so who speaks is inferred from the run of the decade.

thinai_evidence.note: herdsmen driving the herds home in the rainy evening

reading: The friend says that, as the cloud with its thunder of shaking voice drinks the wave-tossed sea and roars so that the serpent with its ripe gem cowers, and in the evening that hides the sun the heavy rain hangs low, the beauty spots will spread over her breasts.
nuance: The spots (சுணங்கு) on a woman's breasts are a sign of happiness and union, the opposite of the pallor of the other verses; the friend predicts the body's change from waiting to joy. The gem-bearing serpent that shrinks at thunder is a stock belief of the rains.

thinai_evidence.note: the thunder and heavy rain of the evening

comparisons.tenor: the cloud as a drinker of the sea

reading: The friend calls the heroine of fine jewels to come out and see the woodland with her: the rain has made the whole forest its own, the sharp buds of the lovely kodal look like snakes ready to strike, the mullai has put out buds, and fine sand flows down every stream.
nuance: The proof is no longer reported but shared: 'come, let us see' (போதராய் காண்பாம்) invites the heroine out of the house into the season itself. The same words could be the returned man's to his wife; the run of the decade favours the friend.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest taken over by the rains and the mullai in bud

comparisons.tenor: the sharp kodal buds, like snakes raising their hoods to strike

reading: The friend tells the heroine of the striped-bangled arm that this rain has bloomed in full, the cloud thundering in grace, the kurukilai flowering and the chosen herds of cows oozing sweet milk; will our man not come?
nuance: 'Will our man come?' (வருவார் நமர்கொல்) is a question whose answer the whole season has given; the cows streaming milk for their calves are the plainest picture of a return home, though the verse draws no match, so they stay scene.

thinai_evidence.note: cows dripping milk and the woodland in flower in the rains

comparisons.tenor: the rain-season spoken of as a flower in full bloom

title: மருதம் 31-40
theme: Marutham: the wife and her friend answer the straying husband of the field town and refuse his bard (31-39), measuring what his love gave and took through the lily, the bee and the crushed cane; the last verse names a girl of the town by her family's flowers (40).
source_issues: 31-40: no colophon thurai; every speech situation is inferred from the verse.
31 line 4: தோட்டு does not construe cleanly (ear-ring, company, or a corruption); the verse is marked uncertain.
35 line 1: எதிர்மலரேல் தூதும் reads as a corruption of எதிர்மலர்மேல் ஊதும், 'hums over the fresh flower'.
36 line 1: மரைலருஞ் is probably மரைமலரும் (செந்தாமரை மலரும்); line 2 நொந்தான் reads as நொந்தால், 'if she is hurt'.
37 line 2: வயவல லூரன் is probably வயல் ஊரன்.
38 line 3: எல்லு is unclear.
39 line 1: ஆங்கண கழுமிய may be ஆங்கண் கழுமிய; line 2 பெடைகதூஉம் leaves unclear whether the female fish or the male is the biter.

reading: The lord of the town of loud waters, where the bent-horned buffalo wallowing in the field-pond hears the drum beaten against the field workers and runs off with its strength gone, still holds, the speaker says, his rightful bond (கிழமை) with her.
nuance: The buffalo that bolts at the field drum invites a reading of the man startled out of his pleasures, but the poem gives only that one match and never states the situation it would point to, so it stays scene; the last word, தோட்டு, does not construe cleanly, and whether the claim of கிழமை is a concession or a bitter irony turns on it.

reading: The lord of the town of spreading fields of thick-stalked red paddy in ear, where the tall marutham tree with its arrow-straight trunk sheds fragrant pollen on the petals of the blue lily, has fastened a sickness on us too.
nuance: எமக்கும், 'on us too', is the barb: the sickness he gives is not hers alone but shared with the women he goes to. The tree that scatters its pollen on whatever lily lies under it reads easily as the man spending his love freely, but only that one correspondence is clear, so it is a near miss for ullurai (condition 3) and stays scene.

reading: The friend tells the man of the good town of kaanji trees that, like the friendship of the base, he has consumed the young beauty that was his own, and now at the last stands taking in the fresh beauty of the street of bright-breasted women he holds dear as his eyes.
nuance: The simile is from the ethics of friendship, not from the fields: a friend who eats while there is something to eat and leaves when it is gone. உடைய, 'your own', makes the wife's youth his property, which makes spending it and turning away a loss to himself as much as to her.

reading: The woman says the lord of the town of fields where red paddy ripens would not, for some days, give his love to any but her; so get up, bard: you have gone into the street of the broad-hipped, bamboo-shouldered women and stand there for your own gain.
nuance: The bard is shown not as the husband's go-between to the wife but as one who frequents the other women's street for what it brings him (வாரி). Who speaks is not certain: the other woman could say 'he gives himself to none but me', and the sense of வாரிக்கு is not secure.

reading: The man of the good town of cool fields is like the bent bee that hums over freshly opened flowers in the hot season: he enjoys the young beauty of well-jewelled women and leaves them with nothing but their bodies.
nuance: மேனி ஒழிய, 'only the body left', is the point of the simile: the bee takes the honey and the flower stands, emptied. The verse speaks of the women in general (நல்லார்), so the wife counts herself among many.

reading: The woman tells the bard not to come again and again pressing his words: even on the days the lord of the town of paddy fields was joined with us, we of the soft shoulders and bright bangles never had the gracious regard of his eyes that 'our younger sisters' have.
nuance: எங்கையர், 'our younger sisters', is the polite family word turned to irony for the women he goes to; நாட்டம், his eyes' regard, is what she says she never had, which makes the bard's assurances of his love pointless.

nuance: She sets a sign against the bard's speech: the disordered hair answers his praise without argument. Whose hair it is, the other woman's or her own, the Tamil leaves open, and எல்லு is unclear.

reading: The lord of the town where, in the dark pond, the big-backed vaalai fish bites at the full-blown blue lily, no longer as on the days he desired us, has eaten up our beauty, and we have become the chewed refuse of sugarcane.
nuance: The closing image is the bitterest in the decade: not a flower left standing but the cane-pith spat out after the juice is gone. பெடை may make the biter the female fish, which would point the bite at the other woman rather than the man; the ullurai is tagged on the reading that the fish is the man.

title: நெய்தல் 41-50
theme: Neythal: the heroine and her friend on the shore of backwaters and screw-pine, complaining of trysts that proved false and of pallor and slipping bangles, pressing the sea lord to come and marry (41-48, 50); and the man's first-sight doubt whether the girl of the njazhal grove is peacock, woman or sea goddess (49).

source_issues.issue: The text flag says sangamtamil.com lacks this verse; our text cannot be checked against that witness.
குருதினம் (line 2) is probably a misprint for குருகினம், 'flock of herons', the form Akananuru 260.3 has in the same shore scene; read as such.
தணியும்எள் (line 4) is probably a misprint for தணியும்என், 'my (shoulders)'; read as such.
Line 4 ends on the non-finite உரைத்து with no main verb, so the verse reads as incomplete or elliptical.

reading: The heroine tells her friend that the lord of the cool shore, with its neythal gardens and brimming backwaters, is no longer as he was the day she first saw him in the screw-pine-ringed seaside grove; the trysts he set have proved false, and she asks whether the bond of the noble is really so frail.
nuance: ஐயகொல் ஆன்றார் தொடர்பு turns a maxim into a reproach: she does not say he lied, but asks whether the bond of the worthy (ஆன்றார்) is so slight, which quietly puts him outside that class. The first sight in the grove (கண்டநாள்) is the measure he has fallen from.

thinai_evidence.note: the neythal-flowered shore, the backwater and the seaside grove

reading: The friend asks the lord of the cool sea shore, where the old bent-trunked punnai puts out buds like pearls and the leaping waves heave, to grant his grace to the girl who is like a painted flowering creeper: his chest with its fine green ornaments.
nuance: What the friend asks him to give is his chest (மார்பு), so arul here is not pity but the embrace and the claim it makes; the plea for grace is a plea for him to take her openly.

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai of the shore and the sea-lord

comparisons.tenor: the heroine, slender and bright as a painted flowering creeper
the punnai buds, white and round as pearls

reading: The friend tells the heroine, girl of fine jewels whose sweet speech never parts from good sense, that the trysts set by the lord of the long backwater, where the tide of the shark-tossed sea moves and prawns wheel along their path, never lose their closeness with her.
nuance: நின்னில் செறிவுஅறா செய்த குறி can also mean that the marks of their meetings never leave her body, so that the friend has guessed the secret (an opening of the friend's discovery) rather than reassured her. The striking shark beside the wheeling prawns invites a hidden reading, but it gives only a mood, not two pairs, so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the long sea and its backwater

reading: The friend asks the lord of the ford, where the tide with its young fish moves over the dark backwater and gem-clear water spreads, whether it is fitting for him to stay away from the side of the creeper-like girl whose good nature never fails, without even the grace of thinking of her.
nuance: The verse plays on நீர் three ways: the gem-clear water (மணிநீர்), her unfailing nature (குணநீர்மை) and his lack of the nature of remembering (நினைநீர்மை). Her constancy is set against his forgetting in the same word.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater and the ford

comparisons.tenor: the heroine, slender as a creeper

reading: The friend tells the lord of the ford, where fishermen's daughters with jewelled girdles on hood-shaped hips string into garlands the bright pearls the sea has washed up and heaped, and play, of the sickness that has entered her friend's body.
nuance: The playing girls who make ornaments of what the sea gives freely stand against the friend's girl, who is ill; the contrast is left unstated. The last line has no finite verb (உரைத்து), so the friend's message is cut off at 'telling of her sickness'.

thinai_evidence.note: the fisherfolk and the pearls the sea casts up

comparisons.tenor: the girls' hips, broad as a snake's jewelled hood

reading: The friend tells the lord of the curving backwater, where flocks of herons cry on the wide shore of the fragrant seaside grove, that he must come to join her for good, so that the sickness he caused, which wastes her beauty, may end.
nuance: மருவி வரல் asks for a coming that stays, not another visit, so the plea is for marriage; and உன்நோய், 'your sickness', lays the girl's illness at his door.

thinai_evidence.note: the seaside grove and the curving backwater

reading: The heroine asks her friend whether the lord of the shore of the surging sea has abandoned her, now that she is not as she was that day in the lovely flowered grove by the backwater: pallor spreads like flowers over her gem-bright body and the bangles slip down her soft shoulders.
nuance: அற்றைநாள் போலான, 'not as on that day', is the same measure as in verse 41, but here it is her own body, not his conduct, that has changed; the question துறந்தான்கொல் she cannot answer reads itself on her skin.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater grove and the sea-lord

reading: As the tall chariot with ringing bells cuts its way, crabs scatter over the gleaming sand and the fierce sun that parches hurries away, the evening, deepening in colour, comes on.
nuance: The speaker is not named, and the chariot can be the man's coming at dusk (a hope) or the sun's own car leaving (a dread of evening). கண்வாள் அறுப்ப is obscure: the wheel's blade-like rim cutting the sand is the likeliest sense.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore sand at sunset, neythal's hour

reading: The man, struck at first sight, asks his companions whether she was a peacock, a young woman, or a goddess dwelling in the waves of the great sea, for his heart aches from the eyes that looked at him by the flowering grove of young njazhal where the koel calls.
nuance: This is the first-sight doubt (ஐயம்) of kalavu, and the shore supplies its goddess: not the hill's anangu but one who lives in the waves. The pain is placed in her look (நோக்கிய கண்ணின்), not her beauty.

reading: The heroine asks her friend whether the lord of the shore of creeping waves, his bright chest where Tiru dwells, will come to their front yard, where coral, pearls and crystal, mixed together, are brought as if in praise and heaped up at the edge.
nuance: Who heaps the gems is not said (the waves, or the fisherfolk), and புகழக் கொணர்ந்து makes it an offering. A reader may hear in the treasure piled at her door the bride-wealth she hopes he will bring, but the act is not tied to him, so it is left as scene rather than iraicchi.
